modules.title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
modules.standfirst: Three particles, two numbers, one table. Short questions, quick marks — and the 2023 commentary's most alarming line: "many students seemed to have absolutely no concept of what was meant by period number." Every question here is counting, done in the right order.

From the 2023 mark scheme commentary:

"Several students got period and group number mixed up."

"Many students seemed to have absolutely no concept of what was meant by period number."

And a persistent one-mark leak: the charge on a sodium ion is +1 / 1+ / Na⁺ — writing just "positive" was explicitly ignored (no mark). Sign and size, every time.

subsections.html: An atom is a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus (protons + neutrons) wrapped in shells of almost weightless electrons. Two numbers on the periodic table encode everything the exam asks. Learn to read them, and every question in this module becomes counting.

subsections.heading: Atoms, elements and molecules
subsections.html:
Spec 1.14 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(a)

An atom is the smallest particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms covalently bonded together.

An element contains only one type of atom. A molecule can be of an element or of a compound:

  • Cl₂, O₂, H₂ — molecules of elements (two atoms, but the same kind).
  • HCl, H₂O, CO₂ — molecules of compounds (different elements bonded).
  • O on its own — a single atom, not a molecule.

That is the whole of the 2023 January multiple-choice question: "which is a molecule of an element?" — Cl₂.

subsections.heading: The three particles
subsections.html:
Spec 1.15 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(a)

Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus and carry almost all the mass; electrons orbit in shells and carry the negative charge.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeWhere
Proton1+1nucleus
Neutron10nucleus
Electron1/1836 (almost 0)−1shells around the nucleus

Edexcel's version of the table prints the electron's mass as 1/2000 — either is accepted. Atoms are neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons: +1 and −1 cancel.

subsections.heading: Atomic number and mass number — counting the particles
subsections.html:
Spec 1.16 · 2021 Q1 · 2022 Q2 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q7(a)

Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Everything else is subtraction.

Atomic number is the number of protons — that alone. The 2022 scheme ignored any mention of electrons. Mass number is protons + neutrons, because those are the particles with mass.

Worked example — ¹¹₅B

  1. Protons = the small bottom number (atomic number) = 5.
  2. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 11 − 5 = 6.
  3. Electrons = protons, because the atom is neutral = 5.

For an ion, change only step 3: add one electron for each − charge, remove one for each + charge. I⁻ from iodine-127 (53 protons): 53 p, 127 − 53 = 74 n, 53 + 1 = 54 electrons.

subsections.heading: Isotopes
subsections.html:
Spec 1.16 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q7(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(b)

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

So isotopes have the same atomic number and a different mass number. ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl both have 17 protons; one has 18 neutrons, the other 20.

Isotopes have identical chemical properties. Chemistry is decided by electrons, and both isotopes have 17 electrons arranged 2.8.7. The extra neutrons only change the mass.

✗ "Isotopes have different numbers of protons." — that would make them different elements.
✗ "Isotopes have a different mass." — true, but not the definition; no mark.
✓ "Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons." — two marks, one for each half.

subsections.heading: Relative atomic mass — the weighted average
subsections.html:
Spec 1.16, 1.17 · 2023 Q9a · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q3(c) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q7(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q7(a)

Ar is the mean mass of an element's atoms, weighted by how common each isotope is.

Relative atomic mass from isotopesAr = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) ÷ 100Σ means "add up for every isotope" · isotope mass = the mass number · % abundance = how common that isotope is

Worked example — copper, ⁶³Cu 69.5% and ⁶⁵Cu 30.5%

  1. Multiply each mass by its percentage: 63 × 69.5 = 4378.5 and 65 × 30.5 = 1982.5
  2. Add them: 4378.5 + 1982.5 = 6361
  3. Divide by 100: 6361 ÷ 100 = 63.61
  4. Round as asked: 63.6 to 3 significant figures

Check: the answer must sit between the isotope masses, nearer the more common one. 63.6 is between 63 and 65, near 63. ✓

Three isotopes work the same way. Magnesium (2024 Edexcel): (24 × 79.0 + 25 × 10.0 + 26 × 11.0) ÷ 100 = 2432 ÷ 100 = 24.3. This is why chlorine's Ar is 35.5 even though no chlorine atom weighs 35.5.

subsections.heading: Electronic configurations — the 2.8.8 rule
subsections.html:
Spec 1.19 · 2023 Q1 · 2025 Q6a · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q1(a) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q1(a)

Electrons fill shells from the inside out: 2 in the first shell, then 8, then 8, then the rest.

  1. Find the number of electrons. For an atom this is the atomic number.
  2. Fill the first shell with 2.
  3. Fill the second shell with up to 8, then the third with up to 8.
  4. Put whatever is left in the fourth shell (only potassium and calcium in the first 20).
  5. Check the digits add up to the number of electrons.
  • Sodium, 11 electrons → 2.8.1
  • Silicon, 14 electrons → 2.8.4 (2024 Edexcel)
  • Phosphorus, 15 electrons → 2.8.5 (2025's one-marker, and 2023 Edexcel's)
  • Calcium, 20 electrons → 2.8.8.2

In a shell diagram, draw the electrons as dots or crosses on circles, in pairs where you can, and write the symbol or "nucleus" in the centre.

subsections.heading: Group and period — reading the table
subsections.html:
Spec 1.18, 1.22 · 2022 Q2b · 2023 Q1 · 2024 Q1 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q1 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1

Group = number of outer-shell electrons. Period = number of occupied shells.

The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number. Its layout is the electron structure:

  1. Write the configuration, e.g. 2.8.3.
  2. Group = the last number (outer electrons) → Group 3. The reason mark is "because it has 3 electrons in its outer shell".
  3. Period = how many numbers there are (shells) → Period 3.
  4. Identity = add the numbers to get the atomic number → 13 → aluminium.

Groups run down in columns; periods run across in rows. The exception: Group 0 (also called Group 8), the noble gases, have full outer shells — helium has 2, the rest 8.

✗ "2.8.3 is in period 3 because it has 3 outer electrons." — that is the group reason.
✓ "Group 3: three electrons in the outer shell. Period 3: three occupied shells."

It is a coincidence when group and period match. Calcium, 2.8.8.2, is Group 2, Period 4 — the 2023 January Edexcel answer.

subsections.heading: Ions and their charges
subsections.html:
Spec 1.22 · 2023 Q1 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q1(e) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1(b)

Atoms lose or gain electrons to get a full outer shell, and the charge is the number of electrons moved.

  1. Groups 1, 2, 3 (metals) lose their outer electrons → ions of 1+, 2+, 3+.
  2. Groups 5, 6, 7 (non-metals) gain enough to reach 8 → ions of 3−, 2−, 1−.
  3. The ion's configuration is the atom's, with electrons removed or added. Na 2.8.1 → Na⁺ 2.8. Cl 2.8.7 → Cl⁻ 2.8.8.

Protons never change. An ion with three more protons than electrons has a charge of 3+. Write the charge with its size: +1, not "positive".

subsections.heading: Metals and non-metals
subsections.html:
Spec 1.20, 1.21 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1

Metals are on the left and centre of the table; non-metals are on the right — and two tests tell them apart.

TestMetalNon-metal
Electrical conductivityConducts (as a solid)Does not conduct (graphite is the exception)
Oxide dissolved in waterBasic oxide — alkaline, pH above 7Acidic oxide — pH below 7

Magnesium burns to MgO, a basic oxide. Sulfur burns to SO₂, which dissolves to give an acidic solution. "An element that forms a basic oxide" was a 2024 Edexcel answer — lithium, a metal.

subsections.heading: Why a group reacts alike — and why noble gases don't
subsections.html:
Spec 1.23, 1.24 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q1(b) · 2024 Q1c

Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in the same way.

Reactions happen at the outer shell. Lithium (2.1), sodium (2.8.1) and potassium (2.8.8.1) each lose one outer electron, so all form 1+ ions and similar compounds.

The noble gases (Group 0) have a full outer shell. They do not need to lose, gain or share electrons, so they are unreactive and exist as single atoms. An element with a full outer shell has 0 electrons available for bonding — 2024's answer.

The noble gas answer — two marks

1. It has a full outer shell (8 electrons, or 2 for helium) 1

2. So it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons 1

The two lookups everything follows from

Group = outer electrons. Period = occupied shells. Get those two straight and every configuration, group, period and ion-charge question is arithmetic.

Protons = atomic number. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Electrons = protons (adjust for an ion's charge).

questions.promptHtml: An atom has the electronic configuration 2.8.3. Without being told the element, state its group, its period, the charge on its ion, and — using a periodic table — its identity.
questions.answerHtml:
Group 3 — three outer electrons. Period 3 — three occupied shells. Ion: loses the three outer electrons → 3+ (configuration 2.8).

Identity: 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 electrons = 13 protons → atomic number 13 → aluminium.

Same-numbers-different-meanings is the trap: "3" appears as both group and period here by coincidence. Group counts the outer electrons; period counts the shells. The 2023 cohort mixing them up is why this question keeps returning.

questions.promptHtml: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Explain why the two isotopes react identically, and calculate Ar.
questions.answerHtml:
Identical chemistry: both have 17 protons and therefore 17 electrons in the same arrangement (2.8.7). Chemical behaviour is decided entirely by the electrons — the extra two neutrons in ³⁷Cl change only the mass.

Ar = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

Check: between 35 and 37, closer to 35 (the abundant one). ✓

questions.promptHtml: Why does an atom of element X with 14 protons, 14 electrons and 15 neutrons have a mass number of 29 — and why are answers of 14, 15 and 28 each wrong in a different way?
questions.answerHtml:
Mass number counts what has mass in the nucleus: protons + neutrons = 14 + 15 = 29.

The wrong answers (this was 2022's actual MCQ, distractors and all): 14 is the proton count — the atomic number, not the mass number. 15 is just the neutrons. 28 is protons + electrons — but electrons weigh ≈1/1836 of a proton, effectively nothing, and never contribute to the mass number.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium's ion is Na⁺ but its configuration is 2.8.1. Talk through what the atom loses, what the ion's configuration becomes, and why the exam refuses the answer "positive" for the charge.
questions.answerHtml:
The single outer electron is lost (it is the easiest route to a full outer shell). The ion's configuration is 2.8 — eleven protons now hold ten electrons, so the net charge is +1.

"Positive" was ignored (scored nothing) in 2023 because it answers a different question — direction without size. Mg loses two electrons and is also "positive", but its ion is 2+. The charge is a number with a sign: +1, 2+, 3−, written either way round, or as the symbol Na⁺.

questions.promptHtml: Element Y is in Group 0 (the noble gases). How many electrons does it have available for bonding, and what does that predict about its chemistry?
questions.answerHtml:
Zero. A Group 0 element has a full outer shell — no tendency to lose, gain or share anything. (2024's answer line accepted "0".)

Prediction: unreactive. Noble gases form almost no compounds and exist as single atoms. A full shell is the stable arrangement every other atom reaches by ionic or covalent bonding.

questions.promptHtml: Argon (Ar 39.9) comes before potassium (Ar 39.1) in the periodic table, even though it is heavier. Why is that the right place for it?
questions.answerHtml:
The table is in order of atomic number, not mass. Argon has 18 protons, potassium 19, so argon comes first.

It also has to be that way for the groups to work. Argon (2.8.8) has a full outer shell and belongs with the unreactive noble gases. Potassium (2.8.8.1) has one outer electron and reacts like sodium. Ordering by mass would put each in the wrong group. Argon is heavier only because its common isotope has more neutrons — and neutrons do not affect chemistry.

questions.promptHtml: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water in the same way. Explain this using electronic configurations — and say why the number of shells does not change the type of reaction.
questions.answerHtml:
Li 2.1, Na 2.8.1, K 2.8.8.1 — each has one electron in its outer shell. In a reaction each atom loses that one electron to form a 1+ ion. Same outer shell → same reaction → same type of product (a hydroxide and hydrogen).

The inner shells are full and take no part. More shells change how easily the outer electron is lost (it is further from the nucleus, so less strongly attracted), which changes how fast the reaction goes — but not what kind of reaction it is.

questions.promptHtml: An ion X³⁺ has the electronic configuration 2.8. Identify X, and explain each step of your reasoning.
questions.answerHtml:
Step 1: the ion has 2 + 8 = 10 electrons.

Step 2: a 3+ charge means the atom lost 3 electrons, so the atom had 10 + 3 = 13 electrons.

Step 3: a neutral atom has protons = electrons, so 13 protons → atomic number 13 → aluminium (2.8.3, Group 3 — which fits a 3+ ion).

The trap is reading 2.8 as neon. The configuration belongs to the ion; the element is set by the protons, which never change.

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Describe two tests that could be used to decide whether an element is a metal or a non-metal. Give the result for a metal. (2)
(b) Sulfur burns in air. The oxide formed dissolves in water to give a solution of pH 3. Explain what this shows about sulfur. (2)
questions.answerHtml:

modules.title: Bonding and Structures
modules.standfirst: Three bond types, four structures, and one iron law: properties follow structure. The killer distinction on every paper is bonds versus intermolecular forces — confuse them once in an answer and the whole explanation scores zero.

subsections.html: Atoms bond three ways: give electrons away (ionic), share them (covalent), or pool them (metallic). But melting points and conductivity are set by the structure — giant or simple molecular — not by the bond type alone. Work out the structure first; everything else follows from it.

subsections.heading: Which kind of bond? Look at the elements
subsections.html:
Spec 1.37, 1.44, 1.53C · 2025 Q6b

Metal + non-metal → ionic. Non-metal + non-metal → covalent. Metal on its own → metallic.

Every atom is trying to get a full outer shell. How it does that depends on its partner:

ElementsBondWhat the electrons doExample
Metal + non-metalIonicTransferred from metal to non-metalNaCl, MgO, Ca₃P₂
Non-metal + non-metalCovalentShared in pairsH₂O, NH₃, CO₂, diamond
Metal onlyMetallicDelocalised — free to moveMg, Cu, Fe

Decide this first. Explaining an ionic compound with sharing, or a molecule with ions, scores zero — the 2025 Ca₃P₂ scheme gave nothing for any mention of sharing.

subsections.heading: Ionic bonding — electron transfer
subsections.html:
Spec 1.37, 1.40 · 2021 Q3c · 2023 Q2a · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q4(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(b)

Metal atoms lose their outer electrons and non-metal atoms gain them, so both end up with full outer shells as ions.

  1. Write both configurations. Mg 2.8.2 and O 2.6.
  2. Say how many electrons the metal loses. Mg loses two → Mg²⁺, 2.8.
  3. Say how many the non-metal gains. O gains two → O²⁻, 2.8.
  4. Balance the numbers. If they don't match, use more atoms: Na loses one, O needs two, so two Na atoms per O → Na₂O.

The 2023 marker: "Needed the idea of 2 electrons to score — several just said electrons moved from magnesium to oxygen without specifying how many." Always give the number.

Drawing an ionic dot-and-cross diagram

1. Draw the metal ion's shell empty (outer electrons gone), or show only the full shell underneath. Put it in square brackets with the charge: [Na]⁺.

2. Draw the non-metal ion with a full outer shell of 8, using a different symbol for the gained electron(s): [Cl]⁻ with 7 dots and 1 cross.

3. Brackets and charges on both ions. Only outer electrons need be shown.

subsections.heading: The ionic bond is an attraction
subsections.html:
Spec 1.41 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(c) · 2025 Q6b

An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

The transfer makes the ions; the attraction is the bond. "Transfer of electrons" alone is not a description of the bond, and "sharing" is always wrong here.

Formula from charges (2025 Q6b): calcium forms Ca²⁺, phosphorus forms P³⁻. The charges must cancel: 3 × (2+) = 6+ balances 2 × (3−) = 6−, so the formula is Ca₃P₂. Module 3 drills this.

subsections.heading: Giant ionic lattices — melting point and conductivity
subsections.html:
Spec 1.42, 1.43 · 2023 Q6e · 2025 Q6e · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q6

Every ion in a giant ionic lattice is held by strong attractions to all the oppositely charged ions around it, so it takes a lot of energy to melt.

The high-melting-point answer — three marks

1. It has a giant ionic lattice / structure 1

2. With strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions 1

3. So a lot of energy is needed to overcome them 1

Any mention of covalent bonds, molecules or intermolecular forces: 0 marks.

Conductivity: the charge carriers are the ions.

  • Solid: ions are in fixed positions in the lattice, so they cannot move — no conduction.
  • Molten or dissolved in water: the ions are free to move and carry the charge — it conducts.

Electrons never enter this answer. "Electrons can't move in the solid" does not score.

subsections.heading: Covalent bonding — a shared pair pulled by two nuclei
subsections.html:
Spec 1.44, 1.45 · 2021 Q2c · 2022 Q10a · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(a)

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons, held by the electrostatic attraction between that pair and the nuclei of both atoms.

"Describe the forces in a covalent bond" — two marks

1. (Electrostatic) attraction between the shared pair of electrons 1

2. and the nuclei of both atoms 1

2021 and 2022 both refused the mark for "attracted to the nucleus". The plural is the mark.

Covalent bonds are strong. That matters later: what is weak in a simple molecular substance is never the bond.

subsections.heading: Dot-and-cross diagrams for molecules
subsections.html:
Spec 1.46 · 2021 Q2d · 2023 Q4a · 2024 Q3a · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(a)

Share just enough pairs so that every atom ends with a full outer shell — 2 for hydrogen, 8 for everything else.

  1. Count each atom's outer electrons. H 1, C 4, N 5, O 6, Cl 7.
  2. Work out how many bonds each needs. H needs 1 more, O needs 2, N needs 3, C needs 4.
  3. Draw the shared pairs in the overlap, one dot and one cross per pair.
  4. Add the lone pairs left over on each atom.
  5. Check every atom: H has 2, every other atom has 8 in its shell.
MoleculeShared pairsLone pairs
H₂, HCl, Cl₂1 single bondCl keeps 3 lone pairs
H₂O2 (O–H)2 on O
NH₃3 (N–H)1 on N
CH₄4 (C–H)none
O₂a double bond — 2 pairs2 on each O
CO₂two double bonds, O=C=O2 on each O
N₂a triple bond — 3 pairs, 6 electrons1 on each N
C₂H₄ (ethene)C=C double bond + 4 C–Hnone
C₂H₆ (ethane)C–C + 6 C–Hnone

Marks are lost to miscounted lone pairs, not to untidy circles. The schemes accept any mix of dots and crosses.

subsections.heading: Simple molecular substances — why strong bonds still boil low
subsections.html:
Spec 1.47, 1.51 · 2021 Q2b · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q3(b)

Melting or boiling a simple molecular substance only separates the molecules; it overcomes the weak intermolecular forces and breaks no covalent bonds.

H₂, Cl₂, CO₂, water and alkanes have strong covalent bonds inside each molecule, but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. That is why they are gases, liquids, or solids with low melting points.

The two-mark script for "strong bonds, low boiling point"

1. There are only weak forces of attraction between the molecules (weak intermolecular forces) 1

2. So little energy is needed to overcome them / separate the molecules 1

Any reference to breaking covalent bonds: 0/2. The bonds are bystanders.

Covalent substances usually do not conduct: the molecules are neutral, so there are no ions and no free electrons to carry charge.

subsections.heading: Bigger molecules, higher boiling points
subsections.html:
Spec 1.48 · 2024 Q9b · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(b)

As relative molecular mass increases, the intermolecular forces get stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

  1. The molecules get bigger (higher Mr).
  2. So the intermolecular forces between them get stronger.
  3. So more energy is needed to overcome them — a higher boiling point.

Two exam versions: longer alkanes boil higher (2024 school), and the halogens F₂ → Cl₂ → Br₂ → I₂ go from gas to liquid to solid (2023 January Edexcel). The forces are between molecules, never "between atoms".

subsections.heading: Giant covalent structures — diamond and graphite
subsections.html:
Spec 1.49, 1.50 · 2022 Q10b · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q8(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(c)

In a giant covalent structure every atom is covalently bonded into one huge network, so melting means breaking millions of strong covalent bonds.

Here, and only here, "covalent bonds are broken on melting" is the right phrase. That is why diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide have very high melting points.

PropertyDiamondGraphite
Bonding of each carbonBonded to 4 others — rigid 3-D (tetrahedral) networkBonded to 3 others — flat hexagonal layers
HardnessVery hard — strong bonds in every directionSoft, slippery — layers slide over each other
Conducts?No — no free electrons; all 4 outer electrons are in bondsYes — one delocalised electron per carbon moves along the layers
UseCutting toolsLubricant, electrodes

For the Edexcel six-marker, give each point for both forms: bonded to 4 vs 3, no delocalised electrons vs delocalised electrons, hard vs soft.

Edexcel allows "weak forces between the layers" of graphite. The school's 2022 scheme cancelled marks for the word intermolecular in graphite — graphite has no molecules. Safe phrase: "the layers can slide over each other".

subsections.heading: C₆₀ fullerene — carbon that is molecular
subsections.html:
Spec 1.50 · 2022 Q10c · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q8(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q10(b)

C₆₀ is made of separate molecules of 60 carbon atoms, so it is simple molecular and melts far lower than graphite.

  1. Graphite is giant covalent.
  2. Melting graphite breaks covalent bonds.
  3. C₆₀ has a simple molecular structure.
  4. Melting C₆₀ only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules.
  5. Breaking covalent bonds needs much more energy than overcoming intermolecular forces.

That list is the mark scheme — "any four from" these five, on both the school's 2022 paper and two Edexcel papers.

subsections.heading: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals
subsections.html:
Spec 1.52C, 1.53C, 1.54C · 2025 Q4a · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q4(c)

A metal is a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, held together by the electrostatic attraction between them.

In the 2-D diagram, draw rows of circles labelled + (the positive ions) with electrons (e⁻) scattered between them. The two labels are positive ions and delocalised electrons — "protons" was rejected.

  • Conduct electricity: the delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.
  • Malleable: the ions are in layers that can slide over each other without the bonding breaking.
  • High melting point: strong attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.

2025 rejected intermolecular forces in the malleability answer. Metals have no molecules.

subsections.heading: Identifying a mystery substance from its properties
subsections.html:
2021 Q3a · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q3 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q2

Two facts — does it conduct, and when? how high is its melting point? — identify the structure every time.

  1. Conducts as a solid? Yes → metal (graphite is the one exception).
  2. Conducts only when molten or dissolved? → giant ionic.
  3. Never conducts, low melting point? → simple molecular.
  4. Never conducts, very high melting point? → giant covalent (e.g. diamond).

2021's grid: mp −101 °C, never conducts → simple molecular (a gas at 20 °C since bp −35 °C); mp 1063 °C, conducts solid → metal; mp 801 °C, conducts molten only → ionic; mp 3550 °C, never conducts → giant covalent (diamond). To say whether something is a gas at a temperature, compare that temperature with its boiling point.

The one distinction everything follows from

Giant structures: strong bonds/attractions are overcome on melting. Simple molecular: weak forces BETWEEN molecules are overcome — the covalent bonds never break. Choose the story before you write; mixing them scores zero.

Conduction: metals and graphite — delocalised electrons. Ionic — ions, only when molten or dissolved. Molecules — nothing.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording

Covalent bondA shared pair of electrons, electrostatically attracted to the nuclei of both atoms (plural!)
Metallic bondingLattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, with electrostatic attraction between them
Intermolecular forcesThe weak forces of attraction between molecules — overcome on boiling; not bonds
CompoundA substance containing two or more elements chemically bonded/combined (reject: mixture)
Malleable (metal)Can be hammered into shape because layers of ions slide over one another
Delocalised electronsElectrons not tied to one atom, free to move through the structure

questions.promptHtml: The H–H bond is one of the strongest single bonds known, yet hydrogen boils at −253 °C. Resolve the contradiction — and explain why "some of the covalent bonds break on boiling" scores 0/2 rather than 1/2.
questions.answerHtml:
No contradiction: boiling and bond-breaking are different events. Boiling only has to separate whole molecules from each other, and between H₂ molecules there are just weak intermolecular forces — very little energy overcomes them, hence −253 °C. The strong H–H bond travels intact inside every molecule of the gas.

It scores 0/2 because the error isn't a missing detail — it is the wrong physical story. An answer built on bond-breaking describes a chemical decomposition, not boiling, so neither marking point is present. That is why the schemes treat one mention of bond-breaking as fatal rather than partial.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium chloride at 801 °C and diamond at 3550 °C both have giant structures. What is being overcome when each one melts, and why is "strong bonds" an incomplete answer for NaCl?
questions.answerHtml:
NaCl: the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice. The three-marker wants the structure named (giant ionic), the attraction identified (between oppositely charged ions), and the energy statement (a lot needed to overcome it).

Diamond: actual covalent bonds — every carbon is pinned to four others, and melting means breaking that network. This is the one place "bonds break on melting" is the right answer.

"Strong bonds" alone fails for NaCl because it never says what kind of attraction or between what — and worse, it invites covalent language, which zeroes the answer. Name the particles: ions, oppositely charged.

questions.promptHtml: Graphite and C₆₀ fullerene are both pure carbon with covalent bonds. Why does graphite survive to ~3600 °C while C₆₀ melts far lower — and which single word in a student's answer would destroy the graphite half?
questions.answerHtml:
Different structures. Graphite is giant covalent: one continuous network, so melting must break covalent bonds — hugely expensive. C₆₀ is simple molecular: separate 60-atom balls, held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces; melting just pulls the balls apart and leaves every bond intact. Covalent bonds need far more energy than IMF — that comparison is its own mark.

The destroying word: "intermolecular" anywhere near graphite. Graphite has no molecules, so it can have no intermolecular forces — the 2022 scheme cancelled both graphite marks when they appeared.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why copper conducts electricity as a solid, sodium chloride only when molten, and chlorine never — naming the moving particle in each case.
questions.answerHtml:
Copper: delocalised electrons move through the lattice of positive ions — mobile charge exists already, so the solid conducts.

Sodium chloride: the charge carriers are the ions themselves. Solid: locked in the lattice — no conduction. Molten (or dissolved): ions free to move — conducts. Electrons never enter this story.

Chlorine: neutral molecules, no ions, no delocalised electrons — no charged particle free to move, ever.

Conduction answers live or die on naming the right particle: electrons for metals (and graphite), ions for ionic compounds, nothing for covalent substances.

questions.promptHtml: Use the charges rule to explain why calcium phosphide is Ca₃P₂ and not CaP — and why a sharing-based explanation was awarded zero.
questions.answerHtml:
Calcium (Group 2) forms Ca²⁺; phosphorus (Group 5) gains three electrons to form P³⁻. A formula must be electrically neutral: 2+ and 3− don't cancel one-for-one. The smallest balance is three calciums (6+) against two phosphides (6−) → Ca₃P₂.

Sharing scored zero because this is a metal + non-metal — an ionic compound. Explaining an ionic formula with covalent ideas is the same mistake as intermolecular forces in graphite: the wrong model, not a partial answer. Metal + non-metal → transfer and charges, always.

questions.promptHtml: Metals can be hammered into sheets without shattering; ionic crystals crack. Explain both from their structures.
questions.answerHtml:
Metal: the lattice is layers of identical positive ions in a shared electron sea. Hammering makes the layers slide — but every new position looks like the old one: positive ions still surrounded by the delocalised electrons that hold them. The bonding survives the slide → the metal changes shape without breaking (malleable).

Ionic crystal: sliding a layer by one position puts like charges next to each other — positive against positive. Attraction flips to repulsion and the crystal shatters.

For the exam: malleability = layers (of ions) slide over each other — and no intermolecular forces anywhere near this answer (2025 rejected them).

questions.promptHtml: Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid at room temperature. All four are X₂ molecules with one covalent bond. Explain the trend.
questions.answerHtml:
All four are simple molecular, so melting and boiling only overcome the intermolecular forces. The covalent bond inside each molecule plays no part.

Down the group the molecules get bigger — Mr rises from 38 (F₂) to 254 (I₂). Bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling points rise, and by iodine the forces are strong enough to hold a solid at room temperature.

The same argument explains why long-chain alkanes boil higher than short ones.

questions.promptHtml: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon in giant covalent structures. Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
questions.answerHtml:
Carbon has 4 outer electrons. In diamond each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds, so all four electrons are held in bonds. None are free to move — no conduction.

In graphite each carbon forms only 3 bonds. The fourth electron is delocalised — it can move along the layers and carry charge. So graphite conducts, like a metal.

Conduction always needs a charged particle that is free to move. Ask that question first, whatever the structure.

questions.promptHtml:
Sodium (2.8.1) reacts with chlorine (2.8.7) to form sodium chloride.

(a) Describe the changes in electronic configuration when the atoms form sodium chloride. (3)
(b) Explain why sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Sodium loses one electron 1; chlorine gains one electron 1; Na becomes 2.8 AND Cl becomes 2.8.8 1 — wrong number of electrons transferred caps at 2; any covalent language caps at 1

(b) Solid: ions are fixed in the lattice / cannot move 1; molten: ions are free to move (and carry charge) 1 — no marks for electrons moving

markScheme.point: (a) Sodium loses one electron ; chlorine gains one electron ; Na becomes 2.8 AND Cl becomes 2.8.8 — wrong number of electrons transferred caps at 2; any covalent language caps at 1

There are only weak forces of attraction (weak intermolecular forces) between the molecules 1; so little (heat) energy is needed to overcome the forces / separate the molecules 1

questions.promptHtml: Magnesium oxide has a melting point of 2852 °C. Explain why magnesium oxide has a high melting point. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Giant ionic structure/lattice 1; strong (electrostatic) attraction between oppositely charged ions 1; a lot of energy is needed to overcome the attractions 1

Mention of covalent bonds, molecules or intermolecular forces: 0 marks — the 2025 rule.

questions.promptHtml: Graphite and C₆₀ fullerene both contain covalent bonds but have different structures. Explain why C₆₀ fullerene has a much lower melting point than graphite. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Any four from this list of five:

  • graphite is giant covalent 1
  • melting graphite breaks covalent bonds 1
  • C₆₀ is (simple) molecular 1
  • melting C₆₀ overcomes intermolecular forces (between molecules) 1

The fifth point, which can replace any one above: covalent bonds need much more energy to break than intermolecular forces need to overcome. Putting intermolecular forces in graphite cancels the graphite marks.

modules.title: Formulae and Equations
modules.standfirst: The grammar of the subject. Few questions test it alone — instead it leaks marks in every other topic: a wrong formula, a missed balancing number, HBR instead of HBr, an equation with no state symbols. Two rules — charges cancel, atoms balance — fix it once and earn everywhere.

intel.html:

The recurring commentary lines:

"Many got close with the equation but did not include balancing numbers." — 2024, thermite.

"REJECT wrong case: HBR / hbr" — 2024; the schemes penalise wrong capitalisation in formulae and even in names ("spelling must be correct").

2021's state-symbol scheme accepted capital letters, but the safe habit is lower-case (s), (l), (g), (aq) — and knowing which is the real test: soluble salt (aq), insoluble product (s).

subsections.html: Chemical formulae are not memorised one by one — they are built from ion charges. Equations are then balanced by counting atoms, never by editing formulae. Two rules, used again and again.

subsections.heading: Reading a formula — counting the atoms
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25, 1.39 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q9(a)

A small number after a symbol counts that atom only; a small number after a bracket counts everything inside; a big number in front counts the whole formula.

  • H₂O — 2 hydrogen, 1 oxygen.
  • Ca(OH)₂ — 1 calcium, and the bracket doubles O and H: 2 oxygen, 2 hydrogen.
  • 3H₂O — three whole water molecules: 6 hydrogen, 3 oxygen.

Worked example — Na₂SO₄·7H₂O

  1. Different elements: Na, S, O, H → 4.
  2. Atoms before the dot: 2 Na + 1 S + 4 O = 7.
  3. Atoms after the dot: 7 × H₂O = 7 × 3 = 21.
  4. Total: 7 + 21 = 28 atoms.

The "·7H₂O" is water of crystallisation — seven water molecules for each Na₂SO₄. That was the 2023 Edexcel multiple choice, both parts.

subsections.heading: Ion charges you can read off the table
subsections.html:
Spec 1.38 · 2024 Q8a · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(a)

For Groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, the group number gives the charge.

GroupChargeExamples
1+1Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺
2+2Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺
3+3Al³⁺
5−3N³⁻ (nitride), P³⁻ (phosphide)
6−2O²⁻ (oxide), S²⁻ (sulfide)
7−1F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ (fluoride, chloride, bromide, iodide)

Metals lose electrons (positive); non-metals gain them (negative). Module 1 explains why.

subsections.heading: Ions you must learn by heart
subsections.html:
Spec 1.38 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q9(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q6(a)

Six metal ions and six other ions are on the spec list and cannot be worked out from the table — learn them.

  • Metal ions: Ag⁺ (silver), Zn²⁺ (zinc), Cu²⁺ (copper(II)), Pb²⁺ (lead(II)), Fe²⁺ (iron(II)) and Fe³⁺ (iron(III)).
  • Other ions: H⁺ (hydrogen), OH⁻ (hydroxide), NH₄⁺ (ammonium), NO₃⁻ (nitrate), CO₃²⁻ (carbonate), SO₄²⁻ (sulfate).

The Roman numeral in a name is the charge: iron(III) = Fe³⁺, copper(II) = Cu²⁺, lead(II) = Pb²⁺. Lead oxide, PbO, contains Pb²⁺ because O²⁻ is 2− — the 2022 Edexcel answer.

subsections.heading: Building a formula — the charges must cancel
subsections.html:
Spec 1.39 · 2023 Q4b · 2024 Q8a · 2025 Q6b · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(a)

A compound has no overall charge, so you take just enough of each ion for the positive and negative charges to cancel.

  1. Write the two ions with their charges. Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
  2. Find the lowest number both charges go into. 3 and 2 → 6.
  3. Work out how many of each ion make that. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 Al³⁺; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 O²⁻.
  4. Write the numbers as subscripts. Al₂O₃.
  5. Check: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6. Total zero. ✓

The shortcut is to "cross" the charge numbers — each ion's charge becomes the other's subscript — then simplify. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ cross to Mg₂O₂, which simplifies to MgO.

  • Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl
  • Mg²⁺ + Cl⁻ → MgCl₂
  • Mg²⁺ + N³⁻ → Mg₃N₂ (2024's table)
  • Ca²⁺ + P³⁻ → Ca₃P₂ (2025)

subsections.heading: Brackets around compound ions
subsections.html:
Spec 1.39 · 2023 Q4b · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q10(b) · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(d)

If you need more than one of an ion made of several atoms, put it in brackets before writing the number.

  1. Write the ions. Ammonium carbonate: NH₄⁺ and CO₃²⁻.
  2. Balance the charges. Two NH₄⁺ (2+) cancel one CO₃²⁻ (2−).
  3. Bracket the ion you need more than one of. (NH₄)₂CO₃.

Without brackets, NH₄₂CO₃ means 42 hydrogen atoms. Only one of the ion? No brackets: NH₄Cl, NaOH, CuSO₄. More examples: Ca(OH)₂, Mg(NO₃)₂, Al₂(SO₄)₃, Fe(OH)₃.

subsections.heading: Naming compounds
subsections.html:
Spec 1.39 · 2023 Q4b · 2024 Q8 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(a)(ii)

The metal (or ammonium) is named first, unchanged; the non-metal part comes second with its ending changed.

  • -ide = only the one non-metal element: chloride (Cl⁻), oxide (O²⁻), nitride (N³⁻), phosphide (P³⁻).
  • -ate = the element plus oxygen: sulfate (SO₄²⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻), carbonate (CO₃²⁻).
  • Hydroxide = OH⁻; ammonium = NH₄⁺.
  • Roman numerals for metals with more than one ion: iron(II) chloride FeCl₂, iron(III) chloride FeCl₃.

MgO = magnesium oxide. NH₄Cl = ammonium chloride. Spelling is marked — the 2024 scheme said the name's "spelling must be correct".

subsections.heading: Elements that exist as molecules of two atoms
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(a)

Seven elements are always written as pairs in equations: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

Every other element is written as a single symbol: Mg, Fe, C, S, Na. So hydrogen gas is H₂, never H; chlorine is Cl₂, never Cl. A lone "Cl" or "O" in an equation loses the formula mark.

subsections.heading: Word equations — naming what reacts and what forms
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · every paper

Reactants go on the left, products on the right, and most reactions on the course follow a handful of patterns.

PatternExample
metal + acid → salt + hydrogenmagnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
base + acid → salt + watercopper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper(II) sulfate + water
carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxidecalcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
metal + oxygen → metal oxidemagnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + watermethane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogensodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen

Write the word equation first if you are unsure. It tells you exactly which formulae to write.

subsections.heading: Balancing — change the big numbers, never the formulae
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2024 Q5a · 2025 Q4b · 2023 Q9b · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(c)

A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides, and you balance it only by putting numbers in front of formulae.

Worked example — magnesium burning: Mg + O₂ → MgO

  1. Write correct formulae. Mg + O₂ → MgO. These are now fixed — never change a subscript.
  2. Count each element on both sides. Mg: 1 left, 1 right. O: 2 left, 1 right. Oxygen is unbalanced.
  3. Fix one element with a big number. Put 2 in front of MgO: Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Now O: 2 = 2.
  4. Recount everything. Mg: 1 left, 2 right. Put 2 in front of Mg.
  5. Final check. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Mg 2 = 2, O 2 = 2. ✓

Tip: balance elements that appear on their own (O₂, C, Mg) last — changing their number doesn't upset anything else.

The school's set pieces: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe · 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ · Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO · Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃. Schemes usually give one mark for formulae and one for balancing, and "ALLOW multiples".

subsections.heading: Harder balancing — brackets and burning
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2024 Q8b · 2025 Q6c–d · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(c)

Count brackets and water molecules carefully, and leave oxygen to the very end.

Worked example — ethane burning: C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

  1. Carbon first. 2 C on the left → 2CO₂.
  2. Hydrogen next. 6 H on the left → 3H₂O.
  3. Now count the oxygen on the right. 2CO₂ = 4 O, 3H₂O = 3 O. Total 7.
  4. Balance O₂ last. 7 ÷ 2 = 3½ O₂. That gives C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
  5. Remove the half by doubling everything. 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Recount: C 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 14 = 14. ✓

Both versions score — Edexcel accepts the ½.

Brackets: in Ca₃(PO₄)₂ there are 2 × 4 = 8 oxygens. All eight leave as CO, so you need 8CO and 8C. The 2024 Edexcel nitric acid equation balances as 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃: N 4 = 4, H 4 = 4, O 8 + 2 + 2 = 12 = 12.

subsections.heading: State symbols — and which one is the real test
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2021 Q8a · 2022 Q3b · 2024 Q10a · 2025 Q4b · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q6(a) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q9(a)

A state symbol says what each substance is physically like in the flask: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.

The papers' favourite: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).

  1. Water is (l) — it is the liquid itself, not dissolved in anything.
  2. Acids, alkalis and dissolved salts are (aq). 2024's commentary: many wrote zinc nitrate as (s) or (l); it is a soluble salt in solution. Check the solubility rules in module 4.
  3. Precipitates are (s) — insoluble products are solid even though they form in solution: PbCl₂(s), BaSO₄(s).
  4. Gases are (g): H₂, O₂, CO₂, Cl₂.
  5. Metals and solid oxides are (s): Mg(s), CuO(s), PbO(s).

Dissolving a solid in water is X(s) → X(aq) — the 2023 January Edexcel multiple choice.

subsections.heading: Equations for reactions you have never seen
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2025 Q6d · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(b)

The question gives you every formula you can't work out, so copy them exactly and just balance.

Worked example — calcium phosphide + water → calcium hydroxide + phosphine (PH₃)

  1. Formulae: Ca₃P₂ (from the charges), H₂O, Ca(OH)₂ (Ca²⁺ with two OH⁻), PH₃ (given).
  2. Balance the element that appears in one place on each side: 3 Ca → 3Ca(OH)₂; 2 P → 2PH₃.
  3. Count H and O on the right: 3Ca(OH)₂ has 6 O and 6 H; 2PH₃ has 6 H. So 6 O and 12 H.
  4. Balance water: 6H₂O gives 6 O and 12 H. ✓
  5. Answer: Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃

2022 Edexcel did the same with methanoic acid (HCOOH) and sodium carbonate: the pattern "acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂" gives 2HCOOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2HCOONa + CO₂ + H₂O.

The two rules everything follows from

Formulae: charges cancel. Equations: atoms balance — adjust the big numbers in front, never the small ones.

subsections.heading: The ion bank
subsections.html:
PositiveNegative
Group 1 → +1 (Na⁺, K⁺) · Group 2 → +2 (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺) · Group 3 → +3 (Al³⁺)Group 7 → −1 (Cl⁻, Br⁻) · Group 6 → −2 (O²⁻, S²⁻) · Group 5 → −3 (N³⁻, P³⁻)
Ag⁺ · Zn²⁺ · Cu²⁺ · Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺ · Pb²⁺ · H⁺ · NH₄⁺OH⁻ · NO₃⁻ · CO₃²⁻ · SO₄²⁻

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Diatomic moleculeAn element that exists as molecules of two atoms: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂
-ide endingCompound of just the two elements named (chloride, oxide, phosphide)
-ate endingCompound containing the element plus oxygen (sulfate, nitrate, carbonate)

questions.promptHtml: Why is magnesium chloride MgCl₂ but sodium chloride just NaCl? Explain from the charges, and state what the "crossing trick" is actually doing.
questions.answerHtml:
Compounds are electrically neutral. Mg²⁺ carries two positives, and each Cl⁻ only one negative — so it takes two chloride ions to cancel one magnesium: MgCl₂. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel one-for-one: NaCl.

The crossing trick (charge of one ion becomes subscript of the other) is just a quick way of making total + equal total −. That is why the result must always be simplified (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ "cross" to Mg₂O₂ → reduce to MgO).

questions.promptHtml: A student balances Mg + O₂ → MgO by rewriting it as Mg + O₂ → MgO₂. Chemically, what has the student done wrong — and what is the legal fix?
questions.answerHtml:
They have invented a different substance. MgO₂ is not magnesium oxide — the formula of a compound is fixed by its ion charges (Mg²⁺, O²⁻ → MgO) and cannot change during balancing. Editing subscripts changes what reacts, not how much.

The legal fix uses big numbers only: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO — two Mg and two O on each side, formulae untouched. (With state symbols, 2025's version: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).)

questions.promptHtml: In Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO, show the oxygen count that makes 8 the right number for both carbon and CO.
questions.answerHtml:
Left side oxygen: (PO₄)₂ = 2 × 4 = 8 oxygens. Calcium (3) and phosphorus (2) already match Ca₃P₂ — so all 8 oxygens must leave inside CO, one each: 8CO. Eight CO needs eight carbons: 8C.

Recount: Ca 3 = 3, P 2 = 2, O 8 = 8, C 8 = 8. ✓ The general skill: brackets multiply everything inside, and a careful count of each element beats guessing. This equation appeared two years running (2024, 2025).

questions.promptHtml: The same reaction — zinc + nitric acid → zinc nitrate + hydrogen — gets four state symbols. Give them, and explain the two that students got wrong in 2024.
questions.answerHtml:
Zn(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂(g).

The two casualties: zinc nitrate, widely written (s) or (l). It is a soluble salt (all nitrates are soluble) sitting dissolved in the solution it formed in — (aq). It only becomes (s) after you deliberately crystallise it. And the acid: dilute acid is a solution, always (aq), never (l).

The habit: for every substance ask where is it, physically, in the flask? — not what it could be in a bottle somewhere.

questions.promptHtml: Ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid to give ammonium sulfate. Build the product's formula from its ions, then write and balance the full equation.
questions.answerHtml:
Formula: NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ — two ammoniums cancel one sulfate → (NH₄)₂SO₄, brackets because the compound ion is doubled.

Equation: the product contains two NH₄ groups, so two ammonia molecules are needed: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄. Count: N 2 = 2, H (6 + 2) = 8 = 8, S 1 = 1, O 4 = 4. ✓

(2023 asked exactly this, copied from 2022 Edexcel 1C Q10 — the balancing 2 was required.)

questions.promptHtml: "2H₂O" and "H₄O₂" contain the same atoms. Why is only one of them acceptable in an equation?
questions.answerHtml:
"2H₂O" means two water molecules, each H₂O. "H₄O₂" claims to be one molecule with four hydrogens and two oxygens — a substance that doesn't exist.

The big number counts how many of a substance; the small numbers say what the substance is. Balancing changes amounts, so it may only touch the big numbers. That's why the formulae are written first and then frozen.

questions.promptHtml: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Why does iron need a Roman numeral in its name when sodium never does?
questions.answerHtml:
Sodium is in Group 1 and only ever forms Na⁺, so "sodium chloride" can only mean NaCl.

Iron is a transition metal and forms two ions, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. "Iron chloride" could be either. The Roman numeral gives the charge: iron(II) chloride = Fe²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ = FeCl₂; iron(III) chloride = Fe³⁺ + 3Cl⁻ = FeCl₃. Same for copper(II) and lead(II) — learn them with the numeral attached.

questions.promptHtml: Lead(II) nitrate solution and potassium chloride solution are mixed and a solid forms. Explain how you would know which state symbol each substance gets, without being told.
questions.answerHtml:
Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KCl(aq) → PbCl₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq).

Both reactants are described as solutions, so both are (aq). For the products, use the solubility rules: chlorides are soluble except silver and lead(II), so PbCl₂ is insoluble — the solid that formed, (s). Potassium salts and nitrates are always soluble, so KNO₃ stays dissolved, (aq).

State symbols are chemistry, not guesswork: the solubility rules decide (s) or (aq) for every salt.

questions.answerHtml:
NaCl 1; MgCl₂ 1; Mg₃N₂ 1; (NH₄)₂CO₃ 1; Fe(OH)₃ 1; Al₂(SO₄)₃ 1

Wrong case or missing brackets is penalised — capitals and subscripts are part of the answer.

modules.title: Acids, Alkalis and Salt Preparation
modules.standfirst: Three salt-making methods, and the exam's favourite trick is making you pick the right one. The 2025 commentary on crystallisation is the longest the teachers have ever written — every line of it is a mark someone lost.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2021 Q1, Q5, Q10c (~14)Litmus colours and acid formulae; find the mistake in each step of a salt plan; insoluble BaSO₄ method; observations for Mg + acid; ion that makes a solution acidic

2023 Q10 (4)CuSO₄ + NaOH: what would be SEEN; pure dry sample of the precipitate

The 2025 crystallisation commentary, condensed — each line was a real answer that scored 0:

"Adding another chemical in step 1 scores 0 — the salt is no longer pure."

"'Filtering out the sodium sulfate' scores 0 — it is not a precipitate. Sodium salts are always soluble."

"Filtering before crystallising is the wrong order — max 2."

"'Heat the solution' without 'until crystallisation point' reads as heating to dryness — max 1."

And from 2023: "Students lost marks by stating that the filtrate must be washed and dried. In a double displacement reaction, the salt you want is the residue."

subsections.html: An acid in water releases H⁺ ions; an alkali releases OH⁻. Everything else — indicators, neutralisation, the three salt preparations — is about where those ions and their partners end up.

subsections.heading: Acids and alkalis — H⁺ and OH⁻
subsections.html:
Spec 2.31 · 2021 Q10c · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q6(a) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(b)

An acid in water is a source of hydrogen ions, H⁺; an alkali in water is a source of hydroxide ions, OH⁻.

  • Acids: hydrochloric acid HCl, sulfuric acid H₂SO₄, nitric acid HNO₃.
  • Alkalis: sodium hydroxide NaOH, potassium hydroxide KOH, calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂, ammonia solution.

The water matters. Hydrogen chloride dissolved in an organic solvent forms no H⁺ ions, so it does not turn litmus red. In water it forms H⁺ ions and becomes hydrochloric acid — the 2024 Edexcel four-marker.

"Which ion makes the solution acidic?" — the hydrogen ion, H⁺. If you give the name and the formula, both must be right.

subsections.heading: The pH scale
subsections.html:
Spec 2.29 · 2022 Q1

pH runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.

pHClassificationExample
0–3Strongly acidicdilute hydrochloric acid
4–6Weakly acidicvinegar, rain water
7Neutralpure water, salt solution
8–10Weakly alkalinesoap, baking soda solution
11–14Strongly alkalinesodium hydroxide solution

The lower the pH, the more H⁺ ions. The spec's bands are exact — pH 10 is weakly alkaline, pH 11 is strongly alkaline.

subsections.heading: Indicators
subsections.html:
Spec 2.28, 2.30 · 2021 Q1 · 2022 Q1 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q4(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q2(b)

An indicator changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.

IndicatorIn acidIn alkali
Litmusredblue
Phenolphthaleincolourlesspink
Methyl orangeredyellow

Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators. It gives the approximate pH: red (pH 0–3) → orange/yellow (4–6) → green (7) → blue (8–10) → purple (11–14).

  1. Add a few drops of universal indicator to the solution (or dip in the paper).
  2. Compare the colour with the colour chart.
  3. Read off the pH.

To show a solution is acidic: blue litmus turns red — state the change, not just the final colour.

subsections.heading: Neutralisation and proton transfer
subsections.html:
Spec 2.32, 2.35, 2.36 · 2022 Q1d · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q4(g)

In neutralisation the acid donates H⁺ (a proton) and the base accepts it — H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

A hydrogen ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its electron, so it is just a proton. That gives the spec's definitions:

  • An acid is a proton donor.
  • A base is a proton acceptor.

"Explain why this is an acid–base reaction" — two marks

1. The acid gives an H⁺ ion, which is a proton 1

2. The OH⁻ ion accepts the proton, forming water 1

Alkalis neutralise acids: add exactly the right amount and the solution is neutral, pH 7, containing just a salt and water.

subsections.heading: Bases and alkalis — not the same thing
subsections.html:
Spec 2.38

A base is any substance that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.

  • Bases: metal oxides (CuO, MgO), metal hydroxides (Cu(OH)₂, NaOH) and ammonia.
  • Alkalis are the soluble ones: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂ (slightly), ammonia solution.

So every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali. Copper(II) oxide is a base — it neutralises acid — but it is insoluble, so it is not an alkali.

subsections.heading: Naming the salt — the acid decides the surname
subsections.html:
Spec 2.37 · 2022 Q1d · 2021 Q5a

The metal (or ammonium) from the base gives the first name; the acid gives the second.

  1. First name from the metal: magnesium, zinc, copper(II), sodium — or ammonium from ammonia.
  2. Second name from the acid: hydrochloric → chloride; sulfuric → sulfate; nitric → nitrate.
  3. Put them together: potassium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → potassium chloride + water.

That's why a sulfate cannot be made from nitric acid — 2021's find-the-mistake question.

subsections.heading: The three acid reactions and what you see
subsections.html:
Spec 2.37 · 2021 Q10c · 2024 Q10a

Acids react with metals, bases and carbonates, and every one of them makes a salt.

ReactionProductsWhat you see
acid + metalsalt + hydrogeneffervescence; the metal gets smaller and disappears
acid + base (oxide or hydroxide)salt + waterthe solid disappears; often a colour change (CuO + acid → blue solution)
acid + carbonatesalt + water + carbon dioxideeffervescence; the solid disappears; the gas turns limewater milky

The spec leaves nitric acid + metals out of what you must describe, but both the school (2024, zinc) and Edexcel (January 2023, magnesium) set it anyway. Treat it like any other acid + metal.

Observation questions: say what your eyes see — effervescence/bubbles, the solid disappears, a colour change. "Hydrogen is given off" is a deduction, not an observation, and the schemes ignore it. 2021 also rejected extra wrong observations bolted on ("white flame") — do not decorate.

subsections.heading: The solubility rules — the map that picks the method
subsections.html:
Spec 2.34 · 2022 Q7a · 2024 Q2b · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(a)

Six rules tell you whether any salt dissolves, and every salt question starts by checking them.

  • All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts — soluble. ("Sodium salts are always soluble" — the 2025 marker, twice.)
  • All nitrates — soluble.
  • Chlorides — soluble, except silver and lead(II).
  • Sulfates — soluble, except barium, calcium and lead(II).
  • Carbonates — insoluble, except sodium, potassium, ammonium.
  • Hydroxides — insoluble, except sodium, potassium (calcium slightly).

Worked example — does a precipitate form?

Potassium carbonate solution + calcium nitrate solution.

  1. Swap the partners: the new pairs are potassium nitrate and calcium carbonate.
  2. Check each against the rules: potassium nitrate — soluble (potassium, and a nitrate). Calcium carbonate — carbonates are insoluble, and calcium is not an exception.
  3. Conclusion: yes — calcium carbonate precipitates.

Sodium chloride + ammonium nitrate → sodium nitrate and ammonium chloride, both soluble → no precipitate.

subsections.heading: Method 1 — soluble salt from an acid + excess insoluble solid
subsections.html:
Spec 2.39, 2.42 · 2024 Q10b · 2021 Q5a · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(a)

React the acid with more insoluble solid than it can use, filter off the extra, then crystallise the salt from the solution.

Use this for salts of magnesium, zinc, copper and other metals whose oxide, carbonate or the metal itself is insoluble. The required practical: hydrated copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

  1. Warm the dilute acid in a beaker.
  2. Add the solid a little at a time, stirring, until it is in excess — some stays undissolved. This makes sure all the acid is used up.
  3. Filter off the excess solid. The filtrate is the salt solution.
  4. Heat the filtrate until the crystallisation point — crystals just start to form on a cold glass rod. Never to dryness.
  5. Leave to cool and crystallise.
  6. Pour off or filter the remaining liquid, and dry the crystals with a named method: pat with filter paper, or leave in a warm place.

The two killers, straight from the schemes: heating to dryness collapses the answer to 1 mark (it drives off the water of crystallisation, and some salts decompose); and "leave the crystals to dry" without a method was refused the final mark in 2024 — name how.

Why excess? ✗ "to make more salt". ✓ "so that all the acid reacts" — so the solution contains only the salt and water.

subsections.heading: Titration — finding exactly how much acid neutralises the alkali
subsections.html:
Spec 2.33C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q4 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q2

A titration adds acid from a burette to a measured volume of alkali until the indicator just changes colour.

  1. Use a pipette to put exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask. A pipette is more accurate than a measuring cylinder.
  2. Add a few drops of indicator — methyl orange or phenolphthalein, not universal indicator.
  3. Fill the burette with acid and read the start volume.
  4. Add acid, swirling the flask to mix, until the indicator just changes colour — the end point. Stand the flask on a white tile to see the colour change clearly.
  5. Read the final volume. The difference is the titre.
  6. Repeat until you have concordant titres — within 0.20 cm³ of each other.

Why not universal indicator? It changes colour gradually through many colours, so there is no sharp end point — 2022 Edexcel.

subsections.heading: Method 2 — soluble salt from an acid + alkali
subsections.html:
Spec 2.40C · 2025 Q2a

When both reactants are soluble, there is no excess to filter off, so a titration finds the exact volumes first.

This is for sodium, potassium and ammonium salts.

  1. Titrate with an indicator to find the exact volume of acid that neutralises 25.0 cm³ of alkali.
  2. Repeat with the same volumes but no indicator, so the salt isn't coloured.
  3. Heat the solution to the crystallisation point.
  4. Leave to cool and crystallise.
  5. Pour off the remaining liquid and dry the crystals in a warm place.

2025 asked only for steps 3–5 — and adding any new chemical at that stage scored zero: the solution already contains only the salt and water.

subsections.heading: Method 3 — insoluble salt by precipitation
subsections.html:
Spec 2.41C, 2.43C · 2022 Q7b · 2023 Q10 · 2025 Q7a · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b)

Mix two solutions that each carry one ion of the insoluble salt; it forms as a solid that you filter, wash and dry.

Choose two soluble starting compounds — nitrates and sodium salts always are. For the required practical, lead(II) sulfate: lead(II) nitrate solution + sodium sulfate solution (or dilute sulfuric acid).

  1. Mix the two solutions — the schemes reject mixing solids.
  2. Filter — the salt you want is the residue on the paper.
  3. Wash the residue with distilled water — this rinses away the soluble by-product.
  4. Dry — filter paper, a warm oven, or leave in a warm place. No direct heating with a Bunsen (2022 rejected it).

Wrong-method answers are the biggest single loss on salt questions. Describing the excess-base method for a precipitation scored 1 of 4 in 2025 and 1 of 3 in 2023. And it is the residue that is washed and dried — 2023's marker: "the salt you want is the residue", not the filtrate. If the product is insoluble, there is no crystallisation step anywhere.

subsections.heading: Choosing the method — the ten-second decision
subsections.html:
every salt question · 2021 Q5a

Check whether the salt you want is soluble, then check whether its partner reactant is soluble — that picks the method.

  1. Is the target salt insoluble? (check the rules) → Method 3: mix solutions, filter, wash the residue, dry.
  2. Soluble, and the partner is an insoluble solid (metal, oxide or carbonate)? → Method 1: excess solid, filter, crystallise.
  3. Soluble, and both reactants soluble (Na/K/NH₄ salt from acid + alkali)? → Method 2: titrate, then crystallise.

2021's find-the-mistake question was this decision in disguise: nitric acid can't make a sulfate; magnesium carbonate is insoluble so there is no "solution of magnesium carbonate"; and boiling to dryness wrecks the hydrated crystals.

The one decision everything follows from

Look up the solubility first. Insoluble target → precipitate, filter, wash the residue, dry. Soluble target → make a solution of just salt + water, then heat only to the crystallisation point — never to dryness.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the soluble-salt method demand an excess of the solid, when excess sounds wasteful — and how does the excess then leave the story?
questions.answerHtml:
The excess guarantees that all the acid has reacted. If any acid survived, it would stay dissolved in the filtrate and end up concentrated in your crystals — the product would be contaminated with acid you cannot see.

An excess of an insoluble solid is easily removed: filter it off. That is the whole design of the method — the impurity you deliberately created is the one impurity filtering can remove. (2024's one-marker: "so that all the nitric acid reacts". "To make more salt" misses the point entirely.)

questions.promptHtml: Heating the filtrate "until crystals just start to form" and then stopping feels unfinished. Why is stopping there exactly right, and what goes wrong for a hydrated salt if you keep heating to dryness?
questions.answerHtml:
Stopping at the crystallisation point leaves a hot saturated solution. As it cools, solubility falls and the salt comes out of solution slowly as well-formed crystals, leaving the remaining impurities behind in the liquid you then pour off.

Boiling to dryness does the opposite: everything in the solution — impurities included — is baked onto the dish, and for a hydrated salt the heat also drives off the water of crystallisation, so you get a powdery anhydrous solid instead of the hydrated crystals the question asked for. That is why every scheme caps a heated-to-dryness answer at 1 mark.

questions.promptHtml: In the precipitation method, what exactly does washing the residue with distilled water remove — and why does washing the filtrate instead earn the 2023 marker's special scorn?
questions.answerHtml:
The precipitate on the filter paper is soaked in the reaction mixture, which contains the soluble by-product (sodium nitrate, in the PbBr₂ preparation) and any unreacted solutions. A rinse of distilled water dissolves those away; the insoluble product itself cannot dissolve, so it stays put.

The filtrate is the liquid that passed through: by-product solution. Washing it is washing the waste. The confusion comes from Method 1, where the filtrate is the valuable part — which is exactly why the papers keep asking both: they are testing whether you know which side of the filter paper your product is on. Insoluble product → residue; soluble product → filtrate.

questions.promptHtml: Silver chloride is insoluble. A student proposes making it by adding excess silver to hydrochloric acid, then filtering. Give two separate reasons the plan fails, and the correct recipe.
questions.answerHtml:
Reason 1 — wrong method for the product: even if the reaction worked, an insoluble product forms wherever it is made — mixed in with the excess solid — and filtering would collect both together. The excess-solid method only works when the product stays dissolved.

Reason 2 — the reaction doesn't happen: silver is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids at all.

Correct recipe: precipitation from two soluble starting compounds — silver nitrate solution + sodium chloride solution (nitrates always soluble, sodium salts always soluble) → AgCl precipitates → filter, wash the residue, dry.

questions.promptHtml: Copper sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. State what you would SEE, name both products, and explain which preparation method this reaction belongs to.
questions.answerHtml:
Seen: a blue precipitate/solid forms (and the blue solution fades). Not "crystals", not "fizzing" — nothing here makes a gas, and 2023 rejected fizzing outright.

Products: copper(II) hydroxide (the blue precipitate — hydroxides are insoluble except Na/K) and sodium sulfate (stays dissolved — sodium salts always soluble).

Method: precipitation (Method 3): filter, wash the residue, dry gently. The question told you a precipitate formed; answers describing excess-base-and-crystallise were the standard way to lose all three method marks.

questions.promptHtml: Aluminium sulfate is used by gardeners to acidify soil: Al₂(SO₄)₃(s) + 6H₂O(l) → 2Al(OH)₃(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq). Using only the state symbols, explain why the products make the soil acidic and not neutral.
questions.answerHtml:
Both an acid and a base are produced — but their states differ. Al(OH)₃ is (s): solid, insoluble, so its OH⁻ ions are locked away and never enter the soil water. H₂SO₄ is (aq): dissolved, so its H⁺ ions are released into solution.

Free H⁺ with no free OH⁻ to cancel it → the soil water is acidic. The general lesson (it earned both marks in 2021): ions only count when they are in solution — (s) means present but unavailable.

questions.promptHtml: Why is universal indicator a poor choice for a titration, when it tells you more about pH than methyl orange does?
questions.answerHtml:
A titration needs to spot one moment: the exact drop where the alkali is neutralised. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein change sharply between just two colours, so that drop is obvious.

Universal indicator changes gradually through red, orange, yellow, green, blue — there is no single clear point to stop at. More information about pH is useless if you can't see the end point. (2022 Edexcel: "no clear end point / colour change is gradual".)

questions.promptHtml: Dry hydrogen chloride gas dissolved in an organic solvent does not change the colour of blue litmus. The same gas dissolved in water turns it red. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
An acid is a source of H⁺ ions in aqueous solution. HCl is a covalent molecule. In water it forms H⁺ ions (and Cl⁻ ions), so the solution is acidic and litmus turns red.

In the organic solvent the HCl molecules stay as molecules — no H⁺ ions form — so there is nothing to change the indicator, and the litmus stays blue. Acidity is about the H⁺ ions, not just the formula. (2024 Edexcel 2C Q7, four marks.)

modules.title: Chemical Calculations
modules.standfirst: The single biggest source of marks on these papers — moles, formulae from experiments, gas volumes, concentrations and yields, threaded through almost every question. One relationship (n = mass ÷ Mr) carries nearly all of it, and every calculation below is laid out as numbered steps you can copy.

The mark schemes are unusually blunt about how these marks die:

"Division by atomic numbers or other inappropriate numbers scores 0/3. Fractions upside down scores 0/3." — 2021, empirical formula. Edexcel's 2022 scheme said the same.

"Did not read the question so did not leave the final answer to 2 sf. Large numbers should always be left in standard form." — 2024.

And the standing rule on every front page: correct answer without working scores full marks, but a wrong answer without working scores zero — show the moles step and the error-carried-forward rules protect you.
