subsections.html: Every calculation on these papers is the same journey: what you're given → moles → whatever was asked (grams of something else, a volume of gas, a concentration, a formula, a yield). The mole is the bridge in the middle; the balanced equation is the exchange rate. Each section below ends in a worked example laid out step by step — copy the layout in the exam.

subsections.heading: Relative formula mass, Mr
subsections.html:
Spec 1.26 · 2024 Q8 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q4(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q6(a)

Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses of every atom in the formula.

Take the Ar values from the periodic table — the larger number in each box, not the atomic number.

Worked example — Mr of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄

  1. Count every atom (the bracket doubles everything inside): N 2, H 8, S 1, O 4.
  2. Multiply each by its Ar: N 2 × 14 = 28; H 8 × 1 = 8; S 1 × 32 = 32; O 4 × 16 = 64.
  3. Add: 28 + 8 + 32 + 64 = 132.

More: Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. Pb(NO₃)₂ = 207 + 2 × (14 + 48) = 331. Mr has no units.

subsections.heading: The mole — n = mass ÷ Mr
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27, 1.28 · every paper · 2024 Q10a

One mole of any substance has a mass equal to its Mr in grams, so dividing a mass by Mr gives the number of moles.

moles = mass ÷ Mr
moles in mol · mass in grams (g) · Mr from the periodic table

Rearranged: mass = moles × Mr. A mole is a counted amount: 6.0 × 10²³ particles. So number of particles = moles × 6.0 × 10²³ (the value is given in the question).

Worked example — how many molecules in 0.081 g of hydrogen? (2024)

  1. Mr of H₂ = 2 × 1 = 2.
  2. Moles = 0.081 ÷ 2 = 0.0405 mol.
  3. Molecules = 0.0405 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 2.43 × 10²².
  4. Round as asked (2 sf) and keep standard form: 2.4 × 10²².

Tonnes to grams: × 10⁶. Kilograms to grams: × 1000. Convert before dividing by Mr.

subsections.heading: Reacting masses — using the equation
subsections.html:
Spec 1.29 · 2021 Q6 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q7(c) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(b)

The big numbers in a balanced equation are mole ratios, so you convert to moles, use the ratio, then convert back.

  1. Moles of what you know = mass ÷ Mr.
  2. Use the ratio from the balanced equation to get moles of what you want.
  3. Convert to what was asked: mass = moles × Mr.

Worked example — mass of CO₂ from 10.5 g of NaHCO₃ (2021)

2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂  ·  Mr: NaHCO₃ = 84, CO₂ = 44

  1. Moles of NaHCO₃ = 10.5 ÷ 84 = 0.125 mol.
  2. Ratio 2NaHCO₃ : 1CO₂, so moles of CO₂ = 0.125 ÷ 2 = 0.0625 mol.
  3. Mass of CO₂ = 0.0625 × 44 = 2.75 g.

Worked example — mass of Cl₂ to make 26.7 g of AlCl₃ (2023 Edexcel)

2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃  ·  Mr: AlCl₃ = 133.5, Cl₂ = 71

  1. Moles of AlCl₃ = 26.7 ÷ 133.5 = 0.200 mol.
  2. Ratio 3Cl₂ : 2AlCl₃, so moles of Cl₂ = 0.200 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.300 mol.
  3. Mass of Cl₂ = 0.300 × 71 = 21.3 g.

subsections.heading: Which reactant is in excess?
subsections.html:
Spec 1.29 · 2025 Q4c · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q10(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(a)

Compare the moles you need with the moles you have — never compare masses.

  1. Moles of each reactant you have.
  2. Use the ratio to find how many moles of one would be needed to react with all of the other.
  3. Compare: if you need more than you have, that reactant runs out (it is limiting); the other is in excess.

Worked example — 1.5 g of Mg with 0.1 mol of HCl (2025)

Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂  ·  Ar: Mg = 24

  1. Moles of Mg = 1.5 ÷ 24 = 0.0625 mol.
  2. Acid needed = 2 × 0.0625 = 0.125 mol.
  3. Compare: only 0.1 mol of acid is there, so the acid runs out and magnesium is in excess.

How much is left over? (2023 January Edexcel) 0.0250 mol of HNO₃ reacts with 0.0250 ÷ 2 = 0.0125 mol of Mg = 0.0125 × 24 = 0.30 g. Started with 0.75 g, so 0.45 g is left.

subsections.heading: Gas volumes — 24 dm³ per mole
subsections.html:
Spec 1.35C · 2022 Q8 · 2023 Q6 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(c)

One mole of any gas takes up 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at room temperature and pressure.

volume = moles × 24 (dm³)  or  volume = moles × 24 000 (cm³)
and back again: moles = volume ÷ 24 (dm³) or volume ÷ 24 000 (cm³)

Check the unit on the answer line before you calculate. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

Worked example — SO₂ from 6.4 tonnes of sulfur (2022 and 2023)

S + O₂ → SO₂  ·  Ar: S = 32

  1. Grams: 6.4 tonnes = 6.4 × 10⁶ g.
  2. Moles of S = 6.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵ mol.
  3. Ratio 1 : 1, so 2.0 × 10⁵ mol of SO₂.
  4. Volume = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 24 = 4 800 000 dm³.
  5. Standard form: 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³ — the third mark was just for this.

subsections.heading: Concentration of a solution — mol/dm³
subsections.html:
Spec 1.34C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(c)

Concentration is the number of moles dissolved in each dm³ of solution.

concentration = moles ÷ volume
concentration in mol/dm³ · moles in mol · volume in dm³

Rearranged: moles = concentration × volume. Volumes are usually given in cm³, so divide by 1000 first: 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³.

Worked example — moles of NaBr in 25.0 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ solution (2024 Edexcel)

  1. Volume in dm³ = 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³.
  2. Moles = 2.0 × 0.0250 = 0.050 mol.

Then carry on as a reacting-mass question: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2NaBr → PbBr₂ + 2NaNO₃, so PbBr₂ = 0.050 ÷ 2 = 0.025 mol → 0.025 × 367 = 9.175 g.

Worked example — concentration of 5.85 g of NaCl in 500 cm³

  1. Moles = 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol.
  2. Volume = 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.500 dm³.
  3. Concentration = 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/dm³.

subsections.heading: Titration calculations
subsections.html:
Spec 1.34C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q4(f) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q2(c)

Use the solution whose volume and concentration you both know to find moles, then the ratio, then divide by the other volume.

  1. Moles of the known solution = concentration × (volume ÷ 1000).
  2. Ratio from the balanced equation → moles of the unknown.
  3. Concentration of the unknown = moles ÷ (its volume ÷ 1000).

Worked example — barium hydroxide (2022 Edexcel)

25.0 cm³ of barium hydroxide is neutralised by 21.5 cm³ of 0.600 mol/dm³ nitric acid.
2HNO₃ + Ba(OH)₂ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O

  1. Moles of HNO₃ = 0.600 × (21.5 ÷ 1000) = 0.0129 mol.
  2. Ratio 2HNO₃ : 1Ba(OH)₂, so Ba(OH)₂ = 0.0129 ÷ 2 = 0.00645 mol.
  3. Concentration = 0.00645 ÷ (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.258 mol/dm³.

The ratio step is where the marks go. Sulfuric acid is the other trap: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH, so moles of KOH = 2 × moles of acid (2023 Edexcel).

subsections.heading: Percentage yield
subsections.html:
Spec 1.30 · 2025 Q7b

Percentage yield compares the mass you actually made with the most you could have made.

% yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100
actual mass = what you weighed · theoretical mass = from a reacting-mass calculation

Worked example — lead(II) bromide (2025)

Expected: 0.150 mol of PbBr₂ (Mr 367). Obtained: 49.6 g.

  1. Theoretical mass = 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g.
  2. Divide actual by theoretical = 49.6 ÷ 55.05 = 0.901.
  3. × 100 = 90.1%.

The scheme rejected 49.6 ÷ 0.150 — a mass divided by moles means nothing. Both numbers must be masses.

Yield is always below 100% in practice: some product stays dissolved, is left on filter paper, or is lost in transfer; the reaction may not finish.

subsections.heading: Empirical formula from masses or percentages
subsections.html:
Spec 1.32, 1.33 · 2021 Q10a · 2025 Q10 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(a) · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, found by turning each mass into moles of atoms.

  1. Divide each element's mass (or %) by its Ar — the relative atomic mass, never the atomic number, and never upside down.
  2. Divide every answer by the smallest one.
  3. If a number isn't close to whole, multiply them all up: ×2 for 1.5, ×3 for 1.33 or 1.67, ×4 for 1.25.
  4. Write the formula from the whole-number ratio.

Worked example — lead oxide, 90.7% Pb and 9.3% O (2025)

StepPbO
1. ÷ Ar90.7 ÷ 207 = 0.4389.3 ÷ 16 = 0.581
2. ÷ smallest (0.438)11.33
3. × 334

Formula: Pb₃O₄. Rounding 1.33 down to 1 would give PbO — wrong.

Worked example — C 40.0%, H 6.7%, O 53.3% (2022 Edexcel)

  1. ÷ Ar: C 40.0 ÷ 12 = 3.33; H 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; O 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33.
  2. ÷ smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2.01, O 1.
  3. Formula: CH₂O.

2021's scheme: "Division by atomic numbers or other inappropriate numbers scores 0/3. Fractions upside down scores 0/3." If your first step is % ÷ Ar, you are safe; anything else scores nothing at all.

subsections.heading: Molecular formula
subsections.html:
Spec 1.32, 1.33 · 2022 Q9 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)

The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found by comparing the Mr with the empirical mass.

  1. Work out the mass of the empirical formula.
  2. Divide the Mr you're given by it — you get a whole number.
  3. Multiply every number in the empirical formula by that.

Worked example — empirical formula C₂H₄Cl, Mr = 127 (2022)

  1. Empirical mass = (2 × 12) + (4 × 1) + 35.5 = 63.5.
  2. 127 ÷ 63.5 = 2.
  3. Molecular formula = C₄H₈Cl₂.

Going the other way (2024 Edexcel): caffeine C₈H₁₀N₄O₂ — every number divides by 2 → empirical formula C₄H₅N₂O.

subsections.heading: Formula of a metal oxide by experiment
subsections.html:
Spec 1.31, 1.36 (practical) · 2024 Q5b, Q7

Weigh the metal and the oxide; the difference is the oxygen, and the two masses give the formula.

By combustion (magnesium oxide):

  1. Weigh an empty crucible and lid, then with the magnesium ribbon inside.
  2. Heat strongly, lifting the lid now and then to let oxygen in — but not so far that white MgO smoke escapes.
  3. Cool and weigh. Reheat and reweigh until the mass is constant — that shows all the magnesium has reacted.
  4. Mass gained = mass of oxygen.

By reduction (copper(II) oxide): heat the oxide in a stream of hydrogen or methane; the mass falls as oxygen is removed, leaving copper. Heat to constant mass.

Worked example — copper oxide reduced

3.18 g of copper oxide leaves 2.54 g of copper. Ar: Cu = 63.5, O = 16.

  1. Mass of oxygen = 3.18 − 2.54 = 0.64 g.
  2. Moles: Cu 2.54 ÷ 63.5 = 0.040; O 0.64 ÷ 16 = 0.040.
  3. Ratio 1 : 1 → CuO.

subsections.heading: Water of crystallisation — finding x
subsections.html:
Spec 1.31 · 2021 Q7 · 2022 Q6 · 2025 Q2b · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q9(b)

Heat the hydrated salt until all the water has gone; the mass lost is the water, and comparing moles of water with moles of salt gives x.

  1. Heat to constant mass — reheat and reweigh until the mass stops changing, so all the water is removed.
  2. Mass of anhydrous salt = mass after heating − mass of the empty container.
  3. Mass of water = mass before heating − mass after heating.
  4. Moles of each: salt ÷ its Mr; water ÷ 18.
  5. x = moles of water ÷ moles of salt.

Worked example — Na₂CO₃·xH₂O (2022)

Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ left = 3.18 g. Water lost = 3.78 g. Mr: Na₂CO₃ = 106, H₂O = 18.

  1. Moles of Na₂CO₃ = 3.18 ÷ 106 = 0.0300 mol.
  2. Moles of H₂O = 3.78 ÷ 18 = 0.210 mol.
  3. x = 0.210 ÷ 0.0300 = 7 → Na₂CO₃·7H₂O.

Every year's follow-up: why might x come out too low? — not heated for long enough, so not all the water was removed. How to improve? — heat to constant mass. To check the liquid given off is water: it boils at exactly 100 °C, or turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate from white to blue.

subsections.heading: Ar from isotopes, and percentage by mass
subsections.html:
Spec 1.17 · 2023 Q9a · 2023 Q6c · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q10(c)

Both are "weighted" sums: Ar weights each isotope by its abundance; percentage by mass takes one element's share of the Mr.

Ar = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) ÷ 100
Copper: (63 × 69.5 + 65 × 30.5) ÷ 100 = 63.61 → 63.6. Module 1 has the full method.

Worked example — % of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (2022 Edexcel)

  1. Mr = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80.
  2. Mass of nitrogen in the formula = 2 × 14 = 28. Count every N atom.
  3. % N = 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%.

Same method for (NH₄)₂SO₄: 28 ÷ 132 × 100 = 21.2% — the 2 outside the bracket doubles the N.

The one journey every question takes

given → moles → (ratio) → moles → answer. If you are stuck, calculate moles of whatever you were given — it is almost always the first mark.

Never rely on memorising these for the exam — the periodic table is given — but knowing the common ones makes checking your own arithmetic fast.

questions.promptHtml: Why does one mole of CO₂ (44 g) and one mole of H₂ (2 g) — wildly different masses — occupy exactly the same volume as gases at room temperature and pressure?
questions.answerHtml:
Because in a gas the particles are so far apart that the volume is almost entirely empty space — the size and mass of the individual molecules barely matter. What sets the volume is the number of particles (and the temperature and pressure), and one mole of anything is the same number of particles: 6.0 × 10²³.

That is the whole reason the molar volume shortcut works: equal moles of any gas → equal volumes → 24 dm³ per mole at rtp. It works for gases only; solids and liquids have their particles touching, so their volumes depend on what they are.

questions.promptHtml: The empirical formula method says "divide the percentage by the Ar". What is that step actually calculating, and why does dividing by the atomic number score zero?
questions.answerHtml:
It converts a mass ratio into a mole ratio — % of mass ÷ mass-per-mole = relative number of moles of atoms. In 100 g of the lead oxide, 90.7 g ÷ 207 g/mol = 0.438 mol of lead atoms. A formula is a ratio of atoms counted, not of grams, so you must get to moles before comparing.

The atomic number is the count of protons — nothing to do with mass. Dividing by it produces a meaningless number, which is why the scheme gives 0/3 rather than just losing one mark: the method itself is wrong, not the arithmetic.

questions.promptHtml: In the water-of-crystallisation practical, the value of x comes out too low even though every weighing was accurate. What happened, how would you detect it, and how do you fix it?
questions.answerHtml:
What happened: the crystals were not heated for long enough, so not all the water of crystallisation was driven off. Some water is still in the "anhydrous" mass, making the salt look heavier and the water lighter — the ratio of water to salt shrinks, so x shrinks.

Detection and fix are the same idea: heat again, cool, reweigh — and repeat until the mass no longer changes. Constant mass is the proof that all the water is gone; a mass still falling means there was more water to lose.

The trap in reverse: if the question says x came out too HIGH, look for the salt decomposing or spitting out of the crucible — mass lost that wasn't water.

questions.promptHtml: A question gives you 1.5 g of magnesium and 0.1 mol of hydrochloric acid, and asks you to "show that the magnesium is in excess" (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂). Why can't you just compare 1.5 g with the acid's mass — and what is the correct comparison?
questions.answerHtml:
Grams of different substances can't be compared — a gram of magnesium contains a different number of particles from a gram of HCl, and the equation works in particles, not grams.

The correct route: 1.5 ÷ 24 = 0.0625 mol Mg. The ratio is 1 : 2, so reacting all of it needs 2 × 0.0625 = 0.125 mol of acid. Only 0.1 mol is available — the acid runs out first, so the magnesium is in excess.

The template for every excess/"show that" question: moles of both → scale one by the ratio → compare needed with available, in moles.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the percentage yield of a real preparation always less than 100% — and why does the exam's yield formula use two masses rather than two amounts in moles?
questions.answerHtml:
Less than 100%: product is physically lost at every step — some stays dissolved in the solution after crystallisation, some is left on the filter paper or washed away, and the reaction may not go to completion. (In 2025's PbBr₂ preparation, ~10% went missing, largely in filtering and washing.)

Why masses: actual ÷ theoretical only makes sense when both are the same kind of quantity. You weigh the actual product, so the theoretical value must be converted all the way to a mass (moles expected × Mr) before dividing. The 2025 scheme specifically rejected 49.6 ÷ 0.150 — a mass divided by moles is a nonsense number.

questions.promptHtml: Chlorine's Ar is 35.5 — not a whole number, though every single chlorine atom has a whole-number mass. Explain, and state what a 75% ³⁵Cl / 25% ³⁷Cl mixture gives.
questions.answerHtml:
Ar is a weighted average over the isotopes as they occur naturally, not the mass of any one atom. Individual atoms are ³⁵Cl or ³⁷Cl; the average of a big natural sample sits in between, pulled towards the more abundant one.

(35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

Sanity check that catches silly errors: the answer must lie between the isotope masses, nearer the more abundant isotope. 2023's copper answer (63.6, close to 63 at 69.5%) passes exactly that check.

questions.promptHtml: 2023 gave a solid metal carbonate XCO₃ that decomposed to give 0.05 mol of CO₂ from 7.40 g. Walk the route from those two numbers to the identity of X, and say where the periodic table comes in.
questions.answerHtml:
Three steps, each one mark:

  1. Ratio: XCO₃ → XO + CO₂ is 1 : 1, so moles of XCO₃ = moles of CO₂ = 0.05.
  2. Mr from the definition of moles: Mr = mass ÷ n = 7.40 ÷ 0.05 = 148.
  3. Subtract the known part: CO₃ contributes 60, so Ar(X) = 148 − 60 = 88. The periodic table's Group 2 metal with Ar 88 is strontium.

This is the pattern for every identify-the-element question: get moles, get Mr, take away what you know, look up what remains — using the question's own clue (a Group 2 metal) to pick the match.

questions.promptHtml: In a titration, 0.0027 mol of sulfuric acid neutralises 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide. A student writes "concentration = 0.0027 ÷ 25.0 = 0.000108 mol/dm³". Find both mistakes.
questions.answerHtml:
Mistake 1 — the ratio. H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Each acid molecule gives two H⁺, so it neutralises two KOH. Moles of KOH = 2 × 0.0027 = 0.0054 mol.

Mistake 2 — the units. Concentration is per dm³, so the volume must be 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³.

Correct: 0.0054 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.216 mol/dm³ (2023 Edexcel 2C Q4). A sanity check helps: bench solutions are usually between 0.1 and 2 mol/dm³ — an answer of 0.000108 should look wrong straight away.

questions.promptHtml:
Sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes on heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂

(a) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced by completely decomposing 10.5 g of NaHCO₃. [Mr of NaHCO₃ = 84; Mr of CO₂ = 44] (2)
(b) Calculate the volume of this carbon dioxide at rtp, in cm³. [1 mol of gas = 24,000 cm³ at rtp] (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) n(NaHCO₃) = 10.5 ÷ 84 = 0.125 mol → ratio 2 : 1 → n(CO₂) = 0.0625 mol 1; mass = 0.0625 × 44 = 2.75 g 1

(b) n(CO₂) = 0.0625 mol 1; volume = 0.0625 × 24,000 = 1500 cm³ 1 — error carried forward from (a) is allowed if the working is shown

markScheme.point: (b) n(CO₂) = 0.0625 mol ; volume = 0.0625 × 24,000 = 1500 cm³ — error carried forward from (a) is allowed if the working is shown

questions.promptHtml:
Hydrated iron(II) sulfate is FeSO₄·xH₂O. A sample is heated to constant mass in a tube: mass of tube 11.96 g, tube + crystals 17.56 g, tube + contents after heating 15.76 g.

(a) State why the crystals are heated to constant mass. (1)
(b) Calculate x, to the nearest whole number. [Mr of FeSO₄ = 152; Mr of H₂O = 18] (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) To make sure all the water (of crystallisation) has been removed 1

(b) mass FeSO₄ = 15.76 − 11.96 = 3.80 g and mass H₂O = 17.56 − 15.76 = 1.80 g → n(FeSO₄) = 3.80 ÷ 152 = 0.025 1; n(H₂O) = 1.80 ÷ 18 = 0.10 1; x = 0.10 ÷ 0.025 = 4 1

markScheme.point: (a) To make sure all the water (of crystallisation) has been removed

questions.promptHtml: A compound of lead and oxygen is 90.7% lead and 9.3% oxygen by mass. Show by calculation that its empirical formula is Pb₃O₄. [Ar: Pb = 207, O = 16] (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Pb: 90.7 ÷ 207 = 0.438 1; O: 9.3 ÷ 16 = 0.581 1; divide by the smaller: 1 : 1.33 1; multiply up: × 3 → 3 : 4 → Pb₃O₄ 1

Divide by Ar, never the atomic number; never round 1.33 down to 1 — a ratio near a third or a quarter is the question telling you to multiply up.

markScheme.point: Pb: 90.7 ÷ 207 = 0.438 ; O: 9.3 ÷ 16 = 0.581 ; divide by the smaller: 1 : 1.33 ; multiply up: × 3 → 3 : 4 → Pb₃O₄

questions.promptHtml: A mass of 6.4 tonnes of sulfur is burned: S + O₂ → SO₂. Calculate the maximum volume, in dm³, of sulfur dioxide produced at rtp. Give your answer in standard form. [Ar of S = 32; molar volume = 24 dm³ at rtp; 1 tonne = 10⁶ g] (3)
questions.answerHtml:
n(S) = 6.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵ mol 1; ratio 1 : 1, volume = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 24 = 4,800,000 dm³ 1; in standard form: 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³ 1

The last mark is only for the standard form — 4 800 000 written out scored 2 of 3. This exact question has appeared on two papers.

markScheme.point: n(S) = 6.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵ mol ; ratio 1 : 1, volume = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 24 = 4,800,000 dm³ ; in standard form: 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³

questions.promptHtml:
A compound G is 37.8% carbon, 6.3% hydrogen and 55.9% chlorine by mass, and has Mr = 127.

(a) Show that the empirical formula of G is C₂H₄Cl. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5] (3)
(b) Determine the molecular formula of G. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 37.8 ÷ 12 = 3.15; 6.3 ÷ 1 = 6.3; 55.9 ÷ 35.5 = 1.57 1 1; divide by smallest → 2 : 4 : 1 → C₂H₄Cl 1

(b) empirical mass of C₂H₄Cl = 63.5; 127 ÷ 63.5 = 2 1; molecular formula = C₄H₈Cl₂ 1

markScheme.point: (b) empirical mass of C₂H₄Cl = 63.5; 127 ÷ 63.5 = 2 ; molecular formula = C₄H₈Cl₂

questions.promptHtml: A preparation of lead(II) bromide is expected to produce 0.150 mol of PbBr₂. The actual mass obtained is 49.6 g. Show that the percentage yield is about 90%. [Mr of PbBr₂ = 367] (2)
questions.answerHtml:
Theoretical mass = 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g 1; % yield = 49.6 ÷ 55.05 × 100 = 90.1% 1

Convert the expected moles to a mass first — the scheme rejected 49.6 ÷ 0.150. Actual mass over theoretical mass, always.

questions.promptHtml: The reaction of zinc with dilute nitric acid produces 0.081 g of hydrogen gas. One mole of hydrogen gas contains 6.0 × 10²³ molecules. Calculate the number of molecules of hydrogen produced. Give your answer to two significant figures. [Mr of H₂ = 2] (3)
questions.answerHtml:
n(H₂) = 0.081 ÷ 2 = 0.0405 mol 1; molecules = 0.0405 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 2.43 × 10²² 1; to 2 sf: 2.4 × 10²² 1

Both instructions carry marks: standard form for the big number, and the stated 2 sf. Read the question twice — that is where 2024's marks went.

questions.promptHtml: Calculate the relative formula mass of: (a) Ca(OH)₂; (b) (NH₄)₂SO₄; (c) CuSO₄·5H₂O. [Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1, N = 14, S = 32, Cu = 63.5] (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74 1

(b) 2 × (14 + 4) + 32 + 64 = 132 1

(c) 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 5 × 18 = 249.5 1

questions.promptHtml: Aluminium chloride is made by this reaction: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. Calculate the mass of chlorine needed to make 26.7 g of aluminium chloride. [Mr: AlCl₃ = 133.5, Cl₂ = 71] (3)
questions.answerHtml: n(AlCl₃) = 26.7 ÷ 133.5 = 0.200 mol 1; n(Cl₂) = 0.200 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.300 mol 1; mass = 0.300 × 71 = 21.3 g 1

questions.promptHtml:
25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 18.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid.

H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution in mol/dm³. (3)
questions.answerHtml: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.150 × 18.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.00270 mol 1; n(KOH) = 0.00270 × 2 = 0.00540 mol 1; concentration = 0.00540 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.216 mol/dm³ 1

questions.promptHtml: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration of the solution in mol/dm³. [Mr of NaOH = 40] (2)
questions.answerHtml: n(NaOH) = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.10 mol 1; concentration = 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³ 1

markScheme.point: n(NaOH) = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.10 mol ; concentration = 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³

questions.promptHtml: 1.3 g of zinc is added to a solution containing 0.0036 mol of hydrochloric acid. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Show that the zinc is in excess. [Ar of Zn = 65] (2)
questions.answerHtml: n(Zn) = 1.3 ÷ 65 = 0.020 mol 1; 0.0036 mol of HCl reacts with only 0.0036 ÷ 2 = 0.0018 mol of Zn, which is less than 0.020, so zinc is in excess 1

markScheme.point: n(Zn) = 1.3 ÷ 65 = 0.020 mol ; 0.0036 mol of HCl reacts with only 0.0036 ÷ 2 = 0.0018 mol of Zn, which is less than 0.020, so zinc is in excess

questions.promptHtml:
An organic compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass.

(a) Show that its empirical formula is CH₂O. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16] (3)
(b) Its relative molecular mass is 60. Find its molecular formula. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 40.0 ÷ 12 = 3.33; 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33 1; divide by the smallest 1; ratio 1 : 2 : 1 → CH₂O 1

(b) Empirical mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30 1; 60 ÷ 30 = 2 → C₂H₄O₂ 1

markScheme.point: (b) Empirical mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30 ; 60 ÷ 30 = 2 → C₂H₄O₂

questions.promptHtml: 0.14 g of lithium reacts completely with water: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced, in cm³, at rtp. [Ar of Li = 7; molar volume = 24 000 cm³ at rtp] (3)
questions.answerHtml: n(Li) = 0.14 ÷ 7 = 0.020 mol 1; n(H₂) = 0.020 ÷ 2 = 0.010 mol 1; volume = 0.010 × 24 000 = 240 cm³ 1

questions.promptHtml:
Crystals of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, are heated to constant mass. The anhydrous barium chloride left has a mass of 5.20 g. The water lost has a mass of 0.90 g.

(a) Explain why the crystals are heated to constant mass. (1)
(b) Calculate the value of x. [Mr: BaCl₂ = 208, H₂O = 18] (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) To make sure all the water is given off 1

(b) n(BaCl₂) = 5.20 ÷ 208 = 0.025 mol 1; n(H₂O) = 0.90 ÷ 18 = 0.050 mol 1; x = 0.050 ÷ 0.025 = 2 1

From 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12.

markScheme.point: (a) To make sure all the water is given off

modules.title: Solubility
modules.standfirst: A small topic — four spec points — that has grown into a ten-mark banker: plot the curve, read the crossing, scale to 100 g, subtract for the crystals. Every mark is graph craft and one definition.

subsections.html: Solubility is a number with strict units: how many grams of solute saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature. The whole topic is that sentence plus a graph of how the number changes with temperature. Nearly every mark is either a definition, a reading off the graph, or one line of arithmetic.

subsections.heading: The four words, exactly
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4 · 2024 Q2

A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution; the solution is saturated when no more solute will dissolve at that temperature.

  • The solute is the substance that dissolves — in this topic, a solid such as potassium nitrate.
  • The solvent is the liquid it dissolves in — almost always water.
  • The solution is the mixture they make together.
  • A saturated solution is one in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature. Some undissolved solid is usually left at the bottom — that is how you know it is saturated.

✗ "A saturated solution is full up." — No temperature, no second mark.
✗ "A saturated solution has lots of solute in it." — "Lots" is not a definition.
✓ "A solution in which no more solute will dissolve at that temperature."

The phrase "at that temperature" carries the mark. A solution saturated at 70 °C is unsaturated at 80 °C, because hot water can hold more.

subsections.heading: What changes solubility — and what only speeds up dissolving
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4, 1.5C · 2024 Q2(a)

Temperature changes how much solid can dissolve; stirring and crushing only change how fast it dissolves.

Two different questions hide in the word "dissolving":

QuestionWhat affects itWhat does not
How much dissolves (solubility)Temperature. For most solids, hotter water dissolves moreStirring, crushing, shaking
How fast it dissolvesStirring, crushing into smaller pieces, warming—

The 2024 scheme wanted temperature. It also allowed the amount of solvent, because more water dissolves more solid in total. It ignored stirring. Stirring gets you to the same final amount sooner — it never raises the amount.

✗ "Stirring increases the solubility."
✓ "Temperature affects solubility. Stirring only makes the solid dissolve faster."

subsections.heading: Solubility in g per 100 g of solvent
subsections.html:
Spec 1.5C · 2024 Q2(d)(ii) · 2025 Q5(c)

Solubility is the mass of solute, in grams, that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to make a saturated solution at a stated temperature.

Three parts, and each one matters:

  1. A mass of solute in grams.
  2. Per 100 g of solvent — not per 100 g of solution, and not per whatever volume you happened to use.
  3. At a stated temperature, because the value changes with temperature.
Solubility from an experimentsolubility = (mass of solute ÷ mass of water) × 100solubility in g per 100 g of water · both masses in g · 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g

Water has a density of 1 g per cm³, so 25 cm³ of water is 25 g of water. That lets the papers swap between cm³ and g of water without comment. It works for water only.

equations.name: Solubility from an experiment
equations.formula: solubility = (mass of solute ÷ mass of water) × 100

subsections.heading: Reading a solubility curve
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6C · 2022 Q4 · 2023 Q12 · 2025 Q5

Every point on a solubility curve is a saturated solution: at this temperature, 100 g of water holds exactly this much.

The x-axis is temperature in °C. The y-axis is solubility in g per 100 g of water. For most solids the curve rises — hotter water dissolves more. To read a value:

  1. Check the label: you are on the curve the question names.
  2. Rule a line up from the temperature to the curve.
  3. Rule a line across to the y-axis and read the value.
  4. Leave both lines on the graph. They are the "working shown" mark.

Where a solution sits compared with the curve tells you its state. On the curve: saturated. Below it: unsaturated — more could still dissolve at that temperature.

2023's commentary: "Several read off the WRONG curve." Two curves are printed so you can grab the wrong one under time pressure. Put your finger on the label before you rule a line.

subsections.heading: Where two curves cross
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6C · 2022 Q4(i) · 2023 Q12(a) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q4(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(a)(i)

Two substances have the same solubility at the temperature where their curves cross.

  1. Find the crossing point.
  2. Rule a vertical line straight down from it to the temperature axis.
  3. Read the temperature and give the unit, °C.

The crossing answer — two marks

1. Working shown on the graph — the vertical line from the crossing 1

2. The temperature read correctly, e.g. 56 °C 1

That is the exact split in 2023 Q12(a) and in 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(a)(i). The answer alone gets one mark.

Below the crossing one substance is more soluble. Above it the other one is. If a question asks "which is more soluble at 30 °C?", read both curves at 30 °C and compare — do not assume the steeper curve wins everywhere.

subsections.heading: Scaling to a different mass of water
subsections.html:
Spec 1.5C · 2022 Q4(ii) · 2025 Q5(c) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q4(c)

The mass that dissolves is in direct proportion to the mass of water, so you scale by multiplying or dividing.

Double the water, double the solid. So you only need a scale factor: new mass of water ÷ 100, or the reverse to get back to per 100 g.

Worked example 1 — more water (2022 Q4)

Solubility of B at 60 °C = 124 g per 100 g of water.

Scale factor for 250 g of water = 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5

Mass dissolving = 124 × 2.5 = 310 g

Worked example 2 — data per 25 cm³ (2024 Edexcel 2C Q4 / school 2025 Q5)

Reading from the graph at 30 °C: about 24 g dissolves in 25 cm³ of water.

25 cm³ of water = 25 g of water, and 100 ÷ 25 = 4

Solubility = 24 × 4 = 96 g per 100 g of water

The scheme gives one mark for the reading and one for the × 4. Forget the × 4 and your answer is in the wrong units, so it scores only the reading.

subsections.heading: How many crystals form on cooling
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6C · 2023 Q12(b) · 2024 Q2(c)(iii) · 2025 Q5(d) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(a)(ii) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(c)(iii)

When a saturated solution cools, the water can hold less, so the extra solute crystallises out.

  1. At the hot temperature the solution is saturated — it holds the hot-temperature amount.
  2. As it cools, the solubility falls.
  3. The water can no longer hold all the solute.
  4. The surplus comes out of solution as crystals. The liquid left is still saturated, at the new, lower temperature.
Mass crystallising on coolingmass of crystals = solubility at hot temperature − solubility at cold temperatureboth read from the same curve · gives the mass per 100 g of water · scale if the water is not 100 g

The two-read subtraction — worked (2023 Q12)

1. Solubility of CuCl₂ at 60 °C, lines shown on the graph = 45 g 1

2. Solubility at 10 °C = 13 g, so mass crystallising = 45 − 13 = 32 g 1

If the solution used 250 g of water, scale at the end: 32 × 2.5 = 80 g.

Watch the units of the graph. In 2024 Edexcel 2C Q4(d) the curves were plotted per 25 cm³, so 21 − 8 = 13 g was already the answer for 25 cm³ of water. No scaling was needed because the question asked about 25 cm³.

2024: "Must show working on the graph." Rule both readings.
✗ "32 g" written on the answer line with a clean graph.
✓ Two sets of construction lines on the graph, then "45 − 13 = 32 g".

equations.name: Mass crystallising on cooling
equations.formula: mass of crystals = solubility at hot temperature − solubility at cold temperature

subsections.heading: Plotting the points and drawing the curve
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6C · 2024 Q2(c) · 2025 Q5(a) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q4(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(c)

Plot every point to within half a small square, then draw one smooth curve through or close to them.

  1. Plot each point with a neat cross, accurate to ± half a small square.
  2. Look at the shape. Solubility points almost always lie on a curve, not a straight line.
  3. Draw a single, smooth curve of best fit in one stroke. Do not join the dots with a ruler.
  4. If it does not pass through every point, leave an even spread of points either side.
  5. With two sets of data, label each curve with its substance.

2024 scheme: "Best-fit curve must be a single line (not sketchy)".
2025 scheme: unlabelled curves lost a mark.
✗ Feathery, doubled-up lines, or dot-to-dot straight segments.
✓ One clean curve per substance, labelled KNO₃ and NaNO₃.

The plotting marks are the easiest on the paper. In 2024 Edexcel 2C Q4 they were four of the ten marks — two for points, two for curves.

subsections.heading: Measuring solubility — the evaporating-basin practical
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7C (practical) · 2024 Q2(d) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b)

Make a saturated solution at a known temperature, evaporate the water from a weighed sample, and weigh the solid left behind.

The school's method, in the order the 2024 flowchart question wanted:

  1. Put a known volume of water in a beaker, at the chosen temperature.
  2. Add the solid a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves and some solid is left over. The solution is now saturated.
  3. Filter to remove the undissolved solid, keeping a measured volume of the clear saturated solution.
  4. Weigh an empty evaporating basin.
  5. Pour the solution into the basin and weigh it again.
  6. Heat gently to evaporate the water, then weigh the basin and dry solid.

Worked example — the 2024 numbers

Mass of salt = (basin + dry salt) − (empty basin) = 78.2 − 50.5 = 27.7 g

This dissolved in 50 cm³ = 50 g of water. Scale factor = 100 ÷ 50 = 2

Solubility = 27.7 × 2 = 55.4 g per 100 g of water

Weighing the basin with the solution is not wasted. It gives you the mass of water directly: mass of water = (basin + solution) − (basin + dry salt). 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b) worked this way — 5.1 g of solid and 15 g of water, so 5.1 ÷ 15 × 100 = 34 g per 100 g.

To measure solubility at another temperature, keep the beaker in a water bath at that temperature and check it with a thermometer, because solubility changes with temperature.

subsections.heading: Evaporate to dryness here, but not when making crystals
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7C · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b)(iv) · links to salt preparation, module 4

The purpose decides the heating: measuring solubility needs all the water gone; making crystals needs most of it left.

GoalHow far you heatWhy
Measure solubilityEvaporate to dryness, gentlyYou need the total mass of dissolved solid, so every gram must come out of solution
Prepare a pure, dry saltHeat only to the crystallisation point, then leave to coolYou want well-formed, hydrated crystals; boiling dry wrecks them

"Gently" matters. Heat a hydrated salt such as copper(II) sulfate too strongly and it loses its water of crystallisation and turns into the anhydrous salt. The mass of solid is then wrong. That was the 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b)(iv) mark.

✗ "Always heat to dryness to get the salt."
✓ "Evaporate to dryness to measure solubility; heat only until crystals start to form to prepare crystals."

subsections.heading: Why some readings are less accurate
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7C · 2022 Q4(iii)

Near 100 °C, water evaporates while you work, so there is less water than you think.

  1. At 95 °C the water is close to boiling, so some of it evaporates during the measurement.
  2. The dissolved solid is then shared between less water than was recorded.
  3. So the values measured at high temperature are less accurate.

The one-mark answer in 2022 was simply "water evaporates". The same idea explains why the temperature must be held steady throughout. If the saturated solution cools while it is being filtered, some solid crystallises out early and is lost.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Solubility = grams of solute that saturate 100 g of water at a stated temperature. Every question is reading, scaling, or subtracting that number.

Saturated: no more solute will dissolve at that temperature.

Same solubility: where the curves cross — rule the line down.

Crystals on cooling: solubility hot − solubility cold, working on the graph, scale last.

Per 25 cm³ → per 100 g: × 4, because 1 cm³ of water = 1 g.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
SoluteThe solid that dissolves in the solvent
SolventThe liquid that does the dissolving
SolutionThe mixture formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent
Saturated solutionA solution in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature (undissolved solid may be present)
SolubilityThe mass of solute, in g per 100 g of solvent, that saturates it at a given temperature

questions.promptHtml: A saturated solution of KNO₃ at 70 °C sits in an open beaker overnight and cools to 20 °C. Describe everything that is different in the morning, with the reasoning.
questions.answerHtml:
Crystals of KNO₃ now sit at the bottom. At 70 °C the water held the full 70-degree solubility; at 20 °C it can hold far less. The surplus had nowhere to go but out of solution — it crystallised.

The remaining liquid is still saturated — but at 20 °C, holding the 20-degree amount. The mass of crystals = (solubility at 70°) − (solubility at 20°), scaled to the actual mass of water. That subtraction is the exam question, every year.

questions.promptHtml: 2025's table gave the mass dissolving in 25 cm³ of water, and the answer line demanded "g per 100 g of water". What conversion is needed, and why does the question feel entitled to swap between cm³ and g of water without comment?
questions.answerHtml:
Multiply the reading by 4 — four lots of 25 make 100.

The silent swap works because 1.00 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.00 g — the density of water is the one conversion factor the papers assume without stating (2024 printed it as a hint; 2025 didn't). So 25 cm³ of water is 25 g of water, and volume-of-water numbers slot straight into solubility units.

It only works for water — never apply it to another liquid or to the solution itself.

questions.promptHtml: Why are solubility values measured at 95 °C systematically less accurate than those at 25 °C — and is the error high or low?
questions.answerHtml:
Near boiling, the water evaporates significantly while the measurement is being made. Less water is present than you think.

The same mass of dissolved salt sitting in less water than recorded means the calculated "per 100 g" figure comes out too high — the salt gets credited to water that has already left. (The one-mark exam answer is just "water evaporates"; the direction of the error is the understanding behind it.)

questions.promptHtml: In the evaporating-basin practical you heat to complete dryness — the exact step the salt-preparation module forbids. Why is it right here and wrong there?
questions.answerHtml:
Different goal, different technique. Here the product is a number: the total mass of dissolved salt. Evaporating everything off and weighing the solid residue measures exactly that — you want every last gram out of solution, and you don't care what the crystals look like.

In salt preparation the product is the substance: well-formed, hydrated crystals. There, heating to dryness wrecks the crystals and drives off the water of crystallisation.

If an exam answer needs one sentence: evaporate to dryness to measure solubility; heat only to the crystallisation point to prepare crystals.

questions.promptHtml: Two curves cross at 68 °C. A student answers "at 68 °C the solutions are the same" and scores one mark of two. What exactly did the second mark want?
questions.answerHtml:
The construction line on the graph. The schemes award a mark for visible working again and again: the line dropped from the crossing in 2023 Q12 and 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3, and the readings for the crystallisation subtraction in 2024 and 2025.

The habit that banks these marks: for any value read from a graph, rule the lines first, read second, and leave the lines on the paper. It also silently protects you — an answer read from the wrong place with lines shown can still earn the method mark.

And "the solutions are the same" is loose wording. Say the solubilities are equal at 68 °C.

questions.promptHtml: A solution contains 40 g of solid X in 100 g of water at 70 °C. The solubility of X is 60 g per 100 g at 70 °C, 40 g at 45 °C and 25 g at 20 °C. Is the solution saturated at 70 °C? What happens as it cools to 20 °C?
questions.answerHtml:
Not saturated at 70 °C. The water could hold 60 g but holds only 40 g, so the point sits below the curve. Another 20 g could still dissolve.

As it cools, nothing visible happens at first. At 45 °C the solubility has fallen to 40 g — exactly what is dissolved — so the solution becomes saturated. That is where crystals first appear.

Below 45 °C crystals keep forming. At 20 °C the water holds 25 g, so 40 − 25 = 15 g has crystallised. Notice it is 40 − 25, not 60 − 25: you subtract from what was actually dissolved, not from the 70 °C solubility.

questions.promptHtml: Sugar stirred into tea disappears much faster than sugar left unstirred. A student concludes that stirring increases the solubility of sugar. Why is that wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
Stirring changes the rate of dissolving, not the amount that can dissolve. It brings fresh water to the surface of the crystals, so they dissolve sooner.

Solubility is the maximum mass that dissolves in 100 g of water at that temperature. Leave the unstirred cup long enough and exactly the same maximum is reached. Only changing the temperature changes that maximum.

This is why the 2024 scheme accepted "temperature" as a factor affecting solubility and ignored "stirring".

questions.promptHtml: A student measures the solubility of copper(II) sulfate but heats the evaporating basin strongly until the blue solid turns white. Explain what has gone wrong and how it affects the result.
questions.answerHtml:
The blue solid is hydrated copper(II) sulfate: its crystals contain water of crystallisation. Strong heating drove that water off and left white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

So the solid weighed at the end is lighter than the salt that was dissolved. A smaller mass of solid gives a solubility that is too low.

The fix is in the word the method uses: heat gently, just enough to evaporate the water from the solution. 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q3(b)(iv) gave its mark for "copper(II) sulfate would lose water / become anhydrous".

These steps for measuring solubility are jumbled: A — gently heat the basin to remove all the water; B — filter to obtain 50.0 cm³ of saturated solution; C — record the mass of basin and salt solution; D — record the mass of the empty basin; E — record the mass of basin and dry salt; F — put 50.0 cm³ of water into a beaker; G — add salt, stirring, until no more dissolves; H — pour the solution into the basin.

modules.standfirst: On every paper for five years straight, always built around the same two practicals and the same three-mark collision-theory explanation. The marks are lost to loose wording and sloppy graphs, not hard chemistry.

The 2025 teacher commentary on this topic is a checklist of how marks were actually lost:

"A lot of students mentioned lowering activation energy so could not score M2" — the catalyst answer needs both halves: alternative pathway and lower activation energy.

"Many students lost M4 as they said m to represent minutes rather than min. This is INCORRECT as m is meters! Also several wrote cm not cm³."

"Several lost M3 by not linking successful collision to time, or missing out successful."

And from 2023: "Really poorly answered. Lots of extremely sloppy graphs — very blunt pencils, and/or drawing sketchy/feathery lines instead of a single one."

Every year the topic is examined through a practical: marble chips + acid (mass loss), Mg or Zn + acid (gas syringe), or H₂O₂ + catalyst (gas syringe). The real Edexcel papers use exactly the same three set-ups. Learn them and you have seen every rates question.

subsections.html: Rate is about how fast a reaction goes — never how much product it makes. Everything in this topic is one idea (particles must collide, hard enough, often enough) applied to five factors and read off two kinds of graph.

subsections.heading: What rate means
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9, 3.10 · 2021 Q8 · 2022 Q3 · 2023 Q7

Rate of reaction is how much reactant is used up, or product is made, per unit time. "Per unit time" is the part that makes it a rate. Without it you have only described an amount.

The simplest rate to work out is the mean (average) rate over a stretch of time:

Mean rate of reactionmean rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time takengas in cm³, mass in g · time in s or min · unit = cm³/s, cm³/min, g/s

Worked example — mean rate with units

Magnesium reacts with acid. 48 cm³ of hydrogen is collected in the first 2.0 minutes.

  1. Write the equation: mean rate = volume ÷ time
  2. Substitute: mean rate = 48 ÷ 2.0
  3. Answer: 24 cm³/min
  4. If seconds are wanted: 2.0 min = 120 s, so 48 ÷ 120 = 0.40 cm³/s

Same idea with mass: a flask loses 0.66 g in 300 s → 0.66 ÷ 300 = 0.0022 g/s.

✗ "24 cm/m" — cm is a length and m is metres.
✗ "24" — no unit, no unit mark.
✓ "24 cm³/min" — cm³ for volume, min for minutes, per unit time.

equations.name: Mean rate of reaction
equations.formula: mean rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time taken

subsections.heading: Three ways to measure it
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9, 3.15, 3.16 · 2021 Q8 · 2022 Q3 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(a)

You measure rate by following something that changes as the reaction goes: the mass of the flask, the volume of gas, or the time for a change to happen.

  • Mass loss on a balance — marble chips + hydrochloric acid in a flask with a cotton wool plug. The CO₂ escapes, so the reading falls.
  • Gas collected in a gas syringe — magnesium or zinc + acid, or hydrogen peroxide decomposing. The volume rises with time.
  • Time for a change to happen — time to collect a set volume of gas, or time to lose a set mass. A shorter time means a faster rate.

Why the mass falls, step by step (2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(a)(i) asked exactly this):

  1. CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
  2. Carbon dioxide is a gas, so it leaves the flask.
  3. The balance reading falls by the mass of CO₂ given off.
  4. When the reaction stops, the mass stays constant.

2022 asked why the cotton wool increases accuracy, and the mark scheme rejected "it stops the gas escaping". The gas must escape or the mass would not change.
✗ "The cotton wool stops the gas escaping."
✓ "It stops acid spray escaping, so the decrease in mass is due only to the gas."

subsections.heading: Reading a rate curve
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q6(b) · 2023 Q7 · 2025 Q1

Every rate curve is steepest at the start, gets less steep, and then goes flat when one reactant runs out. The gradient of the curve is the rate: steeper means faster.

2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(b)(i) gave marks for linked pairs — what the curve does, then why:

  1. The curve is steepest at the start → because the acid concentration is highest, so collisions are most frequent.
  2. The curve becomes less steep → because the acid is used up and becomes less concentrated, so collisions are less frequent.
  3. The curve levels off → because one reactant (here the acid) has been used up, so the reaction has stopped.

Reading a value: draw a vertical line from the time up to the curve and across to the axis — and show those lines. 2023: "They had to show working-out lines on graph to get the full 2 marks."

✗ "The rate is fastest at the start because the particles have the most energy."
✓ "The rate is fastest at the start because the concentration of the acid is highest, so there are more collisions per unit time."

The temperature is the same all the way through, so energy has nothing to do with it. 2023's scheme rejected energy here.

subsections.heading: Worked example — rate at an instant from a tangent
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(c)(iv) · 2022 Q3 · 2025 Q1

The rate at one moment is the gradient of a tangent drawn at that moment. A tangent is a straight line that just touches the curve at that one point without cutting through it.

  1. Find the time on the x-axis and go up to the curve.
  2. Draw a tangent touching the curve at that point only. Use a ruler and a sharp pencil.
  3. Make the tangent long, then draw a large triangle under it.
  4. Read the change in y and the change in x from the axes.
  5. Rate = change in y ÷ change in x.
  6. Give the unit from the axes: cm³/s, cm³/min or g/s.

Worked example — hydrogen collected against time

A tangent is drawn at 40 s. It passes through (0 s, 45 cm³) and (80 s, 305 cm³).

  1. Change in volume = 305 − 45 = 260 cm³
  2. Change in time = 80 − 0 = 80 s
  3. Rate = 260 ÷ 80
  4. Rate = 3.25 cm³/s (about 3.3 cm³/s)

2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(b) marked this exactly: tangent drawn 1; change in volume ÷ change in time 1; answer in the accepted range, 2.75–3.75 cm³/s 1. The range is wide because everyone's tangent is slightly different. The method is what must be right.

Rate at 60 s means the tangent gradient at 60 s, not total change ÷ 60. In 2022 the average-rate answer (0.015 g/s) scored 1 of 3; the tangent gave about 0.005 g/s.
✗ "rate at 60 s = 88 cm³ ÷ 60 s"
✓ "draw a tangent at 60 s; rate = change in y ÷ change in x = … cm³/s"

subsections.heading: Comparing curves and sketching the second one
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q10 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(b)(ii) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q6(c)(i) · 2023 Q7(b) · 2024 Q3(b)

The steepness at the start tells you the rate; the height of the plateau tells you how much product — and only the amount of the limiting reactant can change that height.

What changedStart of the curveFinal plateau
Hotter, powder, catalyst, more concentrated acid (same moles of the limiting reactant)Steeper, from (0,0)Same height, reached sooner
Cooler, bigger chipsLess steep, from (0,0)Same height, reached later
Half the moles of the limiting reactant (e.g. same volume of acid at half the concentration, metal in excess)Less steepHalf the height

Worked example — which reactant sets the plateau?

Like 2022 Edexcel 1C Q6: 0.090 g of magnesium with 0.025 mol of HCl. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

  1. Moles of Mg = 0.090 ÷ 24 = 0.00375 mol
  2. HCl needed = 2 × 0.00375 = 0.0075 mol
  3. 0.0075 mol is less than the 0.025 mol present, so the acid is in excess.
  4. So the magnesium is the limiting reactant. It decides how much hydrogen is made, and so where the curve levels off.

In 2023 Edexcel 1C Q10 it was the other way round: the zinc was in excess, so halving the moles of acid halved the final volume of hydrogen (40 cm³ → 20 cm³) and made the curve less steep.

Two rules for any sketch, from 2023: "the curve had to very obviously start at (0,0) — quite a lot missed the axes slightly." And if the amounts have not changed, the new curve must level off at exactly the same height.

subsections.heading: Collision theory — the idea behind every factor
subsections.html:
Spec 3.11 · every school paper 2021–2025

Particles only react when they collide with at least the activation energy — so anything that makes those successful collisions happen more often speeds the reaction up.

  1. Reactant particles must collide.
  2. The collision must have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Then it is a successful collision.
  3. Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions — how many happen per unit time.

The three-mark template for any factor

1. What changed about the particles (more per unit volume / more energy / more exposed at the surface) 1

2. The word successful, and energy ≥ activation energy where temperature is involved 1

3. Collisions happen more frequently / more per unit time → rate increases 1

2025: "Several lost M3 by not linking successful collision to time, or missing out successful."
✗ "The particles have more chance of colliding."
✓ "There are more successful collisions per unit time."

subsections.heading: Concentration and gas pressure
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10, 3.11 · 2021 Q8(b)(iii) · 2024 Q3(c) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(d)

A higher concentration (or a higher gas pressure) packs more particles into the same volume, so they collide more often. The particles are no faster and no more energetic.

  1. Concentration of the solution increases (or the gas is at higher pressure).
  2. There are more particles in the same volume.
  3. So there are more frequent collisions — more collisions per unit time.
  4. So more successful collisions per unit time, and the rate increases.

For a gas, higher pressure means the same number of particles squeezed into a smaller volume — the same effect as a more concentrated solution. 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9(d) showed rate is directly proportional to acid concentration: double the concentration, double the rate.

✗ "More concentrated acid gives the particles more energy." — the 2024 scheme capped concentration answers that mentioned kinetic energy at 1 mark.
✗ "The concentration of the magnesium increases." — solids have no concentration; 2023's marker penalised it.
✓ "More acid particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions."

2021's scheme also rejected "molecules" or "atoms" for the acid — say particles or ions.

subsections.heading: Temperature
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10, 3.11 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q6(c)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(i) · 2023 Q7(b) · 2025 Q1(c)

Heating gives particles more kinetic energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react — and they collide more often too. Temperature is the only factor where energy belongs in the answer.

  1. Temperature increases, so particles gain kinetic energy.
  2. So more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy — a greater proportion are successful.
  3. Particles also move faster, so collision frequency increases.
  4. So there are more successful collisions per unit time, and the rate increases.

Cooler works the same way backwards: less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions per unit time, slower rate — but, if the amounts are unchanged, the same final amount of product (2023 Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(i)).

2023: "They had to say that more/a greater proportion of collisions are successful. Too many merged this point with collision frequency."
✗ "More energy so more collisions."
✓ "More kinetic energy, so more collisions have energy ≥ activation energy, and collisions are more frequent."

subsections.heading: Surface area
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10, 3.11 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q9(c) · 2022 Q3(d)

Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more particles on its surface, so acid particles hit it more often. Only the surface particles can react.

  1. Smaller chips, or a powder, are used instead of large lumps.
  2. This gives a greater surface area — more particles exposed.
  3. So there are more collisions per unit time between acid particles and the solid.
  4. So the rate increases.

The total amount of solid is unchanged, so the final amount of product is unchanged. The plateau is reached sooner but at the same height.

✗ "Powder has a bigger surface area so it makes more gas."
✓ "Powder has a greater surface area, so more collisions per unit time; the same mass gives the same volume of gas."

subsections.heading: Catalysts — both halves or no mark
subsections.html:
Spec 3.12, 3.13 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q10(c) · 2024 Q3(d) · 2025 Q1(a)

A catalyst speeds a reaction up by giving it an easier route, and is not used up.

The definition — two marks

1. A substance that increases the rate of a reaction 1

2. but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction 1

How it works, as a chain:

  1. The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway.
  2. This pathway has a lower activation energy.
  3. So a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to be successful.
  4. So there are more successful collisions per unit time, and the rate increases.

The school's example is always manganese(IV) oxide catalysing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. The catalyst can be filtered off, dried and weighed at the end — its mass is the same as at the start.

2025: "A lot of students mentioned lowering activation energy so could not score M2".
✗ "The catalyst lowers the activation energy."
✓ "The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy."

subsections.heading: Reaction profiles — activation energy and ΔH (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.14C · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(b)

A reaction profile shows the energy of the reactants, the hump the particles must get over, and the energy of the products. The hump is the activation energy.

  1. Draw the reactants as a flat line on the left.
  2. Draw a hump rising to a peak, then falling to the products line on the right.
  3. Activation energy (Eₐ): a vertical arrow from the reactants line up to the top of the peak.
  4. Enthalpy change (ΔH): a vertical arrow from the reactants line to the products line.
  5. Products lower than reactants = exothermic (ΔH negative). Products higher = endothermic (ΔH positive).

For the catalysed reaction, draw a second curve that starts at the same reactants level, has a lower peak, and ends at the same products level. The catalyst changes Eₐ but not ΔH.

✗ Eₐ drawn from the products line, or from the x-axis, up to the peak.
✗ Catalysed curve ending at a different products level.
✓ Both arrows start at the reactants level; the catalysed curve has a lower peak and the same start and end.

subsections.heading: Practical 1 — marble chips and hydrochloric acid
subsections.html:
Spec 3.15 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q9 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q9 · 2021 Q8 · 2022 Q3

Follow the mass lost as CO₂ escapes, and change only one thing — chip size or acid concentration.

  1. Put a measured volume of dilute hydrochloric acid in a conical flask on a balance.
  2. Add a measured mass of marble chips, put in the cotton wool plug and start the timer.
  3. Record the mass every 30 seconds until it stays constant.
  4. Repeat with smaller chips (same mass) — or with a different acid concentration.
  5. Plot mass lost (or mass) against time for each run and compare the gradients at the start.

Keep the same: mass of marble chips, volume of acid, temperature — and chip size or concentration, whichever you are not testing. Chips left in the flask at the end mean the acid has all reacted.

✗ "Make it a fair test." — scores nothing.
✓ "Use the same mass of marble chips, the same volume of acid and the same temperature."

subsections.heading: Practical 2 — comparing catalysts for hydrogen peroxide
subsections.html:
Spec 3.16 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(a) · 2024 Q3 · 2025 Q1

Add each solid to the same hydrogen peroxide and measure how fast oxygen is made; the fastest rate shows the best catalyst.

The five marks in 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(a) came from these steps:

  1. Put hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe, add the catalyst and start the timer.
  2. Record the volume of oxygen at regular times — or the time to collect a set volume.
  3. Repeat with the same mass of each different catalyst.
  4. Use the same volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, at the same temperature.
  5. Plot volume against time and work out the gradient for each catalyst.
  6. The most effective catalyst gives the fastest rate — the steepest initial gradient, or the shortest time.

With a time-based measurement the comparison flips: a catalyst that makes 20 cm³ in 40 s beats one that takes 90 s. Shorter time = faster rate.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Rate questions are answered with frequency of successful collisions. Name the factor's effect on the particles, keep the word successful, and end with more collisions per unit time.

Concentration / pressure: more particles in the same volume. Temperature: more kinetic energy, more collisions ≥ activation energy. Surface area: more particles exposed. Catalyst: alternative pathway, lower activation energy.

Graphs: steeper = faster. Rate at a time = tangent gradient. Plateau height = amount of the limiting reactant.

subsections.heading: Graph craft — where the easy marks go
subsections.html:
• Sharp pencil, plots exact to the nearest gridline, visible ×.
  • Best-fit curve: one single smooth line, no feathering, through the origin when the data starts there, level exactly at the plateau.
  • Reading a value or a tangent: show the construction lines on the graph — they carry marks on their own.
  • Second-condition sketch: steeper from (0,0), same plateau height — unless the amount of the limiting reactant changed.
  • Ignore an anomalous point when drawing the line — and if asked why an anomaly happened in a rates experiment, "forgot to stir" is the accepted cause on this school's papers.

questions.promptHtml: A student says: "Doubling the concentration doubles the energy of the collisions, so the reaction is faster." There is one correct claim and one wrong claim in that sentence. Which is which?
questions.answerHtml:
Correct: the reaction is faster.

Wrong: concentration does not change the energy of anything. The particles move at the same speed at the same temperature; there are simply more of them in the same volume, so collisions happen more frequently.

Energy language belongs only in temperature answers. The 2024 mark scheme capped concentration answers mentioning kinetic energy at 1 mark of 3 — this exact confusion.

questions.promptHtml: The same mass of marble is used in two runs — large chips, then the same mass ground to powder. Why does the powder react faster, and why is the final volume of CO₂ the same in both runs?
questions.answerHtml:
Faster: grinding exposes far more particles at the surface — greater surface area — so collisions between acid particles and carbonate particles happen more frequently.

Same final volume: the amount of CaCO₃ is unchanged — same mass, same moles — so the same moles of CO₂ are eventually made. Surface area changes how fast you get there, never how much you get.

On the graph: steeper start, same plateau. If your sketch's plateau moves, you have changed the amount, not the rate.

questions.promptHtml: Why does raising the temperature by only 10 °C roughly double the rate, when the collision frequency only rises by a few percent?
questions.answerHtml:
Because frequency is the small effect. The big effect is that the proportion of collisions with energy above the activation energy rises steeply with temperature — many collisions that used to bounce apart now react.

That is why the mark scheme insists on "more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy / a greater proportion are successful" as its own separate mark, and why merging it into "more collisions" loses it. Two different mechanisms: hitting harder (dominant) and hitting more often (minor).

questions.promptHtml: A catalyst does not appear in the chemical equation and its mass is unchanged at the end. So how can it possibly change the rate?
questions.answerHtml:
It takes part, then is regenerated. The catalyst offers the reaction an alternative pathway — a different route from reactants to products — whose activation energy is lower.

The particles' energies are unchanged, but the bar they must clear is lower, so a greater proportion of the same collisions are now successful.

Because the catalyst is chemically unchanged overall, a tiny amount works for a large amount of reactant, and it is still there — same mass — at the end. That "chemically unchanged at the end" phrase is the definition mark.

questions.promptHtml: Two identical H₂O₂ experiments run at 20 °C and 40 °C. Sketch both curves in your head: state three things the 40 °C curve does and one thing it must not do.
questions.answerHtml:
The 40 °C curve:

  1. starts at exactly (0,0), like the original;
  2. rises more steeply from the start;
  3. levels off sooner — but at the same final volume, because the amount of H₂O₂ is the same.

It must not level off at a higher or lower volume. Temperature changes the journey, not the destination — only changing the amount of the limiting reactant moves the plateau.

questions.promptHtml: In the marble-chips experiment the reaction eventually stops while chips are still visible in the flask. What ran out, how would the balance tell you the reaction had stopped, and what would you see in the flask?
questions.answerHtml:
What ran out: the hydrochloric acid — the acid is the limiting reactant. "All the acid has reacted" is the accepted wording.

The balance: the mass stops decreasing — the reading stays constant. (On a graph: the curve levels off.)

In the flask: the fizzing/effervescence stops.

Note the logic: solid left over ⇒ the other reactant finished. This is the same limiting-reactant idea the calculations module uses — the excess is visible, the limiting reagent decides when it ends.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the rate of reaction greatest at the very start — and what is wrong with answering "because the particles have the most energy at the start"?
questions.answerHtml:
Right answer: at the start the concentration of the acid (the reactants in solution) is at its highest — the most particles per unit volume — so collisions are at their most frequent. As reactant is used up, collisions become rarer and the curve flattens.

The wrong answer: energy has nothing to do with it. The temperature is constant, so the particles' energies are the same at the start as at the end. The 2023 scheme explicitly rejected incorrect references to energy here.

questions.promptHtml: A gas syringe collects 88 cm³ of hydrogen in the first 60 s. A student says "so the rate at 60 s is 88 ÷ 60 = 1.5 cm³/s". Why is that wrong, and will the true rate at 60 s be bigger or smaller than 1.5 cm³/s?
questions.answerHtml:
88 ÷ 60 is the mean rate over the whole first minute. The rate at 60 s is the gradient of the tangent at 60 s — a different number.

It will be smaller. The curve is always slowing down: it was steep at the start, when the acid was most concentrated, and flatter by 60 s. The mean mixes the fast early part with the slower later part, so it is bigger than the rate at the end of that minute.

This is why 2022's average-rate answer scored only 1 of 3.

questions.promptHtml:
Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

(b) Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. (2)
(c) Describe how you could show the manganese(IV) oxide is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) A substance that increases the rate of a reaction 1 but is chemically unchanged / not used up at the end 1

(b) Provides an alternative (reaction) pathway 1 with a lower activation energy 1 — both halves needed; "lowers the activation energy" alone drops the pathway mark

(c) Filter it off, wash and dry it, and weigh it: the mass is the same as at the start 1; (it can then catalyse a fresh run just as well) 1

(b) Provides an alternative (reaction) pathway with a lower activation energy — both halves needed; "lowers the activation energy" alone drops the pathway mark

questions.promptHtml:
A student investigates the reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid, collecting the hydrogen in a gas syringe and recording the volume every 15 seconds until the reaction stops.

(a) Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm³/min. (2)

questions.promptHtml:
1.3 g of zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid containing 0.0036 mol of HCl. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ [Aᵣ of Zn = 65]

(a) Show that the zinc is in excess. (2)
(b) The experiment is repeated at a lower temperature. Explain, in terms of particles, why the rate is slower. (3)
(c) The experiment is repeated with the same volume of acid at half the concentration. State two ways the new volume–time curve differs from the original. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Moles of Zn = 1.3 ÷ 65 = 0.02 mol 1; only 0.0036 ÷ 2 = 0.0018 mol of Zn can react, which is less than 0.02, so zinc is in excess 1

modules.title: Electrolysis and Redox
modules.standfirst: Ions to the electrodes, electrons swapped, product decided by reactivity. Examined every year, and the teacher commentary says the same marks die every year: half-equations that invent chemistry, and answers that say "magnesium" when they mean "the magnesium ion".

"Huge number of students wrote Magnesium gains electrons. This is not true! The magnesium ION gains electrons, not the magnesium!!" — 2023.
