subsections.html: Electrolysis is using electricity to break down a compound. Everything on these papers comes down to three questions: can it conduct? — which ions go to which electrode? — which ion wins at each electrode? Each one has a fixed answer pattern, and the headings below take them in order.

subsections.heading: Why things conduct — and why solids never do
subsections.html:
Spec 1.55C, 1.56C · 2023 Q2b · 2024 Q6a · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q4(c) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(c)

To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that are free to move. Ask which particle carries the charge, and whether it can move.

  • Metals conduct as solids and liquids: their delocalised electrons move through the structure.
  • Ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. Melt or dissolve it and the ions are free to move.
  • Covalent compounds do not conduct: they are made of molecules, so there are no ions and no free electrons — no charged particles at all.

Mark script — "Explain why magnesium conducts but magnesium chloride only when molten" (2022 Edexcel 2C Q4, and the school's 2023 Q2)

1. Magnesium has delocalised electrons 1

2. which can move through the structure 1

3. Magnesium chloride conducts only when molten or in solution 1

4. because then its ions are free to move 1

✗ "Solid sodium chloride doesn't conduct because the electrons can't move." — the school's 2024 scheme gave nothing for electron answers about an ionic compound.
✗ "The ions in magnesium move." — the metal conducts by electrons, not ions. The 2023 scheme rejected this too.
✓ "In the solid the ions are in fixed positions and cannot move. When molten, the ions are free to move and carry the charge."

subsections.heading: Anions, cations and the two electrodes
subsections.html:
Spec 1.57C · 2024 Q6b · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(b)(ii)

Opposite charges attract: positive ions go to the negative electrode, negative ions go to the positive electrode.

IonChargeGoes toWhat happens there
Cation — metal ions and H⁺PositiveCathode (negative electrode)Gains electrons — reduction
Anion — halide ions, OH⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻NegativeAnode (positive electrode)Loses electrons — oxidation

A memory hook: a cation is "pawsitive" — cats have paws. And PANiC: Positive is the Anode, Negative is the Cathode.

"Explain how a metal forms at the negative electrode" is always the same chain:

  1. The metal ions are positive (cations).
  2. They are attracted to the negative electrode (cathode).
  3. There each ion gains electrons — it is reduced.
  4. It becomes a metal atom.

Mark script — "Explain how copper forms at the negative electrode" (2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(b), 3 marks from 4 points)

1. Copper ions are positive / Cu²⁺ 1

2. They are attracted to the negative electrode 1

3. where they gain (accept) electrons 1

4. and become copper atoms (any three of these four)

✗ "Sodium atoms move to the negative electrode." — they are not atoms until they get there. The 2024 school scheme rejected this.
✓ "Positive sodium ions are attracted to the negative electrode, where each ion gains an electron to form a sodium atom."

subsections.heading: OIL RIG — oxidation and reduction at the electrodes
subsections.html:
Spec 1.59C, 2.20 · 2022 Q5a · 2023 Q2c · 2025 Q7d · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(d)(iii) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(d)(ii)

Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain of electrons — and it is always the ion that gains or loses them.

OIL RIGOxidation Is Loss · Reduction Is Gainof electrons — the cathode always does reduction, the anode always does oxidation

So "why is this reaction an oxidation?" is a one-line answer. Look at the half-equation: electrons on the right means they were lost, so it is oxidation. Electrons on the left means they were gained, so it is reduction.

  1. Find which side the e⁻ is on.
  2. Right side → electrons lost → oxidation. Left side → electrons gained → reduction.
  3. Name the ion that did it: "the bromide ions lose electrons", "the magnesium ion gains electrons".

✗ "Bromine loses electrons." — bromine is the product. Rejected in 2025 (school) and in 2024 Edexcel 2C.
✗ "Magnesium gains electrons." — "The magnesium ION gains electrons, not the magnesium!!"
✓ "It is oxidation because the bromide ions lose electrons."
✓ "It is reduction because the magnesium ions gain electrons."

equations.name: OIL RIG
equations.formula: Oxidation Is Loss · Reduction Is Gain

subsections.heading: Building a half-equation, step by step
subsections.html:
Spec 1.59C · every school paper · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(d)(ii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(b)(ii)

Balance the atoms first, then balance the charge by adding electrons. Follow the same five steps every time and the "fascinating variations" disappear.

  1. Write the start and finish. The ion on the left, the product on the right. Halogens are diatomic (Cl₂, Br₂). Oxygen in a solution comes from water.
  2. Balance the atoms with big numbers in front.
  3. Add up the charge on each side.
  4. Add electrons (e⁻) to the more positive side until the two totals match.
  5. Check: atoms equal, charges equal. Cathode equations have e⁻ on the left; anode equations have e⁻ on the right.

Worked example 1 — bromide ions at the anode

Step 1: Br⁻ → Br₂

Step 2: two Br atoms on the right, so 2Br⁻ → Br₂

Step 3: left charge = 2 × (−1) = −2 · right charge = 0

Step 4: the right is more positive, so add 2e⁻ there: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

Step 5: −2 = −2 ✓ · electrons on the right, so it is oxidation ✓

Worked example 2 — lead ions at the cathode

Step 1–2: Pb²⁺ → Pb — one lead atom each side already

Step 3: left charge = +2 · right charge = 0

Step 4: the left is more positive, so add 2e⁻ there: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb

Step 5: 0 = 0 ✓ · electrons on the left, so it is reduction ✓

Worked example 3 — oxygen from water at the anode (the one everyone drops)

Step 1: H₂O → O₂ + H⁺ — water is what is really there

Step 2a: balance O: 2H₂O → O₂ + H⁺

Step 2b: balance H: 4 H on the left, so 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺

Step 3: left charge = 0 · right charge = +4

Step 4: add 4e⁻ to the right: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻

Step 5: 0 = +4 − 4 ✓ · also accepted: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻

✗ Cl⁻ → Cl + e⁻, or Cl₃, or Cl⁺ — chlorine is diatomic.
✗ 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ in a solution — there are no O²⁻ ions in a solution. The 2023 year group's favourite wrong answer.
✓ 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻

The Edexcel schemes give two marks for the water equation: one for all the right formulae, one for the balancing. Correct formulae alone still earn a mark.

subsections.heading: The half-equations you will actually write
subsections.html:
Spec 1.59C · every paper

Only about eight half-equations ever come up — learn them as a bank.

At the cathode (reduction — electrons on the left):

  • Metals: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb · Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (molten) · Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg
  • Hydrogen from a solution: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

At the anode (oxidation — electrons on the right):

  • Halogens: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
  • Oxygen from a solution: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)

The number of electrons always equals the charge on the ion × the number of ions. Cu²⁺ needs 2; two Cl⁻ give up 2; Na⁺ needs 1.

subsections.heading: Molten compounds — lead(II) bromide
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q6(c)–(d) · 2025 Q7d

A molten compound has only two ions, so the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode — no choice to make.

  1. Put solid lead(II) bromide in a crucible with two graphite electrodes, connected to a d.c. supply and a bulb or ammeter.
  2. Heat strongly, in a fume cupboard. Nothing happens while it is solid — the bulb stays off.
  3. Once it melts, the ions can move and the bulb lights.
  4. Anode (+): Br⁻ ions lose electrons — brown vapour of bromine: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
  5. Cathode (−): Pb²⁺ ions gain electrons — molten lead, a silvery liquid, collects under the electrode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb.

Why graphite? It is inert (does not react with the products), it conducts, and it has a very high melting point, so it survives the heat. Why a fume cupboard? Bromine vapour is toxic.

✗ "Bromine is seen at the positive electrode." — that is a name, not an observation.
✓ "A brown vapour is seen at the positive electrode." — this is what the 2024 Edexcel scheme accepted.

subsections.heading: Solutions: how to decide the product at the cathode
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C · 2022 Q5b · 2024 Q6b(iv) · 2025 Q3b · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(b)(iv)

At the cathode, the less reactive of the metal and hydrogen is the one that forms. A solution always has H⁺ ions from water as well as the metal ions, so the two compete.

  1. Molten? Then the metal forms. Stop.
  2. In solution? List the positive ions: the metal ion and H⁺ from water.
  3. Find the metal in the reactivity series: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, (H) , Cu, Ag, Au.
  4. Metal below hydrogen (copper, silver) → the metal is deposited.
  5. Metal above hydrogen (potassium, sodium, magnesium…) → hydrogen gas forms instead, and the metal ions stay in solution.

That is why sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen, not sodium. The one-mark answer: "sodium is more reactive than hydrogen" (or "hydrogen is less reactive than sodium").

subsections.heading: Solutions: how to decide the product at the anode
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C · 2021 Q4 · 2022 Q5 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(d)

At the anode, a halide gives its halogen; anything else gives oxygen from the water.

  1. Molten? Then the non-metal from the negative ion forms (Br₂, Cl₂). Stop.
  2. In solution? Is there a halide ion — chloride, bromide or iodide?
  3. Yes → the halogen forms: Cl₂ (pale green gas), Br₂ (orange-brown solution).
  4. No — sulfate or nitrate → oxygen forms, from the water: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

Sulfate and nitrate ions are never discharged at IGCSE. If the question gives you sulfuric acid or copper(II) sulfate, the anode gives oxygen.

subsections.heading: The named solutions, worked through
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C · 2021 Q4 · 2022 Q5 · 2025 Q3

Whatever is not discharged stays behind, and that decides what the solution becomes. Run both flowcharts, then pair up the leftover ions.

SolutionCathode (−)Anode (+)Left in solution
Sodium chloride (concentrated)hydrogen — Na above Hchlorine — halidesodium hydroxide — alkaline
Dilute sulfuric acidhydrogenoxygen — no halidesulfuric acid — you are electrolysing water
Copper(II) sulfatecopper — Cu below Hoxygensulfuric acid — blue fades
Potassium sulfate / potassium nitratehydrogenoxygenunchanged salt — water is electrolysed
Silver nitratesilveroxygennitric acid

Sodium chloride solution turns alkaline. H⁺ is removed at the cathode, so Na⁺ and OH⁻ are left. Universal indicator near the cathode goes blue/purple, and the particle responsible is the hydroxide ion.

Where do OH⁻ ions in copper sulfate solution come from? From water, which dissociates slightly into H⁺ and OH⁻. Not "because the solution is alkaline" — it isn't.

✗ "The indicator turns blue because the solution is alkaline." — true, but the 2025 scheme wanted the particle.
✓ "Blue/purple, because hydroxide ions (OH⁻) are left in the solution."

subsections.heading: Practical: electrolysing a solution and testing the gases
subsections.html:
Spec 1.60C · 2021 Q4b · 2022 Q5 · 2025 Q3a · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(b)(i)

Collect each gas over its electrode, then identify it with the right test.

  1. Pour the solution into a beaker or electrolysis cell with two inert electrodes — graphite or platinum.
  2. Fill a test tube with the solution and turn it upside down over each electrode.
  3. Switch on the d.c. supply. Gas collects in each tube by displacing the solution.
  4. Note what you see at each electrode: bubbles, a coating, a colour.
  5. Test each gas.
GasTestResult
HydrogenLit splintSqueaky pop
OxygenGlowing splintRelights
ChlorineDamp blue litmus paperTurns red, then bleached white

Three follow-ups the papers love:

  • Why add dilute acid to water? Pure water is a very poor conductor; the acid increases its conductivity.
  • Why less oxygen (or chlorine) than expected? Some of it dissolves in the water.
  • Why a fume cupboard for NaCl(aq)? Chlorine is toxic.

✗ "Glowing splint pops." — the 2024 school scheme rejected the glowing splint for hydrogen.
✗ "The acid helps the water carry the current." — the 2021 scheme ignored this.
✓ "A lit splint gives a squeaky pop" · "the acid increases the conductivity".

subsections.heading: Copper(II) sulfate — what you see and how it changes
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C, 1.60C · 2023 Q5 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(a)

With inert electrodes, copper coats the cathode, oxygen bubbles at the anode, and the blue colour fades as the copper ions are used up.

  • Cathode: a pink / brown solid forms — Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
  • Anode: bubbles / effervescence — oxygen. The school's 2023 scheme ignored "oxygen" as an observation.
  • Solution: Cu²⁺ is removed, so the blue fades. H⁺ builds up with SO₄²⁻, so the solution becomes sulfuric acid.

2022 Jan Edexcel 2C gave a graph of the mass of the negative electrode against time. It rises, then goes flat. The two-mark explanation:

  1. The mass increases because copper is deposited on the electrode.
  2. The line goes flat because there are no copper(II) ions left in the solution.

2023 Edexcel 2C opened with a test for the copper(II) ions themselves: add sodium hydroxide solution → a blue precipitate (or a flame test → blue-green flame).

subsections.heading: Calculations: moles of gas, not a special formula
subsections.html:
Spec 1.35C (molar volume) with 1.59C · 2025 Q3a(v)

Electrolysis calculations on this course use ordinary moles: volume ÷ 24 000 cm³, then the ratio from the half-equations. The 4CH1 spec has no Faraday or charge calculations — do not learn any.

Moles of gas at rtpmoles = volume in cm³ ÷ 24 000or volume in dm³ ÷ 24 · then mass = moles × Mr

Worked example — mass of oxygen from its volume (the 2025 Q3 method)

17.8 cm³ of oxygen is collected at rtp. Calculate its mass.

Step 1: moles O₂ = 17.8 ÷ 24 000 = 0.000 742 mol

Step 2: Mr of O₂ = 2 × 16 = 32

Step 3: mass = 0.000 742 × 32 = 0.0237 g (3 s.f.)

Worked example — why twice as much hydrogen as oxygen

Step 1: anode: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ — 4 electrons make 1 O₂

Step 2: cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ — so 4 electrons make 2 H₂

Step 3: the same electrons flow through both, so moles H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1

Step 4: equal moles of gas have equal volumes, so if 36 cm³ of hydrogen collects, expect 18 cm³ of oxygen (a little less, because some dissolves).

subsections.heading: Redox beyond the electrodes — oxygen and electrons
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20 · 2021 Q10b · 2024 Q5a · 2025 Q4b · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q9(a)(iii) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(c)

A redox reaction is one where oxidation and reduction happen together — and you must say which substance does which. The spec tests two definitions:

Oxygen definitionElectron definition
OxidationGain of oxygenLoss of electrons
ReductionLoss of oxygenGain of electrons
Oxidising agentGives oxygenAccepts electrons — is itself reduced
Reducing agentRemoves oxygenDonates electrons — is itself oxidised

How to answer "explain why this is a redox reaction":

  1. Find the substance that gains oxygen (or loses electrons) — it is oxidised.
  2. Find the substance that loses oxygen (or gains electrons) — it is reduced.
  3. Name both, using the reactant names — "iron(III) oxide", not "iron".

Mark script — thermite, 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(iii), school 2024 Q5a)

1. Aluminium gains oxygen, so it is oxidised 1

2. Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced 1

The same pattern did 2022 Edexcel 1C: in PbO + H₂ → Pb + H₂O, lead oxide loses oxygen (reduced) and hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidised).

In electron terms: in Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu, magnesium atoms lose two electrons (oxidised) and copper(II) ions gain them (reduced). Magnesium is the reducing agent because it donates electrons — exactly the two marks in 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(c).

✗ "Oxidation and reduction happen at the same time." — scored nothing in 2024. It names nobody.
✗ "Iron is reduced." — iron is the product. The 2024 teacher: many said IRON rather than IRON OXIDE.
✓ "Aluminium is oxidised because it gains oxygen; iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen."

The sentences everything follows from

Ions move to the oppositely charged electrode; the ION gains or loses electrons there; reactivity decides which ion wins. If your answer names an atom or a metal where it means an ion, it is wrong.

Cathode (solution): metal below hydrogen → metal; above hydrogen → hydrogen.

Anode (solution): halide present → halogen; otherwise → oxygen from water.

Half-equations: balance atoms, then add electrons to balance charge. e⁻ on the right = oxidation; e⁻ on the left = reduction.

questions.promptHtml: Solid sodium chloride sits between two connected electrodes and nothing happens. The moment it melts, a current flows and products appear. What changed — and why would the same experiment described with "electrons become free to move" score zero?
questions.answerHtml:
Melting frees the ions. In the solid, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are locked in a lattice by their attractions; they vibrate but cannot travel, so no charge can flow. Molten, the ions move: Na⁺ to the cathode, Cl⁻ to the anode — the moving ions are the current inside the electrolyte.

"Electrons become free" is a different (wrong) conduction story — that is how metals conduct. An ionic compound never conducts by electron flow; the charge carriers are ions, and the mark schemes reject electron answers outright.

questions.promptHtml: Electrolysing concentrated sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen at the cathode, yet molten sodium chloride gives sodium. Explain the difference — and what universal indicator near the cathode of the solution would show.
questions.answerHtml:
The solution contains a second cation: H⁺ from the water. At the cathode the less reactive species is discharged, and hydrogen is far less reactive than sodium — so H⁺ gains the electrons and H₂ bubbles off, while Na⁺ stays in solution. Molten NaCl has no water, no H⁺, no competition: sodium is the only choice.

Removing H⁺ leaves Na⁺ and OH⁻ behind — sodium hydroxide solution. Universal indicator near the cathode turns blue/purple, because hydroxide ions accumulate there. (2025's marker: most students never realised an alkali was forming, and few could name the OH⁻ ion as the reason.)

questions.promptHtml: Why must the oxygen half-equation in a solution start from water (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻) when 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ balances perfectly well?
questions.answerHtml:
Balancing isn't the test — existing is. A half-equation must start from a species actually present, and a solution of copper sulfate or dilute acid contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ and H₂O — but no free O²⁻ ions.

The oxygen made at the anode really does come from water molecules (or equivalently the OH⁻ from water): 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ — both accepted, because both start from what is really there. This exact wrong answer, 2O²⁻, was the year group's favourite in 2023.

questions.promptHtml: "The magnesium gains two electrons at the cathode." The teacher's comment on this sentence used two exclamation marks. What exactly is wrong with it, and what does the correct sentence look like?
questions.answerHtml:
Before the electrons arrive there is no magnesium — there is a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺. The whole event at the cathode is the ion becoming magnesium: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg. Saying "magnesium gains electrons" describes a neutral atom taking on electrons, which is not what happens and would make Mg²⁻.

Correct: "the magnesium ion gains two electrons (is reduced) to form a magnesium atom." The same precision is demanded at the anode: bromide ions lose electrons; bromine doesn't lose anything — it is the product.

questions.promptHtml: In the water-electrolysis apparatus, twice the volume of gas collects over the cathode as over the anode — but the oxygen tube is always slightly under half. Explain both facts.
questions.answerHtml:
The 2 : 1 ratio: the anode needs 4 electrons to make one O₂; the same 4 electrons at the cathode make two H₂. Twice the moles of hydrogen means twice the volume, because equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes.

The shortfall: some of the oxygen dissolves in the water (oxygen is slightly soluble; the same reason less chlorine than hydrogen collects from NaCl(aq) — chlorine dissolves too). Not a leak, not an error — the accepted one-marker is "some oxygen dissolves".

Related staple: why add dilute acid to the water first? Pure water is a poor conductor; the acid increases its conductivity. (Not "helps carry the current" — name the property.)

questions.promptHtml: The thermite reaction is 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. The 2024 marker complained that "many just said oxidation and reduction are occurring at the same time" and that "many said IRON was reduced rather than IRON OXIDE". Write the answer that scores both marks.
questions.answerHtml:
"Aluminium is oxidised because it gains oxygen (→ Al₂O₃), and iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen (→ Fe)."

Two named species, two named directions, each tied to oxygen. The two rejected shapes: (1) restating the definition of redox without naming anything; (2) "iron is reduced" — iron is the product; the thing that lost oxygen is the oxide. The electron version also scores: iron(III) ions gain electrons.

Bonus connection: aluminium here is the reducing agent — it removes the oxygen — exactly the role carbon plays in extracting iron in the metal-extraction module.

questions.promptHtml: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert graphite electrodes. Predict what happens at each electrode, what you would see, and what the solution contains at the end.
questions.answerHtml:
Cathode: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — a pink/brown coating of copper grows on the electrode.

Anode: no halide present, so oxygen from water: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ — you see effervescence/bubbles (that is the observation; "oxygen" is a name, not a sight).

End state: Cu²⁺ is progressively removed, so the blue colour fades; H⁺ accumulates with the SO₄²⁻, leaving dilute sulfuric acid. This is 2021's products-table row and 2023 Q5 in one story.

questions.promptHtml: A student weighs the negative electrode every five minutes while copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed. The mass rises steadily, then stops changing even though the current is still on. Why does it stop — and what is still happening in the cell?
questions.answerHtml:
Why it rises: Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons at the cathode and copper is deposited, so the electrode gets heavier.

Why it stops: there are no copper(II) ions left in the solution — all the copper has been deposited. The blue colour will have gone too. (This is the 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C mark scheme, word for word.)

What carries on: the current still flows, but now the only cations left are H⁺ ions. So hydrogen bubbles off at the cathode, and oxygen keeps forming at the anode — the cell is now just electrolysing the sulfuric acid, which means electrolysing water. Running the cathode flowchart again with "no copper left" gives exactly this answer.

modules.title: Metal Extraction and the Reactivity Series
modules.standfirst: One list decides everything: how a metal reacts, what displaces what, how a metal is found, and how it is extracted. Add rusting and alloys and you have a topic that turns up in most real Edexcel papers. The reasoning it teaches — carbon as a reducing agent, the more reactive metal wins — is the backbone of redox questions elsewhere.

subsections.html: Metals differ in how easily they react and how tightly they hold on to their compounds. Rank them once — the reactivity series — and reactions with acid, displacement, rusting protection and the choice of extraction method all read straight off the list.

subsections.heading: The reactivity series — learn the order
subsections.html:
Spec 2.17 · used in every question in this module

The reactivity series lists metals from most reactive to least reactive, and you must know the order by heart.

The order — most reactive firstK · Na · Li · Ca · Mg · Al · (C) · Zn · Fe · (H) · Cu · Ag · Aupotassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold · carbon and hydrogen are non-metal markers

Carbon and hydrogen are slotted in as markers. Carbon's position decides extraction: metals below it can be extracted with carbon. Hydrogen's position decides acids: metals below it do not react with dilute acids. A mnemonic helps (Please Send Lions Cats Monkeys And Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries Signed Gerald) — but the exam rewards the order, not the rhyme.

✗ Putting lithium above sodium. It is K, Na, Li in this spec's list.
✗ Swapping zinc and iron. Zinc is above iron — which is the whole reason galvanising works.
✓ K Na Li Ca Mg Al · C · Zn Fe · H · Cu Ag Au.

equations.name: The order — most reactive first
equations.formula: K · Na · Li · Ca · Mg · Al · (C) · Zn · Fe · (H) · Cu · Ag · Au

subsections.heading: Reactions with water and dilute acids
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15, 2.21 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)

The more reactive the metal, the more vigorously it reacts with water and with dilute acid — so the vigour of the reaction ranks the metals.

Metal + watermetal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogene.g. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
Metal + dilute acidmetal + acid → salt + hydrogene.g. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ · Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂
MetalCold waterDilute acid
K, Na, LiFizz, float, move around; K even catches fireNever tried — explosive, too dangerous
CaFizzes steadilyToo vigorous — not done
MgVery slow (reacts well with steam)Vigorous fizzing, tube gets hot
ZnNo visible reactionSteady fizzing
FeNo visible reactionSlow fizzing
Cu, Ag, AuNo reactionNo reaction — below hydrogen

The practical (spec 2.21) compares metals fairly:

  1. Put the same volume of the same concentration of dilute acid into separate test tubes, all at the same starting temperature.
  2. Add the same mass of each metal, in pieces of the same size (same surface area).
  3. Observe the rate of bubbling. You can also measure the temperature rise, or collect the gas and measure its volume in a set time.
  4. Rank the metals: fastest bubbling or biggest temperature rise = most reactive.
  5. Test the gas with a lighted splint: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.

✗ "Potassium should not be added to acid because it is flammable."
✓ "It would react explosively / violently — it is dangerous." That was the 2024 mark.
✗ "Hydrogen relights a glowing splint." That is oxygen.
✓ "A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop."

subsections.heading: Placing unknown metals from observations — the method
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15, 2.16 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(b)

A metal that reacts more vigorously, or displaces more of the others, is higher in the series. The exam gives you letters instead of names so you have to use the evidence, not your memory.

  1. Read every row of the table and mark each metal's reactions: none, slow, steady, vigorous.
  2. If there is a displacement grid, count the ticks for each metal. Each tick means it pushed another metal out.
  3. The metal with the most reactions / most ticks goes at the top. The one with none goes at the bottom.
  4. Check every pair: if A displaces B, A must be above B in your list.
  5. If named metals are included, fit the unknown between them using the order you know. Then name a real metal that sits there.

Worked example — a displacement grid

Three metals A, B and C are each added to solutions of the nitrates of A, B and C. ✓ = a reaction happened.

Metal addedA nitrateB nitrateC nitrate
A—✓✓
B✗—✗
C✗✓—

Step 1. Count ticks: A = 2, C = 1, B = 0.

Step 2. Order: A (most reactive) → C → B (least reactive).

Step 3. Check pairs: A displaces C ✓ (A above C); C displaces B ✓ (C above B). Consistent.

Why the dashes? A metal is never tested with its own salt — a metal cannot displace itself. That was a whole mark in 2023 Jan Q5.

If a question says "metal X is between aluminium and copper", the answer is a real metal from that gap: zinc or iron.

subsections.heading: Displacement in solution — observations and ionic equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.16, 2.20 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(c)–(d) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5

A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt; a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.

Iron in copper(II) sulfate solution:

Word and symbol equationiron + copper(II) sulfate → iron(II) sulfate + copperFe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)

What you see: the blue colour fades (turning pale green), and a pink-brown solid — copper — coats the iron. Magnesium or zinc in copper(II) sulfate does the same, but the solution goes colourless and the mixture gets warm.

The reverse — copper in iron(II) sulfate — gives no reaction. Writing "no reaction, because copper is less reactive than iron" is a full answer.

An ionic equation shows only the particles that change. It is the clearest way to see the electrons move. The method:

  1. Write the balanced equation with state symbols: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
  2. Split every (aq) ionic compound into its ions: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + Cu(s)
  3. Cross out ions that are the same on both sides — the spectator ions. Here, SO₄²⁻.
  4. Write what is left: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
  5. Check the atoms and the total charge balance: 2+ on the left, 2+ on the right.

Worked example — when the charges are different

Copper in silver nitrate solution. Copper is above silver, so it displaces it.

Full: Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s)

Ionic: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)

Charge check: left 2 × (+1) = +2; right +2. Balanced.

Electrons: one Cu atom loses 2 electrons; each of two Ag⁺ ions gains 1. Two lost = two gained.

Seen: the solution turns blue (Cu²⁺ ions) and silvery-grey crystals of silver grow on the copper.

Worked example — magnesium and aluminium ions (2023 Jan style)

Magnesium displaces aluminium from a solution of an aluminium salt.

Unbalanced: Mg + Al³⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Al — charge +3 on the left, +2 on the right. Wrong.

Balance the electrons: each Mg loses 2e⁻, each Al³⁺ gains 3e⁻. The lowest common number is 6.

So: 3Mg + 2Al³⁺ → 3Mg²⁺ + 2Al — charge +6 = +6.

Mark scheme wording: magnesium is the reducing agent 1; magnesium donates / loses electrons to the Al³⁺ ions 1

✗ "Iron displaces magnesium from magnesium sulfate."
✓ "No reaction: iron is less reactive than magnesium / lower in the reactivity series." (2023 Q2(d))
✗ Leaving the sulfate ions in an "ionic" equation.
✓ Spectator ions are crossed out: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).

equations.name: Word and symbol equation
equations.formula: iron + copper(II) sulfate → iron(II) sulfate + copper

subsections.heading: Displacement with a metal oxide — the thermite reaction
subsections.html:
Spec 2.16, 2.20 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b) · 2024 Q5a

A more reactive metal heated with the oxide of a less reactive metal takes the oxygen away from it.

Thermite2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fevery exothermic — the iron is produced molten · balancing numbers are marked

Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it can remove the oxygen from iron(III) oxide. The reaction gives out so much heat that the iron comes out molten — it is used to weld railway lines. The same idea works on a small scale: magnesium heated with copper(II) oxide glows and leaves pink-brown copper: Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu.

Why it is redox — built step by step:

  1. Aluminium gains oxygen, so aluminium is oxidised.
  2. Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so iron(III) oxide is reduced.
  3. Oxidation and reduction happen together, so it is a redox reaction. Aluminium is the reducing agent.

The two-mark script for "explain why this is a redox reaction"

1. Aluminium gains oxygen, so it is oxidised 1

2. Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced 1

Name the oxide, not "iron". "Oxidation and reduction happen at the same time", with nothing named, scores zero.

✗ "Iron is reduced." — Iron is the product. The thing that lost oxygen is iron(III) oxide.
✗ "Exothermic means it needs heat." — It needs heat to start, but exothermic means heat is given out to the surroundings.
✓ "Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it removes the oxygen from iron(III) oxide."

subsections.heading: Rusting — the conditions
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q2(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)

Iron rusts only when both oxygen and water are present. Take either one away and it does not rust.

Rusting — word equationiron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxiderust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O · a brown solid · the iron is oxidised

The classic experiment uses three test tubes, each with an iron nail:

  1. Tube 1 — air and water: nail in ordinary tap water, open to the air. Rusts.
  2. Tube 2 — water, no air: nail in boiled water (boiling removes the dissolved oxygen) with a layer of oil on top (stops oxygen dissolving back in). No rust.
  3. Tube 3 — air, no water: nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride, which absorbs water vapour, and a stopper. No rust.
  4. Conclusion: only tube 1 has both, so both oxygen and water are needed.

Rusting is oxidation: the iron gains oxygen. It is not combustion, neutralisation or decomposition — the real papers have offered all three as wrong options. Rusting uses up oxygen, which is why damp iron wool in a sealed tube of air can be used to find the percentage of oxygen in air (about 21%). Iron powder or wool rusts faster than a nail because it has a larger surface area.

✗ "Iron rusts when it gets wet." — Only one of the two. Both marks need oxygen (air is accepted) and water.
✗ "Rust is iron oxide." — Too vague for the name mark.
✓ "Oxygen and water." · "Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide."
✗ "Aluminium and copper rust too." — Only iron (and steel) rusts. Other metals corrode.

equations.name: Rusting — word equation
equations.formula: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide

subsections.heading: Preventing rusting — barriers, galvanising and sacrificial protection
subsections.html:
Spec 2.19 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q2 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(b) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(a)(iii)

You stop rust either by keeping oxygen and water away from the iron, or by attaching a more reactive metal that reacts instead.

MethodWhat is doneHow it works
BarrierPaint, oil or grease, plastic coating, electroplating (e.g. chromium)Keeps oxygen and water away from the iron. Fails if scratched.
GalvanisingCoat the iron with a layer of zincA barrier and sacrificial: zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron — even if scratched
Sacrificial protectionAttach blocks of a more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium) to ships' hulls, pipesThe more reactive metal oxidises instead of the iron

Sacrificial protection explained as a chain:

  1. Zinc (or magnesium) is more reactive than iron.
  2. So it loses electrons more easily — it is oxidised in preference.
  3. The zinc corrodes instead of the iron. It is "sacrificed".
  4. The iron stays protected as long as some zinc is left, even if the coating is scratched.

The two-mark script for "explain how sacrificial protection / galvanising prevents rusting"

1. Zinc (or a named metal) is more reactive than iron 1

2. so the zinc reacts / oxidises / corrodes instead of the iron 1

"Zinc forms a protective layer" only explains the barrier part. The second mark needs instead of the iron.

✗ "Copper can be used for sacrificial protection." — Copper is below iron. It would make the iron rust faster.
✗ "Paint protects the iron even when scratched." — A scratch exposes the iron to oxygen and water, so it rusts.
✓ "Galvanised iron is still protected when scratched because zinc is more reactive and corrodes instead of the iron."

subsections.heading: Ores, and why gold needs no chemistry
subsections.html:
Spec 2.22C

Most metals are found combined in ores and must be extracted; unreactive metals such as gold are found as the uncombined element.

An ore is a rock containing enough of a metal compound (often an oxide or sulfide) to be worth extracting. The unreactive metals — gold, and sometimes silver — are found native: they are too unreactive to have formed compounds in the first place. The pattern: the more reactive the metal, the more strongly it holds on to its compound, and the more powerful (and expensive) the method needed to get it out.

subsections.heading: Extraction: the carbon line
subsections.html:
Spec 2.23C · 2023 Q2b · 2023 Q9b

Metals below carbon are extracted by heating their oxide with carbon; metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis.

Extraction is reduction — removing oxygen from the metal oxide. Carbon is cheap; electricity is expensive. So the method follows the position:

  1. Find the metal in the reactivity series.
  2. Below carbon (zinc, iron, copper): carbon is more reactive, so heating the oxide with carbon removes the oxygen. Cheap.
  3. Above carbon (aluminium, magnesium and higher): the metal is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove its oxygen.
  4. These metals are extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound. It needs a lot of electricity (and heat to melt the ore), so it is expensive.
Iron — carbon extraction2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂carbon (coke) removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide · the blast-furnace details are not needed
Copper — carbon extraction2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂formulae one mark, balancing the second (2023 Q9b)
Aluminium — electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂at the cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al — the electrons do the job carbon cannot

✗ "Magnesium can't be extracted with carbon because it is too expensive." — That is the effect, not the reason.
✓ "Magnesium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from magnesium oxide." (2023 Q2b — one mark, exactly that.)
✗ "Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide solution." — It is insoluble. Say molten.

equations.name: Aluminium — electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide

subsections.heading: The role-of-carbon two-marker — the school's favourite
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20, 2.23C · 2024 Q8c · 2025 Q6c — identical question, consecutive years

Carbon is the reducing agent: it removes oxygen from the named compound. That one sentence is both marks.

The two-mark script for "explain the role of carbon"

1. Carbon is the reducing agent 1

2. It removes the oxygen from [calcium phosphate / copper(II) oxide / the named compound] 1

Rejected: "reacts with the oxygen", "displaces the oxygen", or naming only half the compound. The oxygen is removed from something — say what.

✗ "Carbon reacts with the oxygen in the calcium phosphate."
✗ "Carbon is more reactive so it displaces the calcium." — ignored in 2025.
✓ "Carbon is the reducing agent. It removes oxygen from calcium phosphate."

subsections.heading: Commenting on an unfamiliar extraction
subsections.html:
Spec 2.24C · 2021 Q10b · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(b)

You are not expected to know the process — the question gives the information, and you apply reactivity and redox to it.

Work through the same checklist every time:

  1. Where is the metal relative to carbon? That tells you whether carbon or something stronger is needed.
  2. What is reduced, and by what? Name the reducing agent and the compound that loses oxygen (or whose ions gain electrons).
  3. Why each condition? An inert gas such as argon stops oxygen in the air reacting with the hot metals. High temperature speeds the reaction.
  4. Cost: electricity, high temperatures, or a reducing agent that was itself expensive to make.
  5. Pollution: for example, roasting sulfide ores gives sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

Worked example — two real processes

Copper pyrites (2021): stage 1 is 2CuFeS₂ + 3O₂ → 2CuS + 2FeO + 2SO₂. The sulfur is oxidised because it gains oxygen (to become SO₂). Stage 2: CuS + O₂ → Cu + SO₂.

Titanium (2022 Edexcel 2C Q6): titanium dioxide is first turned into titanium chloride using chlorine. Then the titanium chloride is heated with magnesium under argon:

TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂ — a displacement: magnesium is more reactive than titanium.

Why argon (2 marks): argon is unreactive / inert 1; so oxygen in the air cannot react with / oxidise the magnesium (or titanium) 1

✗ "The sulfur forms sulfur dioxide." — names the product but doesn't apply the definition. Ignored in 2021.
✓ "The sulfur is oxidised because it gains oxygen."
✗ "Argon is used to keep it safe." — Say why: it is unreactive, so the metal is not oxidised.

subsections.heading: Uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel
subsections.html:
Spec 2.25C

Every use must be linked to a property — "used for wires" scores nothing without "because it conducts electricity".

MetalPropertyUse
AluminiumLow density; resists corrosion (a thin oxide layer protects it); conducts electricityAircraft bodies; overhead power cables (light and conducts); drinks cans; window frames
CopperVery good electrical conductor; ductile (can be drawn into wires); unreactive — does not react with waterElectrical wiring; water pipes
IronPure iron is quite soft; mostly made into steelUsed as steel
Low-carbon (mild) steelStrong and malleable — easily shapedCar bodies, ships, bridges, nails
High-carbon steelHarder and stronger, but more brittleCutting tools, drill bits
Stainless steelResists corrosion — does not rustCutlery, sinks, surgical instruments

Aluminium is above iron in the series, yet it does not corrode away. That is because its surface quickly forms a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that stops further reaction.

subsections.heading: Alloys — why they are harder
subsections.html:
Spec 2.26C, 2.27C · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(c)

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, and the different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding, so the alloy is harder.

An alloy is a mixture of a metal and one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Steel is iron mixed with carbon (stainless steel also contains chromium and nickel).

  1. In a pure metal, all the atoms are the same size and sit in regular layers.
  2. When a force is applied, the layers slide over each other easily — so the pure metal is soft and malleable.
  3. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes are mixed in.
  4. They distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other as easily.
  5. So the alloy is harder / stronger than the pure metal.

The three-mark script (2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(c))

1. In the pure metal the atoms are all the same size / the layers can slide 1

2. The alloy has atoms of different sizes 1

3. which disrupt the layers, so they cannot slide as easily 1

✗ "An alloy is a compound of two metals." — It is a mixture. No chemical bonds between the elements.
✗ "The bonds in an alloy are stronger." — Not the reason the scheme wants.
✓ "Different-sized atoms distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily."

The sentences behind most of the marks

K Na Li Ca Mg Al · C · Zn Fe · H · Cu Ag Au. Above carbon → electrolysis of the molten compound. Below carbon → heat the oxide with carbon. Below hydrogen → no reaction with dilute acids.

Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. A less reactive metal gives no reaction.

Role of carbon: it is the reducing agent; it removes oxygen from [named compound].

Rusting: needs oxygen and water. Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Rusting is oxidation.

Sacrificial protection: zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the iron.

Alloys: different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide — harder.

questions.promptHtml: Gold has been used by humans for 6,000 years; aluminium was more expensive than gold until the 1880s. Explain both facts from the reactivity series.
questions.answerHtml:
Gold sits at the bottom. It is so unreactive that it never formed compounds in the crust. It is found native, ready to pick up and work: no chemistry needed, hence its ancient history.

Aluminium sits above carbon. No fire-and-charcoal method can remove the oxygen from Al₂O₃, because aluminium is more reactive than carbon. Until large-scale electrolysis existed there was no practical way to reduce its ore. The metal was rare not because the ore was rare — it is everywhere — but because the method was missing. Reactivity sets the price of extraction.

questions.promptHtml: Zinc powder is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. State the observations, the equation, and why the reverse experiment (copper in zinc sulfate) does nothing.
questions.answerHtml:
Observations: the blue colour fades to colourless (Cu²⁺ ions leaving the solution), a pink-brown solid (copper) forms, the zinc gets used up, and the mixture warms up. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, or as an ionic equation Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

Zinc is above copper, so zinc atoms lose electrons more easily. They hand two electrons each to Cu²⁺ ions, which become copper atoms. Copper in zinc sulfate would have to do the opposite — give electrons to Zn²⁺ — and copper holds its electrons more tightly than that. No reaction — and writing exactly that is the expected answer.

questions.promptHtml: Reduction is defined as "loss of oxygen" and also as "gain of electrons". Show, using iron(III) oxide and carbon, that the two definitions agree.
questions.answerHtml:
In Fe₂O₃ the iron is present as Fe³⁺ ions, held with O²⁻ ions. When carbon removes the oxygen, what is left is iron metal — neutral Fe atoms.

To get from Fe³⁺ to Fe, each iron ion must gain three electrons: Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe. So the same event can be described two ways. Following the atoms: iron(III) oxide lost oxygen. Following the electrons: the iron ions gained electrons. Both say "reduced".

The electron version is more general — it also works when no oxygen is involved at all, as in Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, or at the cathode in electrolysis.

questions.promptHtml: Why is iron extracted with carbon but aluminium by electrolysis, when both are common structural metals — and what single cost drives the whole decision?
questions.answerHtml:
Iron is below carbon in the series. Heat iron(III) oxide with carbon and the carbon removes the oxygen — and carbon (coke) is cheap.

Aluminium is above carbon. Carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide, so the electrons must be supplied directly — electrolysis of the molten compound, using huge amounts of electricity, plus the energy to keep it molten.

The driving cost is energy — electricity versus cheap carbon. So an answer about extraction cost must tie back to position: not "electrolysis is expensive" alone, but "aluminium's reactivity forces the expensive method".

questions.promptHtml: 2021's copper pyrites question: stage 1 is 2CuFeS₂ + 3O₂ → 2CuS + 2FeO + 2SO₂. Explain why the sulfur is described as oxidised, and why "it forms sulfur dioxide" was not enough for the mark.
questions.answerHtml:
The sulfur starts combined with metals (no oxygen) and ends as SO₂. It has gained oxygen, which is the definition of oxidation the question wants. Full sentence: "the sulfur is oxidised because it gains oxygen."

"It forms SO₂" was ignored because it names the product without applying the definition. The mark tests whether you connect the observation to "gained oxygen". The schemes do this everywhere: give the definition-level reason (gained oxygen / lost electrons), not just the outcome.

questions.promptHtml: A painted iron gate and a galvanised iron gate both get a deep scratch. Only the painted one rusts at the scratch. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Paint is only a barrier. It works by keeping oxygen and water away from the iron. Scratch it and the iron underneath meets oxygen and water, so it rusts — and the rust can spread under the paint.

Zinc is a barrier and a sacrifice. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so even where the iron is exposed, the zinc next to it is oxidised instead. It gives up electrons more readily than iron, so the iron is not oxidised.

The test question: would a coating of copper protect a scratched gate? No — copper is below iron, so the iron would be the one oxidised. It would rust even faster.

questions.promptHtml: Pure iron is soft and bends easily. Adding a small amount of carbon makes steel, which is much harder. How can adding so little make such a difference?
questions.answerHtml:
In pure iron every atom is the same size, so the atoms sit in neat, regular layers. Push on the metal and whole layers slide over each other — that is why it bends.

A carbon atom is a different size from an iron atom. Even a few of them scattered through the structure distort the layers, so the layers catch on each other and cannot slide as easily. The metal is harder.

That is also why more carbon gives a harder but more brittle steel (high-carbon steel for cutting tools), while mild steel stays malleable enough to press into car bodies.

questions.promptHtml: In the rusting experiment, one nail sits in boiled water under a layer of oil, and another sits in a stoppered tube with anhydrous calcium chloride. What is each tube testing, and why does each detail matter?
questions.answerHtml:
Boiled water + oil tests "water but no oxygen". Boiling drives out the dissolved oxygen. The oil layer stops oxygen from the air dissolving back in. Leave out either step and oxygen gets to the nail, so the test fails.

Calcium chloride tests "oxygen but no water". Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs water vapour, so the air is dry. The stopper stops damp air getting in.

Neither nail rusts, but the nail in ordinary water open to the air does. The only thing it has that both others lack is both substances — so oxygen and water are both needed.

subsections.html: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds of hydrogen and carbon only. Everything in this module is sorting that mixture (distillation), naming its members (alkanes, isomers), breaking them up (cracking) and burning them (combustion and its pollution).

subsections.heading: Hydrocarbons and crude oil
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1, 4.7 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1(a)(i) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(a)

A hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon only, and crude oil is a mixture of lots of them.

Two words carry the marks. Compound — the hydrogen and carbon are chemically bonded, not just mixed. Only — the moment a molecule contains an oxygen or a bromine atom, it is no longer a hydrocarbon. 2023 Jan showed a table of structures and asked which was not a hydrocarbon: the answer was the one with an –OH group, because it contains oxygen.

Crude oil is a mixture, not a compound. Its hydrocarbons are not bonded to each other, so they keep their own boiling points — and that is exactly what lets us separate them.

✗ "A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon." — misses only: glucose contains hydrogen and carbon too.
✗ "Crude oil is a hydrocarbon." — it is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
✓ "A hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon only."

subsections.heading: Fractional distillation — the four-marker to memorise
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8 · 2023 Q11 · 2024 Q9a · 2025 Q8a · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(a) · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q3(b)

Heat the crude oil so it boils, let the vapours rise up a column that gets cooler towards the top, and each hydrocarbon condenses at the height where the column is cooler than its boiling point.

Crude oil is separated into fractions — groups of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points. The equipment is the fractionating column; the process is fractional distillation. 2022 asked for the equipment and ignored the process name, so read which one the question wants. The chain, in order:

  1. The crude oil is heated until most of it is vaporised (turned into gas).
  2. The vapours enter the bottom of the column and rise up it.
  3. The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top — a temperature gradient.
  4. Each vapour keeps rising until it reaches a height where the column temperature is below its boiling point.
  5. There it condenses back to a liquid and is tapped off as a fraction.
  6. Short molecules (low boiling points) get near the top; long molecules (high boiling points) condense low down; the shortest leave the top as gas, and bitumen drains from the bottom.

The four-mark script

1. The crude oil is heated / vaporised (before entering the column) 1

2. The vapours rise up the column 1

3. The column is hotter at the bottom than the top (a temperature gradient) 1

4. Each vapour rises until it condenses — at the height where the column temperature drops below its boiling point 1

The two marks that die: forgetting the vapours rise, and saying "turns to liquid" without tying it to the boiling point.

✗ "The crude oil is separated by boiling point." — true, but it describes nothing. No heating, no rising, no condensing: 0 of 4.
✗ "The fractions turn back into liquid at the top." — no link to boiling point, and most don't reach the top.
✓ "The vapours rise up the column, which is cooler at the top, and each condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point."

subsections.heading: The fractions — names, uses and trends
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9, 4.10 · 2021 Q9 · 2022 Q11 · 2024 Q9 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q3(a) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q3(a)

Going down the column, the molecules get longer, so the fractions boil higher, get darker and get thicker.

Fraction (top → bottom)Use
Refinery gasesBottled gas for heating and cooking — lowest boiling point
Gasoline (petrol)Fuel for cars
Kerosene (paraffin)Fuel for aircraft (jet fuel)
DieselFuel for lorries, trains and some cars
Fuel oilFuel for ships and power stations
BitumenRoad surfacing and roofs — most viscous, highest boiling point

A mnemonic for the order: Real Girls Keep Diesel For Businesses — refinery gases, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen.

The three trends the spec names, all increasing down the column: boiling point rises, colour darkens (pale yellow to black), viscosity rises (runny to thick and sticky). All three are caused by the molecules getting longer.

✗ "Bitumen has the lowest boiling point because it is at the bottom." — the bottom is the hottest part; bitumen has the highest.
✗ "Kerosene is used for cars." — cars use gasoline; kerosene is aircraft fuel.
✓ "Refinery gases have the lowest boiling point; bitumen is the most viscous."

subsections.heading: Why longer molecules boil higher
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2024 Q9b

Longer molecules have stronger forces between the molecules, so more energy is needed to pull them apart.

Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. It does not break the covalent bonds inside them. The chain:

  1. A longer hydrocarbon molecule has more atoms and more surface in contact with its neighbours.
  2. So the intermolecular forces between the molecules are stronger.
  3. So more energy is needed to overcome them.
  4. So the boiling point is higher.

The three-mark script (2024)

1. Fraction B has longer chains / larger molecules 1

2. Stronger intermolecular forces between the molecules 1

3. More energy needed to overcome them 1

✗ "Stronger forces between the atoms." — rejected: atoms are held by covalent bonds, which are not broken.
✗ "More covalent bonds need to be broken." — the scheme gave no marks at all for this.
✓ "Longer molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to overcome them."

subsections.heading: Five ways to write one molecule
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2 · 2024 Q4a · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q4(c)(i) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(d)

The same molecule can be written five ways, and each question asks for a particular one — give the one it asks for.

Formula typeWhat it showsButane
MolecularThe actual number of each atomC₄H₁₀
EmpiricalThe simplest whole-number ratio of atomsC₂H₅
GeneralThe formula for the whole family, in terms of nCₙH₂ₙ₊₂
StructuralHow the atoms are arranged, carbon by carbon, without drawing bondsCH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
DisplayedEvery atom and every bond drawn as a linefour C in a row, ten H, every C–H and C–C line drawn

Worked example — molecular to empirical

Find the biggest number that divides into both subscripts, then divide.

Butane C₄H₁₀: both divide by 2 → C₂H₅

Hexane C₆H₁₄: both divide by 2 → C₃H₇

C₄H₆ (2023 Edexcel 1C): both divide by 2 → C₂H₃

Propane C₃H₈: nothing divides into 3 and 8 → empirical formula is C₃H₈, the same as the molecular.

✗ Displayed formula with –CH₃ written as a lump at the end. — Not displayed; the C–H bonds are hidden. Mark lost.
✗ "Empirical formula of ethane is C₂H₆." — it simplifies: CH₃.
✓ In a displayed formula, count: every carbon has exactly four lines coming from it, every hydrogen exactly one.

subsections.heading: Homologous series and the alkanes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.3, 4.4, 4.19, 4.20 · 2021 Q9 · 2022 Q11b · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)(i)

The alkanes are a family of saturated hydrocarbons that all fit the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

General formula of the alkanes — memoriseCₙH₂ₙ₊₂n = number of carbon atoms · double it and add two to get the hydrogens

A homologous series is a family of compounds like this. Two real Edexcel papers asked for two characteristics. Pick any two:

  • the same general formula
  • the same functional group
  • similar chemical properties (they react in the same ways)
  • a trend in physical properties, such as boiling point rising with chain length
  • each member differs from the next by CH₂

A functional group is the atom or group of atoms that decides how a compound reacts. For alkenes it is the C=C double bond.

Alkanes are saturated: they contain only single carbon–carbon bonds, so every carbon already has its full four bonds and nothing more can add on.

Naming — the start of the name counts the carbons; the ending -ane means alkane:

CarbonsPrefixAlkaneFormula
1meth-methaneCH₄
2eth-ethaneC₂H₆
3prop-propaneC₃H₈
4but-butaneC₄H₁₀
5pent-pentaneC₅H₁₂
6hex-hexaneC₆H₁₄

✗ "Triane" for C₃H₈. — 2023: "spelling must be correct". Prefixes are meth, eth, prop, but, pent.
✗ "Alkanes are saturated because they are full of hydrogen." — vague.
✓ "Alkanes are saturated because they contain only single C–C bonds."

subsections.heading: Isomers — a step-by-step method for drawing and naming
subsections.html:
Spec 4.3, 4.5, 4.21 · 2023 Q8 · 2024 Q4b · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q5(a) · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q8(a)(i) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(e) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(a)(iv)

Isomers have the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of atoms — the same atoms, joined up differently.

The two-mark definition — asked on six papers

1. Compounds with the same molecular formula 1

2. but different structural / displayed formulae 1

"Same chemical formula" lost M1 in 2023. Say molecular.

The method for drawing every isomer of an alkane:

  1. Draw the longest chain — all the carbons in one straight line. That is the unbranched isomer (butane, pentane).
  2. Shorten the chain by one carbon and attach that carbon as a CH₃ branch to a middle carbon — never to an end carbon (that just makes the long chain again).
  3. If carbons remain, shorten again and use two branches — on the same middle carbon, or on different ones.
  4. Add hydrogens so every carbon has exactly four bonds.
  5. Check the count: same number of C and H as the molecular formula.
  6. Check it is new: find the longest continuous carbon chain in your drawing. If it matches one you already have, it is the same molecule bent round, not an isomer.
  7. Name it: the longest chain gives the name (but-, pent-); each branch is "methyl"; a number says which carbon it is on.

Worked example — the isomers of C₅H₁₂

Five in a row: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ — pentane

Four in a row + one branch on carbon 2: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ — 2-methylbutane

Three in a row + two branches both on the middle carbon: C(CH₃)₄ — 2,2-dimethylpropane

Check: each has 5 C and 12 H. There are exactly three. For C₄H₁₀ the same method gives two: butane and methylpropane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.

The spec only requires you to name the unbranched isomers (butane, pentane), but the branched names above are what the mark schemes use, so learn them.

✗ Drawing pentane with a bend in it and calling it an isomer. — Bending a chain does not change it. Trace the longest chain: still five.
✗ A CH₃ branch on the end carbon of a four-carbon chain. — That is just pentane again.
✗ A carbon with five bonds. — Count every carbon: exactly four lines.
✓ Longest chain first, then shorten by one and branch in the middle, then check counts and chains.

subsections.heading: Fuels and complete combustion
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6, 4.11, 4.12 · 2024 Q4d · 2025 Q9a–b

A fuel releases heat energy when it burns; with plenty of oxygen, a hydrocarbon burns completely to carbon dioxide and water.

Complete combustion — memorisehydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + waterneeds plenty of air · the carbon goes to CO₂, the hydrogen goes to H₂O

Every carbon atom in the fuel ends up in a CO₂ molecule, and every pair of hydrogen atoms ends up in an H₂O molecule. The reaction type is combustion — one of the three the spec asks you to recognise, with substitution and addition.

✗ "Methane burns to give carbon dioxide and hydrogen." — 2025: "Lots of students said hydrogen instead of water".
✓ "Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water."

subsections.heading: Balancing combustion equations — worked method
subsections.html:
Spec 4.12 · 2024 Q4d · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q8(d), (e)(i)

Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, and oxygen last — because oxygen is the only thing on the left you can freely change.

  1. Write the formulae: fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
  2. Carbon: put the number of C atoms in the fuel in front of CO₂.
  3. Hydrogen: halve the number of H atoms in the fuel and put it in front of H₂O.
  4. Oxygen: count the O atoms on the right. Halve it for the number in front of O₂.
  5. If that gives a half (e.g. 3½ O₂), double everything.
  6. Check each element on both sides.

Worked example 1 — propane, C₃H₈

Carbon: 3 C → 3CO₂

Hydrogen: 8 H → 4H₂O

Oxygen on the right: (3 × 2) + (4 × 1) = 10 O atoms → 5O₂

C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

Worked example 2 — ethane, C₂H₆ (the one that needs doubling)

Carbon: 2 C → 2CO₂

Hydrogen: 6 H → 3H₂O

Oxygen on the right: (2 × 2) + 3 = 7 O atoms → 3½ O₂ — a half, so double everything

2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O — the 2024 school paper's equation

Worked example 3 — working backwards from masses (2024 Edexcel 1C Q8(d) style)

1 mol of an alkane burns completely and makes 396 g of CO₂ and 180 g of H₂O.

Moles of CO₂ = 396 ÷ 44 = 9 → 9 carbon atoms in the fuel

Moles of H₂O = 180 ÷ 18 = 10 → 20 hydrogen atoms in the fuel, so it is C₉H₂₀ (fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂)

Oxygen on the right: (9 × 2) + 10 = 28 O atoms → 14O₂

C₉H₂₀ + 14O₂ → 9CO₂ + 10H₂O

✗ "C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O" — accepted by some schemes, but whole numbers are safer. Double it.
✗ Changing a formula to balance, e.g. writing CO₃. — Never change the small numbers, only the big ones in front.
✓ C, then H, then O; double if you get a half; check every element.

subsections.heading: Incomplete combustion and carbon monoxide
subsections.html:
Spec 4.12, 4.13 · 2025 Q9c · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q8(e)

With too little oxygen, some carbon ends up as poisonous carbon monoxide or as soot instead of carbon dioxide.

In a limited supply of air, there is not enough oxygen to turn all the carbon into CO₂. The hydrogen still becomes water. The possible products are:

  • carbon monoxide, CO — a colourless, odourless, poisonous gas
  • carbon, C — soot, the black smoke and yellow flame
  • water, and usually some carbon dioxide as well
Incomplete combustion of methane2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂Obalance the same way: C, then H, then O

Worked example — octane, C₈H₁₈ (2024 Edexcel 1C Q8(e))

Products given: 5CO, 3C and water.

Carbon: 5 + 3 = 8 ✓

Hydrogen: 18 H → 9H₂O

Oxygen on the right: 5 (in CO) + 9 (in H₂O) = 14 O atoms → 7O₂

C₈H₁₈(l) + 7O₂(g) → 5CO(g) + 3C(s) + 9H₂O(l) — one mark for balancing, one for state symbols

Why CO is poisonous: it reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen. That is the spec's own wording. You may add that it combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells — but only alongside the oxygen point.

✗ "CO is poisonous because it is toxic." — just repeats the question.
✗ "CO binds to haemoglobin." — on its own, 2025's scheme wanted oxygen mentioned.
✓ "Carbon monoxide reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen."

subsections.heading: Acid rain — sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
subsections.html:
Spec 4.14, 4.15, 4.16 · 2023 Q6a · 2025 Q8b · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q3(c) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(g)

Burning fuels releases sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen, which dissolve in rainwater to make acid rain.

Two chains. Each is marked link by link, and skipping a link loses the marks after it.

The sulfur chain:

  1. Some hydrocarbon fuels contain sulfur as an impurity.
  2. When the fuel burns, the sulfur reacts with oxygen to form sulfur dioxide, SO₂.
  3. SO₂ dissolves in rainwater, making it acidic.
  4. This is acid rain — it kills fish and trees and damages limestone buildings.

The nitrogen chain:

  1. Nitrogen and oxygen from the air are drawn into a car engine.
  2. The engine reaches a high enough temperature for them to react.
  3. They form oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ).
  4. These dissolve in rainwater to form nitric acid — acid rain.

The three-mark script — sulfur (2025, 2022 Edexcel 1C)

1. The fuel contains sulfur (impurity) 1

2. Burning produces sulfur dioxide 1

3. which dissolves in rain to cause acid rain 1 — dependent on the first two

✗ "Sulphur oxide causes acid rain." — rejected in 2025. Name it: sulfur dioxide.
✗ "The nitrogen comes from the petrol." — it comes from the air.
✗ "CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, causing global warming." — the wrong question. "Lots spoke about greenhouse gases instead."
✓ "The fuel contains sulfur, which burns to sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain to form acid rain."

subsections.heading: Cracking — making supply match demand
subsections.html:
Spec 4.17, 4.18 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q3(c) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q3(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(b)(i)

Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes, which nobody wants enough of, into shorter alkanes and alkenes, which are in demand.

Crude oil contains more long-chain hydrocarbons than we need and fewer short ones (for petrol) than we want. Catalytic cracking fixes the mismatch:

  1. Take a long-chain alkane from a fraction in surplus, e.g. fuel oil.
  2. Heat it to vaporise it, and pass the vapour over a hot catalyst of silica or alumina at 600–700 °C.
  3. The long molecules break into shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes.
  4. The short alkanes are used as petrol; the alkenes are used to make polymers (plastics).
Cracking decaneC₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄decane → octane (alkane) + ethene (alkene) · catalyst silica or alumina, 600–700 °C

Worked example — finding the missing product

C₁₄H₃₀ → C₁₀H₂₂ + 2 ____

Carbons left: 14 − 10 = 4, shared between 2 molecules → 2 C each

Hydrogens left: 30 − 22 = 8, shared between 2 molecules → 4 H each

Missing product: C₂H₄ (ethene). Check: 10 + 4 = 14 C, 22 + 8 = 30 H ✓

You can spot the alkene: it fits CₙH₂ₙ (twice as many H as C), not CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Cracking always makes at least one, because there are not enough hydrogens to make every fragment saturated.

Why cracking is necessary — the 2024 Edexcel 2C script (any three)

1. There is a surplus of long-chain fractions / not enough supply of short-chain fractions to meet demand 1

2. Alkenes are produced, which are needed to make polymers 1

3. Shorter alkanes are needed for petrol 1

✗ "Cracking separates crude oil into fractions." — that is fractional distillation. Cracking breaks molecules.
✗ "Catalyst: iron, 450 °C." — that is the Haber process. Cracking is silica or alumina, 600–700 °C.
✓ "Long-chain alkanes are broken down into shorter alkanes and alkenes, to match supply with demand."

subsections.heading: Substitution — alkanes with halogens
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6, 4.22 · 2021 Q9c · 2024 Q4c · 2025 Q9d · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q7(f) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q8(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q5(b)

In ultraviolet light, one halogen atom swaps in for one hydrogen atom on an alkane — a substitution reaction.

Alkanes are saturated, so nothing can add on. The only way a bromine atom can get in is to replace a hydrogen:

  1. UV light gives the energy to start the reaction.
  2. One Br atom replaces one H atom on the alkane.
  3. The organic product is a bromoalkane.
  4. The removed H joins the other Br atom as hydrogen bromide, HBr.
Methane + bromineCH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBrneeds ultraviolet light · bromomethane + hydrogen bromide
Any alkane — the patternCₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + Br₂ → CₙH₂ₙ₊₁Br + HBre.g. C₂H₆ → C₂H₅Br (bromoethane) · C₄H₁₀ → C₄H₉Br (2023 Jan Edexcel 1C)

Chlorine works the same way: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. At this level only one hydrogen is replaced (mono-substitution).

Classifying reactions — the spec's three types: combustion (burning in oxygen), substitution (one atom swaps for another — alkanes with halogens), addition (atoms add across a C=C double bond — alkenes only, so never an alkane).

✗ "Displacement" or "reduction". — 2025: "lots said displacement or reduction". It is substitution.
✗ "Heat" as the condition. — ignored. The condition is ultraviolet light (sunlight accepted).
✗ "HBR" or "hbr". — rejected. Write HBr.
✓ "CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr, in UV light — a substitution reaction."

The sentences behind most of the marks

The column: heated oil in at the bottom, vapours rise, hotter below than above, each fraction condenses where the column is cooler than its boiling point. Down the column: longer · hotter · darker · thicker.

Boiling point: longer molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy to overcome.

Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formulae.

Combustion: plenty of air → CO₂ + water; limited air → CO (and soot). CO reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen.

Acid rain: fuel contains sulfur → SO₂ → dissolves in rain. Engine heat → N₂ + O₂ from air react → oxides of nitrogen → nitric acid.

Cracking: long alkanes → shorter alkanes + alkenes, silica/alumina, 600–700 °C, to match supply and demand.

Substitution: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr in UV light.

questions.promptHtml: In the fractionating column, why does bitumen leave at the bottom and refinery gas at the top — walk the physics from "heated crude enters" to both exits.
questions.answerHtml:
The heated crude enters as a mixture of vapours (all but the heaviest, which stay liquid — bitumen drains straight out at the hot bottom). The vapours rise into progressively cooler regions. A long-chain compound has a high boiling point — the column temperature falls below it almost immediately, so it condenses low down (fuel oil, diesel). Short chains have low boiling points — the column never gets cold enough until near the top (gasoline), and the shortest (refinery gases, bp below room temperature) never condense at all and leave as gas.

Every fraction is executing the same rule — rise until your boiling point beats the local temperature — and the exits are just where that happens for each chain length.

questions.promptHtml: Butane and methylpropane are isomers. State three properties they share and one that differs, and explain why the difference exists.
questions.answerHtml:
Shared: molecular formula (C₄H₁₀), Mr (58), and general chemistry (both saturated alkanes — same combustion, same substitution reactions).

Different: boiling point. Butane's straight chain lets molecules lie alongside each other, giving more contact and stronger intermolecular forces; branched methylpropane packs less closely, weaker forces, so it boils lower (−12 °C vs −1 °C).

The principle: molecular formula fixes the chemistry; the shape fixes the physics. That is what "same molecular formula, different structure" means in practice.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a Bunsen flame burn blue with the air-hole open and yellow-sooty with it closed — and why is the closed-hole flame the dangerous one indoors?
questions.answerHtml:
Open hole: plenty of air → complete combustion → CO₂ + H₂O, maximum energy, clean blue flame.

Closed hole: limited oxygen → incomplete combustion → carbon monoxide and unburned carbon (the yellow glow and the soot are hot carbon particles).

The danger: the CO. It binds in the blood and reduces its capacity to transport oxygen — and it is colourless and odourless, so nothing warns you. Every gas appliance question (boilers, heaters in sealed rooms) is this chemistry wearing different clothes.

questions.promptHtml: Acid rain questions offer two different chains — sulfur and nitrogen. For each, state where the element comes from, and identify the step students most often skip.
questions.answerHtml:
Sulfur chain: the sulfur is an impurity in the fuel itself. Burning it gives SO₂; SO₂ + rain → acid rain. The skipped step: saying the fuel contains sulfur — 2025 made the acid-rain mark dependent on it, so answers that opened with "SO₂ is released" had already lost M1 and with it M3.

Nitrogen chain: the nitrogen is from the air, not the fuel. Car-engine temperatures are high enough to make nitrogen and oxygen react → oxides of nitrogen → acid rain. The skipped step: the high engine temperature — without it there is no reason unreactive N₂ would react.

And keep the chains apart from CO₂/greenhouse: acid rain and global warming are different questions with different gases.

questions.promptHtml: Why do alkanes react with bromine by substitution rather than addition, and why does the reaction only start in ultraviolet light?
questions.answerHtml:
Substitution, not addition: alkanes are saturated — every carbon already has four single bonds, so there is nowhere for extra atoms to add. The only way in is to swap: a bromine atom replaces a hydrogen, giving CH₃Br and the displaced hydrogen leaves in HBr. (Addition belongs to alkenes, which have a C=C double bond to open up.)

The UV: the light provides the energy to split Br₂ and start the reaction — in the dark, methane and bromine sit together indefinitely. Exam-level answer: "the reaction requires ultraviolet light" — with heat explicitly ignored by the scheme.

questions.promptHtml: An oil company cracks decane (C₁₀H₂₂) into octane and one other product. Write the equation, identify the other product's family, and explain why the company bothers.
questions.answerHtml:
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ — atoms conserved: 10 = 8 + 2 carbons, 22 = 18 + 4 hydrogens.

C₂H₄ (ethene) fits CₙH₂ₙ — an alkene, unsaturated. Cracking a saturated alkane must produce at least one double-bonded product because hydrogens are conserved but the fragments need fewer of them.

Why: demand and supply are mismatched — customers want petrol-length molecules, the ground supplies too many long ones. Cracking (silica/alumina catalyst, 600–700 °C) converts surplus long fractions into short ones — and the alkene by-product feeds polymer manufacture.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the general formula of the alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂? Work it out from the bonds rather than just learning it.
questions.answerHtml:
Each carbon makes four bonds, so n carbons have 4n bonds to give out.

In a chain of n carbons there are n − 1 C–C bonds joining them. Each of those uses up one bond from two carbons, so they use 2(n − 1) bonds in total.

Every bond left over goes to a hydrogen: 4n − 2(n − 1) = 4n − 2n + 2 = 2n + 2 hydrogens.

Check with butane: 2 × 4 + 2 = 10, so C₄H₁₀ ✓. Branching does not change the count — a branched chain still has n − 1 C–C bonds — which is why isomers share the same molecular formula.

Put a C=C double bond in and it uses up two more bonds, leaving 2n hydrogens — the alkene formula you see in cracking products.

questions.promptHtml: A student draws pentane as a straight chain, then draws it again with the chain bent into an L-shape, and says these are two isomers. Are they? How can you check any drawing?
questions.answerHtml:
No — they are the same molecule. Single C–C bonds can rotate, so a chain drawn bent is just the same chain drawn a different way on paper. Nothing about which atom is bonded to which has changed.

The check: put your pencil on one end carbon and trace the longest continuous chain of carbons without lifting. In the L-shape you still go through all five carbons in a row, so it is still pentane.

A genuine isomer has a different connection: in 2-methylbutane the longest chain is only four carbons, with the fifth carbon hanging off carbon 2 as a branch.

This matters because exam questions give pentane and ask for "the other two isomers" — drawing pentane bent scores nothing.

modules.standfirst: Year 11 topic. It comes up on almost every real paper, and usually as one of three things: sodium or lithium dropped into water, the six-mark halogen displacement explanation, or "explain, in terms of electrons, why X is more reactive than Y". The marks go to further from the nucleus, weaker attraction, and spelling -ine and -ide correctly.

Three mark-scheme lines that cost the most marks in this topic.

2024, on the colour of phenolphthalein in the sodium solution: "REJECT red or purple". The answer is pink, nothing else.

2023, on the six-mark displacement question: "Penalise incorrect use of -ine and -ide". Bromine is the element. Bromide is the ion in potassium bromide.

January 2023, on halogen boiling points: "No M2, M3 or M4 if any mention of breaking covalent/ionic bonds". Boiling a halogen breaks the intermolecular forces. It does not break the covalent bond inside the molecule.
