subsections.html: There is one idea behind this whole module: an atom's outer electrons decide how it reacts. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in the same way. As you go down a group the outer shell gets further from the nucleus, and that single change explains both reactivity trends. Group 1 gets more reactive going down. Group 7 gets less reactive going down. Group 0 has a full outer shell, so it hardly reacts at all.

subsections.heading: Why a group behaves like a family
subsections.html:
Spec 1.23 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(b)(i)

Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, so they have similar chemical properties. Chemical reactions happen at the outer shell, and that is where group members match.

GroupOuter electronsWhat the atom does when it reactsIon formed
1 — lithium 2.1, sodium 2.8.1, potassium 2.8.8.11Loses 1 electronLi⁺, Na⁺, K⁺
7 — fluorine 2.7, chlorine 2.8.77Gains 1 electronF⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻
0 — helium 2, neon 2.8, argon 2.8.8Full shell (2 for helium, 8 for the rest)Does not lose, gain or share electronsNone

✗ "Lithium and sodium react the same because they are both metals." Most metals do not react with water like this.
✗ "They have the same number of electrons." Lithium has 3 electrons and sodium has 11.
✓ "They have the same number of electrons in the outer shell — one."

subsections.heading: Group 1 in water: the family resemblance
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q6(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(a)

Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water to make a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas, and the solution left is alkaline. They give the same products in the same kind of reaction, and that is the evidence that they belong to one family.

Group 1 metal + water — general2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)M = Li, Na or K · metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen
Sodium + water2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)the equation printed in 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4

What you see, and why:

ObservationWhy it happens
FloatsThe metal is less dense than water
Fizzes (effervescence, bubbles)Hydrogen gas is given off
Moves around on the surfaceThe gas pushes the metal along
Gets smaller and disappearsThe metal is used up. It becomes ions in solution.
Melts into a ball (sodium and potassium)The reaction is exothermic and these metals have low melting points
Potassium: lilac flameSo much heat is released that the hydrogen catches fire

The solution is alkaline because it contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻. How that shows up depends on the indicator added:

Indicator in the waterColour at the end
PhenolphthaleinPink (colourless before)
Universal indicatorBlue / purple
Methyl orangeYellow
Red litmusTurns blue

Mark script — "Explain the colour of the phenolphthalein" (2)

1. The phenolphthalein turns pink 1

2. because hydroxide ions (OH⁻) are present — the solution is alkaline 1

✗ "It burns with a flame." For sodium the 2022 scheme said IGNORE references to a flame. It is a wasted line.
✗ "It dissolves and a gas is made." That is too vague to score. Name what you would see.
✓ Pick from: fizzes, moves on the surface, melts into a ball, gets smaller, white trail. The question usually tells you "floats" already, so choose two others.

2024 gave both marks for "moves on the surface", because it covers moves and floats. Read the stem: if it has already given you an observation, that one scores nothing.

subsections.heading: Lithium, sodium, potassium: the differences show the trend
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(a)

Reactivity increases down Group 1: potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium, and sodium more vigorously than lithium, with both water and air.

MetalWith waterFreshly cut surface in air
LithiumFloats, fizzes steadily, moves slowly, gets smaller. Does not melt.Shiny, then tarnishes slowly
SodiumFloats, fizzes quickly, melts into a ball, moves quickly, disappearsTarnishes quickly
PotassiumAll of sodium's signs, faster still. The hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame, sometimes with sparks and a crack.Tarnishes very quickly, almost at once

In air, the shiny metal reacts with oxygen to form a dull layer of oxide. That is tarnishing.

Group 1 metal + oxygen4Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O(s)same pattern for Li → Li₂O and K → K₂O · Group 1 oxides are basic

All three are soft enough to cut with a knife, and they get softer going down. They are stored under oil to keep air and water away from them.

✗ "Potassium reacts faster because it is bigger." Bigger is only the start of the explanation.
✓ "Potassium reacts more vigorously: it melts, and the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame." That is the evidence. The explanation is about electrons and comes in the next section.

subsections.heading: Explaining the Group 1 trend with electrons (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q1(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(b)(ii)

Going down Group 1, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is less strongly attracted and is lost more easily. So reactivity increases.

  1. A Group 1 atom reacts by losing its one outer electron.
  2. Down the group there are more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus. The inner shells also shield it.
  3. So the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker.
  4. So the outer electron is lost more easily, and the metal is more reactive.

Mark script — "Explain, in terms of electron configuration, why sodium is more reactive than lithium" (3)

1. Sodium's outer shell is further from the nucleus. Sodium has more shells (2.8.1 compared with 2.1), so it is a larger atom. 1

2. There is less attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron in sodium 1

3. So the outer electron is more easily lost 1

The 2022 question asked it the other way round ("why is lithium less reactive"). The same three points work in reverse: smaller atom, outer electron more strongly attracted, less easily lost.

✗ "Sodium has more electrons, so it loses them more easily."
✗ "…so its outer electrons are lost more easily." The 2024 scheme ignored the plural "electrons" in M1 and M2 but did not allow it in M3. Sodium loses one outer electron.
✓ "Sodium's outer electron is further from the nucleus, so there is weaker attraction, so it is lost more easily."

Spec 2.3

Continue the trends: rubidium and caesium react like potassium, but more violently, and they have even lower melting points.

Formulae come from the charge. Rubidium forms Rb⁺, just like Na⁺, so rubidium chloride is RbCl, just like NaCl. You do not need to have seen the compound before.

subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q4(c)

In every Group 1 + water equation, 2 mol of metal give 1 mol of hydrogen. Halve the moles of metal to get the moles of H₂.

0.150 g of lithium reacts with excess water and makes 254 cm³ of hydrogen. Show that 1 mol of gas is about 24 000 cm³. 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂ [Aᵣ of Li = 7]

  1. Moles of lithium = 0.150 ÷ 7 = 0.0214 mol

  3. Volume of 1 mol = 254 ÷ 0.0107

The scheme gave a mark for each of those four lines. Show every line. In a "show that" question the method is what you are marked on.

✗ Rounding to 1 significant figure (0.02 mol). The scheme penalised 1 s.f. in M1.
✓ Keep 3 significant figures until the last line.

subsections.heading: The halogens: colours and states
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(a)–(b)

Down Group 7 the halogens get darker in colour and go from gas to liquid to solid. They all exist as diatomic molecules: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

HalogenState at room temperatureColourColour in solution
Fluorine, F₂GasPale yellow — the palest—
Chlorine, Cl₂GasPale yellow-greenVery pale green, almost colourless
Bromine, Br₂LiquidRed-brown, giving off orange-brown vapourOrange (yellow when dilute)

The column you must know best is "colour in solution". Displacement questions are answered with these colours.

✗ "Iodine is purple." Only its vapour is purple. The solid is grey-black.
✗ "Bromine is a gas." Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
✓ Chlorine: pale green gas. Bromine: red-brown liquid. Iodine: grey-black solid.

subsections.html:

1. The boiling points increase down the group 1

2. because the intermolecular forces get stronger 1

3. as the molecules get larger (more mass, more electrons) 1

4. so more energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces

There are four points and three marks. Write all four and you are covered.

✗ "More energy is needed to break the covalent bonds." Under the January 2023 scheme this one phrase cost M2, M3 and M4.
✓ "More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces between the molecules." The Cl–Cl bond inside each molecule does not break when chlorine boils.

subsections.heading: Displacement reactions: the evidence for the Group 7 trend
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q7(d)

A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide. So whichever halogen "wins" is the more reactive one.

Halogen added ↓ / Halide solution →Potassium chloride, KClPotassium bromide, KBrPotassium iodide, KI
Chlorine water (pale green)—Turns orange. Bromine is made.Turns brown. Iodine is made.
Bromine water (orange)No change — stays orange—Turns brown. Iodine is made.
Iodine solution (brown)No changeNo change—

Chlorine displaces two others, bromine displaces one and iodine displaces none. That gives the order chlorine > bromine > iodine.

Chlorine displaces bromineCl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)colourless KBr solution turns orange
Chlorine displaces iodineCl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq)turns brown
Bromine displaces iodineBr₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq)orange turns brown

Mark script — the 2023 six-marker (bromine + KCl, and bromine + KI)

Pair 1, bromine + potassium chloride:

1. No change — stays orange/yellow 1

2. bromine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride 1

3. so chlorine is more reactive than bromine 1

Pair 2, bromine + potassium iodide:

4. Turns brown 1

5. bromine displaces iodine from potassium iodide 1

6. so bromine is more reactive than iodine 1

7. Overall order: chlorine > bromine > iodine. There are seven points available for six marks.

Notice what Pair 1 teaches you: "no reaction" is a result. It is the evidence that bromine is the less reactive one. Always say what you would see, even if what you see is nothing changing.

✗ "Bromide displaces iodide." "Penalise incorrect use of -ine and -ide"
✗ "Chlorine displaces potassium bromide."
✓ "Chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide." The element is -ine. The ion in the salt is -ide.

subsections.heading: Displacement as redox: ionic and half-equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7 · link to module 08 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q7(d) (the scheme accepted the ionic equation)

In a displacement, the more reactive halogen gains electrons and is reduced, and the halide ion loses electrons and is oxidised. The halogen is the oxidising agent.

The potassium ions do nothing. They are spectator ions, so leave them out of the ionic equation:

Chlorine and bromide — ionic equationCl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂charges balance: −2 on each side
Bromine and iodide — ionic equationBr₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂

Split one into two half-equations:

Reduction half-equationCl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻chlorine gains electrons — reduced
Oxidation half-equation2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻bromide ions lose electrons — oxidised

A halogen is more reactive when it is better at gaining electrons, which makes it a stronger oxidising agent. Chlorine takes electrons from bromide ions. Bromine cannot take them back from chloride ions.

✗ "Cl₂ + Br⁻ → Cl⁻ + Br₂" — the atoms and charges do not balance.
✗ "The chlorine is oxidised." Chlorine gains electrons: OIL RIG, so it is reduced.
✓ "Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Chlorine is reduced and bromide ions are oxidised. Chlorine is the oxidising agent."

subsections.heading: Explaining the Group 7 trend with electrons (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8C · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(c)

Going down Group 7, the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so there is weaker attraction for an incoming electron, and one is gained less easily. So reactivity decreases.

  1. A halogen atom reacts by gaining one electron to fill its outer shell.
  2. Down the group there are more shells, so the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded.
  3. So the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly.
  4. So an electron is gained less readily, and the halogen is less reactive.

Mark script — "Explain the relative reactivities of fluorine (2.7) and chlorine (2.8.7)" (4)

1. Fluorine is more reactive than chlorine 1

2. Fluorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus — fewer shells, smaller atom 1

3. so there is a stronger attraction between the nucleus and an electron (less shielding) 1

4. so fluorine accepts an electron more readily 1

M1 is a free mark that people skip. State which is more reactive before you explain why.

FeatureGroup 1Group 7
Atoms react byLosing one electronGaining one electron
Down the group, the outer shell isFurther from the nucleusFurther from the nucleus
So the attraction isWeaker, so the electron is lost more easilyWeaker, so an electron is gained less easily
Reactivity down the groupIncreasesDecreases

When the two groups meet, they form ionic halides: 2Li + Cl₂ → 2LiCl (2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(i)). The scheme rejected any charges written on Li or Cl₂. Testing that the product really is lithium chloride (a red flame, and a white precipitate with silver nitrate) is covered in module 14.

✗ "Fluorine loses electrons more easily." Halogens gain electrons.
✗ "Chlorine has more electrons so it is less reactive."
✓ "Chlorine's outer shell is further from the nucleus, so there is weaker attraction for an extra electron, so it gains an electron less readily."

subsections.heading: Group 0: why the noble gases do not react
subsections.html:
Spec 1.24 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q1(b) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q3(b)(ii) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(a)(i) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4(a)(ii) · 2024 school Q1(c)

Noble gas atoms have a full outer shell of electrons, so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons. That makes them unreactive (inert).

  1. Helium has 2 outer electrons, which fills its only shell. Neon (2.8) and argon (2.8.8) have 8.
  2. A full outer shell is stable.
  3. So the atom has no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, and it does not form bonds.
  4. So the noble gases exist as single atoms (they are monatomic) and hardly ever react.

Mark script — "Explain, in terms of electron configuration, why neon is unreactive" (2)

1. Neon has a full outer shell — 8 outer electrons, 2.8 1

2. so it does not need to lose or gain (or share) electrons 1

Using an unreactive gas. Argon is about 1% of air and is the least reactive gas in it. It is used wherever something must be kept away from oxygen:

  • Titanium is extracted with magnesium (TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂) in a container of argon. Argon is unreactive, so it will not react with the hot magnesium. In air, the oxygen would oxidise the magnesium (2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(b)).
  • Filament light bulbs are filled with argon, so the hot filament does not react with oxygen.
  • Helium is used in balloons because it has a low density and, unlike hydrogen, is unreactive, so it will not burn.

✗ "Argon is used because it protects the magnesium." How does it protect it?
✓ "Argon is unreactive, so it will not react with the magnesium. Oxygen in air would oxidise it."

✗ "Neon is stable." That is only half an answer.
✓ "Neon has a full outer shell, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Same group, same reactions: same number of electrons in the outer shell.

Group 1 down: outer electron further from the nucleus → weaker attraction → lost more easily → more reactive.

Group 7 down: outer shell further from the nucleus → weaker attraction → electron gained less readily → less reactive.

Group 0: full outer shell → does not need to lose, gain or share electrons → unreactive.

Group 1 + water: metal hydroxide + hydrogen. Fizzes, floats, moves, gets smaller. The solution is alkaline because of OH⁻ ions.

Displacement: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

questions.promptHtml: Lithium, sodium and potassium react with water at very different speeds. Why do chemists still say this is evidence that they belong to one family?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the kind of reaction is the same every time. Each metal gives a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, and each leaves an alkaline solution: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂. The same equation fits all three, with only the symbol changed.

The speed is a difference, and differences show a trend (spec 2.2). The similarities show a family (spec 2.1). Both come from the outer shell: each atom has one outer electron to lose, and it is lost more easily further down the group.

questions.promptHtml: Potassium has 19 protons and sodium has 11. With a much more positive nucleus, why does potassium lose its outer electron more easily?
questions.answerHtml:
The extra protons are outweighed by two other effects. Potassium's outer electron is in the fourth shell (2.8.8.1), so it is much further from the nucleus than sodium's (2.8.1). It also has a full extra shell of electrons between it and the nucleus, which shields it.

Attraction falls off quickly with distance. So the net pull on potassium's outer electron is weaker, the electron is lost more easily, and potassium is more reactive. That is why the mark scheme wants "further from the nucleus" and "less attraction". Counting protons or electrons scores nothing.

questions.promptHtml: The outer shell gets further from the nucleus going down both Group 1 and Group 7. So why does reactivity go up in one group and down in the other?
questions.answerHtml:
The two groups react in opposite ways. Group 1 atoms lose an electron, and weaker attraction makes that easier, so reactivity increases.

Group 7 atoms gain an electron. The nucleus has to pull a new electron in, and weaker attraction makes that harder, so reactivity decreases.

It is the same cause (weaker attraction further down) with opposite effects. Always say which job the atom is doing, losing or gaining, before you explain the trend.

questions.promptHtml: Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution and nothing happens. How can "nothing happens" be evidence of anything?
questions.answerHtml:
If bromine were more reactive than chlorine, it would take chlorine's place: Br₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2Br⁻ + Cl₂. The orange colour would fade, because chlorine water is almost colourless.

It stays orange, so bromine cannot displace chlorine. Bromine is not able to take electrons from chloride ions, so chlorine must be more reactive than bromine.

In the 2023 six-marker, the "no change" pair gave three of the marks: the observation, "bromine cannot displace chlorine", and "chlorine is more reactive than bromine".

questions.promptHtml: Going down Group 7, boiling points rise but reactivity falls. A student says: "Iodine's bonds are stronger, so it boils higher and reacts less." What is wrong with this?
questions.answerHtml:
The student has mixed up two different things.

Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. It overcomes the intermolecular forces between I₂ molecules, and those get stronger as the molecules get bigger. The I–I covalent bond does not break when iodine boils. Mentioning broken covalent bonds lost all three explanation marks in January 2023.

Reactivity depends on single atoms gaining an electron. Iodine's outer shell is far from the nucleus, so the attraction for an electron is weak. It is an atom property, not a bond strength property.

questions.promptHtml: Helium has only 2 outer electrons, but argon has 8. Why are both unreactive, and why are they placed in the same group?
questions.answerHtml:
What matters is that the outer shell is full, not the number 8. Helium's only shell holds a maximum of 2, so 2 electrons fill it. Argon's outer shell is full with 8 (2.8.8).

A full outer shell is stable, so neither atom needs to lose, gain or share electrons. Neither forms bonds, both exist as single atoms, and both are chemically similar. That is why helium sits in Group 0 with the others. The school's 2024 scheme accepted "Group 8" for this group, but "Group 0" is the standard name.

questions.promptHtml: Nobody has ever seen enough astatine to test it. How can you confidently predict what happens when chlorine water is added to sodium astatide solution?
questions.answerHtml:
Astatine is below iodine in Group 7, so it is the least reactive halogen. Its outer shell is furthest from the nucleus, so it has the weakest pull on an extra electron.

Chlorine is more reactive, so it would displace astatine: Cl₂ + 2NaAt → 2NaCl + At₂. Every other halogen would displace it too. Going the other way, astatine would displace nothing.

Using a trend to predict an element you have never studied is exactly what spec 2.6 asks you to do.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium melts into a ball on water, but lithium stays solid. Both reactions give out heat. Why the difference?
questions.answerHtml:
There are two reasons, and they add together.

Melting point: sodium melts at 98 °C and lithium at 181 °C. The heat from the reaction is enough to melt sodium but not lithium.

Rate: lithium is less reactive, so it reacts more slowly and releases its heat more slowly. The water carries the heat away before the metal gets that hot.

Potassium has an even lower melting point (63 °C) and reacts even faster. So it melts, and it gives out enough heat to ignite the hydrogen.

modules.title: Gases in the Atmosphere
modules.standfirst: Year 11 topic. It is on most real Edexcel papers as a short, friendly question: the percentages in air, a practical that finds the percentage of oxygen, a colour change and one sentence on climate change. Most lost marks come from the oxygen calculation, when people divide by the wrong starting volume.

"Use of 280 gives an answer of 26 scores 3" — one mark of four is lost for forgetting that the syringe's 100 cm³ of air was part of the starting volume too. The 2022 scheme did the same: 26.2% (68 ÷ 260) scored 2 of 3.

subsections.html: Air is a mixture, and its oxygen is the reactive part. If you let something use up the oxygen in a sealed sample of air, the gas volume shrinks. That shrinkage is the oxygen. The rest of this topic is about what happens when elements react with that oxygen, where extra carbon dioxide comes from, and why it matters.

subsections.heading: What dry air is made of
subsections.html:
Spec 2.9 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(a) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q3(a) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q2

Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, by volume. Learn the four numbers in that order. They come up every year.

Gas% by volumeHow it is asked
Nitrogen, N₂78% (about four-fifths)"Most abundant gas." In 2024 the multiple-choice answer was "80%".
Oxygen, O₂21% (about one-fifth)"Approximate percentage of oxygen": 21%, not 20% or 35%
Argon, Ar0.9% (about 1%)"Gas that is about 1% of dry air"; "trace gas with the highest percentage"; "least reactive gas"
Carbon dioxide, CO₂0.04%"Lowest percentage" of the four

Dry means water vapour is left out, because the amount of water vapour changes from day to day. Hydrogen is not normally found in the atmosphere (2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(a)(iii)).

✗ "Air is mostly oxygen." ✗ "Carbon dioxide is about 1%."
✓ Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon about 1%, carbon dioxide 0.04%. The 1% gas is argon, every time.

subsections.heading: The idea behind every "% oxygen" practical
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10, 2.14 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4(a) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q3(b)(ii)

Something reacts with the oxygen and removes it from the gas, so the fall in gas volume equals the volume of oxygen that was there.

  1. Trap a known volume of air, sealed, over water or between gas syringes.
  2. Let a metal (iron or copper) or a non-metal (phosphorus) react with the oxygen. The product is a solid oxide, or it dissolves in water, so it takes up almost no gas volume.
  3. Nitrogen and argon do not react, so they stay as gas.
  4. Wait until the volume stops changing. Then all the oxygen has been used.
  5. Decrease in volume = volume of oxygen. Divide by the starting volume and × 100.

Why argon (or neon) does not react: it has a full outer shell of electrons, so it does not gain, lose or share electrons. Both 2022 Jan and 2023 Jan asked this for 1 mark.

subsections.heading: Method 1: iron wool in a test tube over water
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10, 2.14 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q3(b)

Wet iron wool rusts and uses up the oxygen, so water rises up the tube to replace it.

  1. Push a ball of wet iron wool to the top (closed end) of a test tube.
  2. Turn the tube upside down in a beaker of water. Measure the length of the column of gas.
  3. Leave it for about a week. Rusting is slow.
  4. The iron reacts with the oxygen. The gas volume falls, so water rises up the tube.
  5. Measure the final length of the gas column once it has stopped changing.
% oxygen from column lengths% oxygen = (initial length − final length) ÷ initial length × 100the tube has the same width all the way, so length stands in for volume

Worked example: 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q3(b)(iii)

Initial column 75 mm, final column 30 mm (a mixture of oxygen and neon).

  1. Decrease = 75 − 30 = 45 mm 1
  2. % oxygen = 45 ÷ 75 × 100 = 60% 1

The mark scheme gave 40% only 1 mark. 40% is 30 ÷ 75, the gas that is left, not the oxygen that was used.

This question used a made-up mixture, so the answer was 60%, not 21%. Always calculate from the numbers you are given. Do not just write 21%.

equations.name: % oxygen from column lengths
equations.formula: % oxygen = (initial length − final length) ÷ initial length × 100

subsections.heading: Method 2: iron and a gas syringe, and the "total volume" trap
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10, 2.14 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(c)

The starting volume of air is the flask (and tube) plus the air in the syringe, and the oxygen used is the drop in the syringe reading.

  1. Wet iron powder (or filings) sits in a conical flask or glass tube, joined to a gas syringe holding air.
  2. Record the syringe reading at the start. Leave the apparatus until the reading stops changing.
  3. The iron uses up the oxygen from all the air: the flask's air and the syringe's air. The plunger moves in.
  4. Oxygen used = start reading − end reading.
  5. Total air at the start = volume of flask and tube + start syringe reading.
% oxygen with a gas syringe% oxygen = (syringe start − syringe end) ÷ (apparatus volume + syringe start) × 100the bottom line is ALL the air at the start, not just the flask

Worked example: 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(c), 3 marks

Flask and tube hold 260 cm³. Syringe goes from 90 cm³ to 22 cm³.

  1. Oxygen = 90 − 22 = 68 cm³ 1
  2. Total air at start = 260 + 90 = 350 cm³ 1
  3. 68 ÷ 350 × 100 = 19.4% 1

2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(c) was the same with a 280 cm³ flask and 100 → 27 cm³: 73 ÷ 380 × 100 = 19.2 = 19% to two significant figures (4 marks: 73, 380, 19.2, 19).

Why wet? Water is needed for iron to rust. Why powder? A powder has a larger surface area, so the iron rusts faster and you get the results sooner. The product is rust, Fe₂O₃, a brown coating on the iron.

Iron reacting with oxygen4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide · water is needed too

✗ "68 ÷ 260 × 100 = 26.2%": this leaves the syringe's air out of the total. The 2022 scheme gave it 2 of 3.
✗ The product is "red": the 2022 scheme said "IGNORE red alone".
✓ "68 ÷ (260 + 90) × 100 = 19.4%" · rust is brown (orange-brown and red-brown were allowed).

equations.name: % oxygen with a gas syringe
equations.formula: % oxygen = (syringe start − syringe end) ÷ (apparatus volume + syringe start) × 100

subsections.heading: Method 3: passing air over heated copper
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10, 2.14 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4

Pushing the gas back and forth over hot copper removes the oxygen as black copper(II) oxide, and the syringe reading falls until it stays the same.

  1. Two gas syringes are joined by a glass tube packed with copper powder. One syringe holds a measured volume of air.
  2. Heat the copper. Cold copper does not react with oxygen quickly, so heating increases the rate and gives the particles enough energy to react.
  3. Push the gas from syringe A to B over the hot copper, then back again. Record the reading on syringe A. Repeat many times.
  4. The copper turns from pink-brown to black: copper(II) oxide forms.
  5. When the readings stay the same, all the oxygen has reacted.
  6. Let the apparatus cool to room temperature before the final reading, because hot gas takes up more volume.
Copper reacting with oxygen2Cu + O₂ → 2CuOpink-brown copper → black copper(II) oxide · oxidation

Worked example: 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4(b)(ii), 3 marks

Syringe A starts at 78 cm³ and ends at a steady 58 cm³. The tube and connecting tubes hold 175 cm³.

  1. Oxygen = 78 − 58 = 20 cm³ 1
  2. Total gas = 175 + 78 = 253 cm³ 1
  3. 20 ÷ 253 × 100 = 7.9% 1

That sample was an oxygen and argon mixture, not air, so 7.9% is correct.

Why the answer may not be accurate (the three the scheme accepted): a leak in the apparatus; the temperature was not the same for all readings; the apparatus was not left to cool.

✗ "Copper(I) oxide". The scheme allowed plain "copper oxide", but said "REJECT copper(I) oxide".
✓ "Copper(II) oxide", which is black.

subsections.heading: Method 4: phosphorus, a non-metal
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10, 2.14

Phosphorus also reacts with oxygen and removes it, which shows that a non-metal works as well as a metal. The spec names both: iron (metal) and phosphorus (non-metal).

  1. A small piece of phosphorus is placed in a sealed volume of air above water, for example in a bell jar or an upturned tube. This is a teacher demonstration: phosphorus catches fire easily.
  2. The phosphorus reacts with the oxygen to make phosphorus oxide, a white solid that dissolves in the water.
  3. The oxygen is used up, so the water rises to replace it, by about one-fifth of the volume.
  4. Wait for the apparatus to cool, then measure how far the water has risen and work out the percentage exactly as in Method 1.
Phosphorus reacting with oxygen4P + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀phosphorus(V) oxide · an acidic oxide, because phosphorus is a non-metal

Whatever reacts with the oxygen, the logic and the calculation are the same. Fall in volume = oxygen, and divide by all the gas you started with.

subsections.heading: Checking your answer and finding errors
subsections.html:
Spec 2.14 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4(b)(i), (iii) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(b)

For air, a good answer is close to 21%. An answer far below that means not all the oxygen reacted, or the final reading was taken while the gas was still warm.

ProblemEffect on the % oxygen
Not left long enough / not enough iron or copper, so not all the oxygen reactedToo low. The volume did not fall far enough.
Final reading taken while the gas is still warm (copper method)Too low. Warm gas takes up more volume.
Only the flask volume used as the total, not flask + syringeToo high. You divided by too small a number.
Calculated the gas left ÷ startAbout 79–80%. That is the nitrogen and argon, not the oxygen.

Reading a syringe: read the scale level with the end of the plunger, to the nearest 1 cm³. If you write the start and end readings the wrong way round, you get 1 of the 2 marks (2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(b)).

subsections.heading: Burning elements in oxygen: magnesium, hydrogen, sulfur
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q4(a) · 2025 school Q4(b)

Elements burn in oxygen to form oxides. This is combustion, and the element is oxidised because it gains oxygen. Elements burn more brightly in pure oxygen than in air, because pure oxygen is about five times more concentrated than the oxygen in air.

ElementWhat you seeProduct
MagnesiumBright white light (flame); leaves a white powder (ash)Magnesium oxide, MgO: a white solid, a basic oxide
HydrogenBurns with a pale blue, almost invisible flame; droplets of water form on a cold surfaceWater, H₂O: a neutral oxide
SulfurMelts, then burns with a blue flame (bright blue in oxygen, pale in air); a colourless, choking gas formsSulfur dioxide, SO₂: an acidic oxide
Magnesium burning2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)2025 school: equation 1 mark, state symbols (s)(g)(s) 1 mark
Hydrogen burning2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)the only product is water
Sulfur burningS(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)sulfur dioxide · link: SO₂ from burning fuels causes acid rain (module 10)

Magnesium burning: 2 marks (2022 Edexcel 2C Q4(a))

1. Bright / white light, or bright / white flame 1

2. White powder / solid / ash forms 1

✗ "A white precipitate forms." The scheme said "REJECT white precipitate". A precipitate forms in a solution. Burning magnesium leaves a powder.
✗ "2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO₂" or "Mg + O → MgO": oxygen is O₂, and magnesium oxide is MgO.
✓ "2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s); bright white light; white powder."

subsections.heading: Oxides: basic for metals, acidic for non-metals
subsections.html:
Spec 1.20 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(a) · 2021 school Q10(c)

Metal oxides are basic and non-metal oxides are acidic. A metal oxide reacts with acids, and the oxides that dissolve give alkaline solutions. A non-metal oxide that dissolves in water gives an acidic solution.

OxideWith waterpH / indicatorCharacter
Magnesium oxide, MgOMgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂Above 7: universal indicator blue or purple, red litmus turns blueBasic
Sodium oxide, Na₂ONa₂O + H₂O → 2NaOHWell above 7Basic
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃Below 7: blue litmus turns redAcidic
Carbon dioxide, CO₂CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃Slightly below 7: this is why rainwater is slightly acidicAcidic

An acidic solution contains hydrogen ions, H⁺. It shows the normal acid reactions. For example, magnesium fizzes (effervescence) and disappears in it. The school's 2021 Q10(c) gave 4 marks for exactly this: H⁺; blue litmus turns red; effervescence; magnesium dissolves.

✗ "Sulfur dioxide is an acid." It is an acidic oxide. It forms an acidic solution when it dissolves in water.
✗ "Magnesium oxide is acidic because it contains oxygen." All oxides contain oxygen. The element decides the character.
✓ "Magnesium is a metal, so its oxide is basic. Sulfur is a non-metal, so its oxide is acidic."

subsections.heading: Is it a metal or a non-metal?
subsections.html:
Spec 1.20, 1.21 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(a)

Metals conduct electricity and form basic oxides; non-metals (except graphite) do not conduct, and form acidic oxides. You can also tell from where the element is in the Periodic Table.

TestMetalNon-metal
Electrical conductivity of the elementConducts (it has delocalised electrons)Does not conduct. Graphite is the exception.
Oxide, dissolved or tested with indicatorBasic: alkaline solution, pH above 7Acidic: pH below 7
Position in the Periodic TableLeft and centre, to the left of the stepped lineRight, to the right of the stepped line (and hydrogen)

In 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(a), lithium was the answer for "a good conductor of electricity" and for "an element that forms a basic oxide". Both are metal properties. Diamond has a giant covalent structure but does not conduct. Bromine is the liquid element.

✗ "Carbon is a metal because graphite conducts." Carbon is a non-metal. It is on the right of the stepped line, and its oxide, CO₂, is acidic.
✓ Use two pieces of evidence: conductivity and oxide character, or position.

subsections.heading: Thermal decomposition of metal carbonates
subsections.html:
Spec 2.12 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q7(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q2(b)(i)

When heated, a metal carbonate breaks down into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. This is thermal decomposition. "Thermal" means by heat, and "decomposition" means one substance breaking into two or more.

Metal carbonate decomposing (general)metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxideMCO₃ → MO + CO₂ for a metal that forms M²⁺ ions
Copper(II) carbonate decomposingCuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂green solid → black solid · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(b)(iii), 1 mark
CarbonateColour changeEquation
Copper(II) carbonateGreen → black (copper(II) oxide)CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂
Zinc carbonateWhite → yellow when hot, white again when coolZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂
Calcium carbonateWhite → white (needs very strong heating)CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

To show the gas is carbon dioxide, bubble it through limewater, which turns milky. The full gas tests are in module 14.

✗ "Blue to black" or "green to orange". Both were wrong options in 2022 and 2023. Copper(II) carbonate is green, and copper(II) oxide is black.
✗ "Oxidation" or "neutralisation" as the type of reaction.
✓ "Thermal decomposition; green to black; CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂."

subsections.heading: Calculating from a carbonate decomposition
subsections.html:
Spec 2.12 · 2023 school Q3

The mass lost on heating is the mass of carbon dioxide given off, and one mole of MCO₃ gives one mole of CO₂.

Worked example: 2023 school Q3, identify X in XCO₃

7.40 g of a Group 2 carbonate, XCO₃, gives off 2.20 g of carbon dioxide. [Mᵣ of CO₂ = 44]

  1. n(CO₂) = 2.20 ÷ 44 = 0.05 mol 1
  2. XCO₃ → XO + CO₂ is 1 : 1, so n(XCO₃) = 0.05 mol 1
  3. Mᵣ(XCO₃) = mass ÷ moles = 7.40 ÷ 0.05 1 = 148 1
  4. CO₃ = 12 + (3 × 16) = 60, so Aᵣ(X) = 148 − 60 = 88 1
  5. X = strontium (Aᵣ 88, Group 2) 1

If the question gives the mass of solid left, subtract: mass of CO₂ = mass before − mass after. Heat to constant mass, so that you know the decomposition is complete.

subsections.heading: Carbon dioxide, the greenhouse effect and climate change
subsections.html:
Spec 2.13 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(d) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q2(b)

Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat in the atmosphere, so increasing amounts may contribute to climate change.

  1. Burning fuels such as alkanes (complete combustion), and thermal decomposition of carbonates, release carbon dioxide. Respiration releases it too.
  2. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas. It absorbs heat (infrared) given off by the Earth and traps it in the atmosphere.
  3. More CO₂ traps more heat, so the average global temperature rises. This is global warming, and it leads to climate change.
  4. Effects: melting polar ice caps, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires. Extra CO₂ also dissolves in the sea, so the oceans become more acidic.

Why more CO₂ is a problem: 2 marks (2023 Edexcel 2C Q2(d))

1. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas (it traps heat in the atmosphere) 1

2. It causes climate change / global warming, or a named effect such as melting ice caps, rising sea levels or flooding 1

Which reactions make CO₂? In 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q2(b)(i), the two ticks were complete combustion of an alkane and thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate. The wrong options were cracking (it makes smaller hydrocarbons), magnesium + hydrochloric acid (it makes hydrogen) and rusting (it uses up oxygen).

✗ "CO₂ makes a hole in the ozone layer." This was rejected in 2022 and 2023.
✗ "CO₂ causes acid rain." This was ignored. Acid rain comes from SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen (module 10).
✓ "CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, so more of it causes climate change, e.g. rising sea levels."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Air: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon 0.9%, carbon dioxide 0.04%.

% oxygen: fall in volume ÷ all the gas at the start (apparatus + syringe) × 100. Wait until the volume stops changing, and let it cool.

Iron: must be wet; powder has a larger surface area, so it reacts faster; brown Fe₂O₃. Copper: heat it; turns black (copper(II) oxide).

Burning: Mg gives bright white light and a white powder; S gives a blue flame and SO₂; H₂ gives water.

Oxides: metal → basic; non-metal → acidic. CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂, green to black. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, so it causes climate change.

questions.promptHtml: In the iron-and-syringe experiment, why do you divide by the flask volume plus the syringe reading, and not by the flask volume alone?
questions.answerHtml:
The flask and the syringe are joined, so they hold one sample of air. The iron takes oxygen from all of it, including the air that started in the syringe. That is why the plunger moves in.

So the fall in the syringe reading is the oxygen from the whole sample, and it has to be divided by the whole sample. Divide by the flask alone and the bottom number is too small, so the answer is too big: about 26% instead of 19–21%. That mistake cost one mark in both 2022 and 2023.

questions.promptHtml: In the heated-copper experiment, why do you keep pushing the gas back and forth until the reading stops changing, and why must you let it cool before the last reading?
questions.answerHtml:
Each pass only removes some of the oxygen. Only the gas touching the hot copper reacts. When the reading stays the same on several passes, there is no oxygen left to remove. That is the 2022 Jan answer: "results are the same".

Gas expands when it is hot. A reading taken while the gas is warm is too large, so the decrease looks smaller and the % oxygen comes out too low. Cooling to room temperature makes the start and end readings a fair comparison.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a test tube of wet iron wool over water take about a week, when heated copper does the same job in minutes?
questions.answerHtml:
Rusting at room temperature is a slow reaction. The particles have little energy, and only the surface of the iron is exposed.

Heating the copper gives the particles much more energy, so far more collisions succeed and the oxygen is removed quickly. This is the same collision theory as in module 7. That is also why iron powder is better than lumps: a larger surface area gives more collisions per second, so the reaction is faster.

questions.promptHtml: Iron, copper and phosphorus are very different elements. Why do all three give the same answer for the % oxygen in air?
questions.answerHtml:
Each one only has to do one job: react with all the oxygen and turn it into something that is not a gas, such as a solid oxide or an oxide that dissolves in the water.

Nitrogen and argon are left behind in every method. So the fall in gas volume always measures the same thing, the oxygen, whatever removed it. The spec asks you to know that both a metal and a non-metal can do this.

questions.promptHtml: Magnesium oxide makes universal indicator turn blue. Sulfur dioxide solution turns it red. Explain the difference in terms of what the elements are.
questions.answerHtml:
Magnesium is a metal, so its oxide is basic. It reacts with water to form magnesium hydroxide, which gives an alkaline solution with OH⁻ ions, so the pH is above 7.

Sulfur is a non-metal, so its oxide is acidic. It dissolves in water to form an acid, which gives H⁺ ions, so the pH is below 7.

This is one of the two tests the spec gives for classifying an element. The other is electrical conductivity.

questions.promptHtml: When copper(II) carbonate is heated, the solid gets lighter. When copper is heated in air, the solid gets heavier. Both make black copper(II) oxide. How?
questions.answerHtml:
Carbonate: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. The carbon dioxide is a gas and escapes, so the solid loses the mass of the CO₂.

Copper: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. Oxygen from the air joins onto the copper, so the solid gains the mass of that oxygen.

Mass is conserved both times. The difference is whether a gas leaves the solid or joins it.

questions.promptHtml: Carbon dioxide is only 0.04% of the air. How can such a small amount affect the climate?
questions.answerHtml:
Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases, so they do not trap heat in this way. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs heat given off by the Earth and traps it in the atmosphere.

So even a small percentage matters, and a small rise in that percentage is a large increase in the amount of this particular gas. More CO₂ traps more heat. That is why burning fuels may contribute to climate change. The spec says "may contribute", so write it as a cause, not a certainty about the size of the effect.

questions.promptHtml: A student calculates the % oxygen in air as 16%. Give two likely reasons, and explain why a mistake in this experiment usually makes the answer too low rather than too high.
questions.answerHtml:
Reasons: not all the oxygen had reacted (not left long enough, or not enough iron or copper), or the final reading was taken while the gas was still warm and expanded.

Why usually low: the method depends on the volume falling as far as it can. Anything that stops the reaction from finishing, or makes the gas take up extra room at the end, makes the fall smaller, so the percentage comes out lower.

The main way to get too high an answer is a calculation slip, such as leaving the syringe volume out of the total.

subsections.html: This module builds on the reactivity series you met in Module 9 (Metal Extraction). There the list was used to decide how a metal is extracted. Here you see the evidence for the order — reactions with water, acids and other metals' compounds — then what reactivity means for iron in the real world: it rusts, and we stop it with barriers, zinc and magnesium. The module ends with why we use alloys rather than pure metals.

subsections.heading: The order, and the two kinds of evidence
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15, 2.17 · recap of Module 9 · used in every question below

The more vigorously a metal reacts with water or acid, the higher it sits in the reactivity series.

Reactivity series (spec 2.17)K · Na · Li · Ca · Mg · Al · (C) · Zn · Fe · (H) · Cu · Ag · Aumost reactive on the left · carbon and hydrogen are markers, not metals

There are two ways to put metals in order:

  1. How fast they react with water or dilute acid — watch the bubbles (hydrogen) and the temperature rise. Faster = more reactive.
  2. Displacement — a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound. If A displaces B, A is above B.

Hydrogen's place matters: metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to make hydrogen; metals below hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) do not react at all.

equations.name: Reactivity series (spec 2.17)
equations.formula: K · Na · Li · Ca · Mg · Al · (C) · Zn · Fe · (H) · Cu · Ag · Au

subsections.heading: Metals with water
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(a)

A metal that reacts with water makes a metal hydroxide and hydrogen; only the most reactive metals do this with cold water.

MetalWith cold waterWith steam
Potassium, sodium, lithiumVery fast — floats, fizzes, moves around; potassium catches fire (lilac flame)(too dangerous)
CalciumSteady fizzing; water goes cloudy (calcium hydroxide)(too dangerous)
MagnesiumVery slow — a few bubbles over daysBurns with a bright white glow → magnesium oxide + hydrogen
Zinc, ironNo visible reactionReact when heated → metal oxide + hydrogen (iron only slowly)
Copper, silver, goldNo reactionNo reaction
Sodium with water2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen
Calcium with waterCa + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂steady fizzing · the solution is alkaline
Magnesium with steamMg + H₂O → MgO + H₂with steam the product is the oxide, not the hydroxide

If a table says a metal reacts "very fast" with water, it is from the top of the series (Group 1 or calcium).

subsections.heading: Metals with dilute acids
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(a)(iii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)

A metal above hydrogen reacts with a dilute acid to give a salt and hydrogen; the faster the fizzing, the more reactive the metal.

Metal + acid (general)metal + acid → salt + hydrogenhydrochloric acid → chlorides · sulfuric acid → sulfates
MetalWith dilute HCl or H₂SO₄
K, Na, Li, CaNot done — the reaction is violent / explosive
MagnesiumVigorous fizzing, metal disappears quickly, tube gets warm
AluminiumSlow at first (oxide layer), then fast
ZincSteady fizzing
IronSlow bubbling; solution turns pale green (Fe²⁺)
Copper, silver, goldNo reaction — below hydrogen
Magnesium + hydrochloric acidMg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Zinc + sulfuric acidZn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂zinc sulfate + hydrogen
Iron + sulfuric acidFe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂iron forms iron(II) salts with dilute acids — 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(i)
Aluminium + hydrochloric acid2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂word equation: aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chloride + hydrogen

The gas is hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Gas tests are covered fully in Module 14.

✗ "aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chlorine + hydrogen"
✗ "iron + sulfuric acid → iron sulfide + hydrogen"
✓ Chloride from hydrochloric acid; sulfate from sulfuric acid. Sulfide means no oxygen at all.

subsections.heading: Why aluminium looks less reactive than it is
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15, 2.25C

Aluminium is covered by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that stops water and acid reaching the metal underneath.

That is why aluminium reacts slowly with acid at first and then speeds up once the acid has eaten through the layer. It is also why aluminium is used outdoors without rusting away: the oxide layer protects it from corrosion. On the series it is still above zinc and iron — thermite proves it.

subsections.heading: Practical: metals in dilute acid
subsections.html:
Spec 2.21 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)

To compare magnesium, zinc and iron fairly, change only the metal and compare how fast each makes hydrogen.

  1. Put the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of the same concentration of dilute hydrochloric (or sulfuric) acid into three test tubes.
  2. Measure the starting temperature of the acid.
  3. Add the same mass of each metal, in the same form (all powder, or pieces of the same size) so the surface area is the same.
  4. Observe the rate of bubbling, and record the temperature rise — or collect the hydrogen in a gas syringe and measure the volume in a set time.
  5. The most bubbles / biggest temperature rise / most gas = the most reactive.

Expected order: magnesium > zinc > iron. Copper can be added as a comparison: no bubbles at all.

Mark script — describe how to compare three metals with acid

1. Same volume and concentration of acid 1

2. Same mass and surface area (form) of each metal 1

3. Measure something: rate of bubbles, temperature rise or volume of gas in a set time 1

4. The fastest reaction / greatest rise shows the most reactive metal 1

subsections.heading: Reading an unknown-metal table
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(a)

Rank the metals by the water results first, then use the acid results to separate the ones that did not react with water.

The 2024 paper gave four metals (the letters are not symbols):

MetalWith waterWith dilute HCl
Pno reactionno reaction
Qvery fast reaction(not done)
Rno reactionslow reaction
Sslow reactionfast reaction
  1. Q reacts very fast with water → most reactive (a Group 1 metal). The acid test is not done because it would be explosive / dangerous.
  2. S reacts slowly with water and fast with acid → next (like magnesium or calcium).
  3. R does not react with water, but does with acid, slowly → next. R could be zinc (or iron).
  4. P does nothing with either → least reactive, below hydrogen: copper, silver or gold.

Answer: Q, S, R, P. One mark for the whole order.

✗ Reason the acid test was not done: "it is volatile" / "it is vigorous" — the 2024 scheme ignores both.
✓ "The reaction would be explosive / dangerous / violent."

subsections.heading: Displacement from salt solutions as evidence
subsections.html:
Spec 2.15, 2.20 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(c)–(d)

A metal coats itself with a less reactive metal from a salt solution; if nothing happens, the metal in the solution is more reactive (or is the same metal).

Module 9 gave you the basic rule. Exam questions turn it into a results table. January 2023 put magnesium, then metal X, into four sulfate solutions:

SolutionMagnesium addedMetal X added
aluminium sulfategrey coatingno change
magnesium sulfateno changeno change
copper(II) sulfatebrown coatingbrown coating
sulfate of Xgrey coatingno change
  1. Magnesium displaces Al, Cu and X → magnesium is the most reactive.
  2. X displaces only copper → X is below aluminium but above copper.
  3. Order: magnesium, aluminium, X, copper. X could be zinc or iron.
  4. No change with magnesium sulfate: magnesium cannot displace itself.
Iron in copper(II) sulfateFe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cublue fades to pale green · pink-brown copper forms
Displacement as an ionic equationZn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)the sulfate ion is a spectator and is left out

The copper that forms is a pink-brown (or brown / orange-brown) solid. Iron added to magnesium sulfate does nothing because iron is less reactive than magnesium.

✗ "The brown coating is copper(II) ions" / "Cu²⁺" — the 2023 January scheme rejects both.
✓ "Copper" — the metal atoms, which are the solid.

subsections.heading: Displacement and electrons: the reducing agent
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q5(c)

In every displacement the more reactive metal loses electrons, so it is oxidised and is the reducing agent.

Magnesium and aluminium ions3Mg(s) + 2Al³⁺(aq) → 3Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Al(s)each Mg loses 2e⁻ · each Al³⁺ gains 3e⁻
  1. Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻: magnesium loses electrons — it is oxidised.
  2. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al: aluminium ions gain electrons — they are reduced.
  3. Magnesium donates the electrons that reduce Al³⁺, so magnesium is the reducing agent. Al³⁺ is the oxidising agent.

Mark script — "explain which substance is the reducing agent"

1. Magnesium is the reducing agent 1

2. Because it donates / loses electrons (to the aluminium ions) 1

Full definitions of oxidation, reduction and the agents in electron terms are in Module 8 (Electrolysis and Redox).

subsections.heading: Displacement from oxides: thermite
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b) · 2024 school Q5(a)

Aluminium takes the oxygen from iron(III) oxide because aluminium is more reactive than iron; the reaction is very exothermic.

Thermite reaction2Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + Al₂O₃started with a burning magnesium fuse · the iron comes out molten
  • Exothermic: heat (thermal energy) is given out to the surroundings. Enough to melt the iron — used to weld railway lines.
  • Why aluminium displaces iron: aluminium is more reactive (higher in the reactivity series) than iron.
  • Redox: aluminium gains oxygen so it is oxidised; iron(III) oxide loses oxygen so it is reduced.
  • Aluminium is the reducing agent; iron(III) oxide is the oxidising agent.

✗ "Exothermic means energy is released" — the 2024 scheme ignores "energy" on its own.
✓ "Heat / thermal energy is given out to the surroundings."

✗ "Oxidation and reduction happen at the same time." — no species named, no marks.
✓ "Aluminium gains oxygen and is oxidised; iron(III) oxide loses oxygen and is reduced."

subsections.heading: Rusting: what it needs and what it makes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q2(a) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(a) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)

Iron rusts only when both water and oxygen are present; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide.

Rusting — word equationiron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxidesimplified formula Fe₂O₃ · a brown / orange-brown solid
Rusting — symbol equation4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂Ox varies — that is why rust has no single formula
  • Rusting is oxidation: the iron gains oxygen (and loses electrons, Fe → Fe³⁺).
  • It is slow, and it is exothermic. Hand warmers use fast rusting of iron powder.
  • Iron powder rusts faster than a nail: larger surface area, so a faster reaction. That is why 2022's oxygen-in-air experiment used wet iron powder.
  • Only iron and steel rust. Other metals corrode.

✗ "Rust is iron oxide" — ignored. ✗ "Iron(II) oxide" — rejected.
✓ "(Hydrated) iron(III) oxide" or Fe₂O₃.

✗ Colour of rust: "red" alone — the 2022 scheme ignores it.
✓ "Brown", "orange-brown" or "red-brown".

equations.name: Rusting — word equation
equations.formula: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide

subsections.heading: The three-tube experiment
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q4(a)(i)

Each tube removes one condition; only the tube with both air and water shows rust.

TubeSet-upResultWhat it shows
AIron nail in tap water, open to the airRustsWater + oxygen → rust
BNail in boiled water with a layer of oil on topNo rustOxygen is needed
CNail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride, tube stopperedNo rustWater is needed
  1. Boiling the water drives out the dissolved air (oxygen).
  2. The oil layer stops air dissolving back into the water.
  3. Anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent — it absorbs water vapour from the air.
  4. The stopper stops moist air getting in.

Conclusion: iron needs both water and oxygen to rust. Remove either one and it does not rust.

subsections.heading: Preventing rust: barrier methods
subsections.html:
Spec 2.19 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q2(a)(ii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(iii)

A barrier method coats the iron so that water and oxygen cannot reach its surface.

  • Painting — bridges, cars, railings.
  • Oiling or greasing — bike chains, moving machine parts (paint would crack off).
  • Plastic coating — garden wire, fridge shelves.
  • Electroplating with another metal, e.g. chromium plating.

The weakness: if the barrier is scratched or chipped, water and oxygen reach the iron and it rusts at that point.

✗ Asked for a barrier method: "sacrificial protection" — the 2024 scheme rejects it. It is a different method.
✓ "Painting", "oiling", "greasing" or "coating with plastic".

subsections.heading: Galvanising and sacrificial protection
subsections.html:
Spec 2.19 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q2(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q2(b) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(a)(iii)

A more reactive metal in contact with iron is oxidised instead of the iron, so the iron does not rust.

Sacrificial protection: blocks of magnesium or zinc are bolted to ship hulls, oil rigs and underground pipes. The block corrodes away and must be replaced from time to time; the iron stays intact.

Galvanising: iron or steel is coated with a layer of zinc (e.g. dipped in molten zinc). It protects in two ways:

  1. The zinc is a barrier that keeps water and oxygen off the iron.
  2. If the zinc is scratched, zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc reacts / is oxidised instead of the iron — sacrificial protection keeps working.
Sacrificial zincZn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻zinc loses electrons in place of the iron (Fe → Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ does not happen)

Mark script — explain how sacrificial protection works (2)

1. A more reactive metal (e.g. zinc or magnesium) is attached to / coats the iron 1

2. The more reactive metal reacts / is oxidised / corrodes instead of the iron 1

Never "rusts instead". Never just "an element".

subsections.heading: Uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel
subsections.html:
Spec 2.25C (triple only)

Every use must be linked to a property: say what the metal does and why that property suits the job.

MaterialKey propertiesUses
AluminiumLow density; resists corrosion (oxide layer); good conductor of electricity and heatAircraft bodies (as an alloy), overhead power cables, drinks cans, foil, window frames
CopperVery good electrical conductor; ductile (draws into wires); unreactive — does not react with waterElectrical wiring, water pipes, bases of saucepans
Iron (from the blast furnace)About 4% carbon: hard but brittle; pure iron is too softMostly turned into steel
Low-carbon (mild) steelLittle carbon: soft, malleable, easily shaped, strongCar bodies, ship panels, nails, wire
High-carbon steelMore carbon: harder and stronger, but more brittleCutting tools, drill bits, chisels, knives
Stainless steelIron with chromium (and nickel): resists corrosion, hardCutlery, sinks, surgical instruments, chemical plant

Overhead power cables are aluminium, not copper: aluminium has a much lower density, so the cables are lighter and need fewer pylons. They usually have a steel core for strength.

✗ "Aluminium is used for aeroplanes because it is light."
✓ "Aluminium has a low density (and its alloys are strong), and it resists corrosion."

✗ "Copper is used in wires because it conducts."
✓ "Copper is a very good conductor of electricity and is ductile, so it can be drawn into wires."

subsections.heading: Alloys, and why they are harder
subsections.html:
Spec 2.26C, 2.27C (triple only) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q6(c) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(a) · 2025 school Q4(a)

In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily and the alloy is harder.

Alloy — definitionalloy = a mixture of a metal and one or more other elementsusually other metals or carbon · steel = iron + carbon · brass = copper + zinc
  1. In a pure metal, all the atoms (positive ions) are the same size and sit in regular layers. The layers can slide over one another, so the metal is soft and malleable. (Metallic bonding itself is in Module 2.)
  2. An alloy contains atoms of different sizes.
  3. The different-sized atoms distort / disrupt the layers.
  4. So the layers cannot slide over each other as easily — the alloy is harder and stronger.

Mark script — why is the alloy stronger than the pure metal? (3)

1. In the pure metal all the atoms are the same size, so layers can slide over each other 1

2. The alloy has atoms of different sizes 1

3. This disrupts the structure, so the layers cannot slide as easily 1

A labelled diagram can score all three: a regular grid of equal circles next to a grid with some bigger circles.

✗ "The molecules in the alloy can't slide." — metals have no molecules; the 2022 and January 2023 schemes reject "molecules".
✓ "The layers of atoms / ions cannot slide."

✗ "The alloy has stronger bonds." — not the reason.
✓ "Atoms of different sizes make it harder for the layers to slide."

equations.name: Alloy — definition
equations.formula: alloy = a mixture of a metal and one or more other elements

subsections.html:
The sentences behind most of the marks

Order: K Na Li Ca Mg Al (C) Zn Fe (H) Cu Ag Au. Faster with water or acid = more reactive. Below hydrogen = no reaction with acid.

Rusting: needs water and oxygen; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide; rusting is oxidation.

Sacrificial: a more reactive metal is oxidised / corrodes instead of the iron.

Alloys: atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding, so alloys are harder.

questions.promptHtml: Aluminium is above zinc in the reactivity series, yet aluminium foil barely reacts with dilute acid at first and aluminium window frames do not corrode. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Aluminium reacts instantly with oxygen in the air to form a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide. That layer sticks to the metal and stops water, oxygen and acid reaching the aluminium underneath.

In acid the reaction is slow until the oxide has been dissolved, then it speeds up. Outdoors the layer never goes away, so the frame is protected. The metal is reactive; its coating is not.

questions.promptHtml: Why does copper not react with dilute hydrochloric acid, while magnesium fizzes rapidly?
questions.answerHtml:
A metal reacts with acid by displacing hydrogen from it. Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series can do this.

Magnesium is well above hydrogen, so it gives up electrons easily and makes hydrogen gas fast. Copper is below hydrogen, so it cannot displace it — no bubbles, no salt, no reaction.

questions.promptHtml: In the three-tube rusting experiment, why is the water boiled, why is oil added, and why do you need all three tubes rather than just one?
questions.answerHtml:
Boiling drives out dissolved air, so there is no oxygen in the water. The oil stops air dissolving back in. That tube has water but no oxygen.

One tube can only show that rusting happens. To prove both water and oxygen are needed you must remove each one separately: no oxygen (boiled water and oil), no water (calcium chloride). Tube A, with both, shows what happens when nothing is removed — the comparison.

questions.promptHtml: A painted steel gate and a galvanised steel gate are both scratched through to the steel. Explain why only one of them starts to rust.
questions.answerHtml:
Painted gate: paint is only a barrier. Once scratched, water and oxygen reach the bare steel, and it rusts at the scratch.

Galvanised gate: the zinc is also a barrier, but zinc is more reactive than iron. At the scratch the zinc is oxidised instead of the iron — it gives up its electrons first. The iron is protected until the nearby zinc is used up.

questions.promptHtml: Why do the mark schemes reject "the zinc rusts instead of the iron", when zinc is clearly corroding?
questions.answerHtml:
Rusting has a precise meaning: the oxidation of iron to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. Zinc does not make rust; it forms zinc compounds.

So the correct words for zinc or magnesium are corrodes, reacts or is oxidised. Saying zinc "rusts" shows the examiner you do not know what rust is.

questions.promptHtml: In the January 2023 question, magnesium was put into four sulfate solutions and then metal X was. Why was the magnesium table alone not enough to find the full order?
questions.answerHtml:
Magnesium displaced aluminium, copper and X. That tells you magnesium is top, but nothing about how Al, X and Cu compare with each other.

Metal X displaced only copper, and not aluminium. So X is below aluminium and above copper. You need one test for each pair you want to compare — the second table supplied the missing pairs: Mg > Al > X > Cu.

questions.promptHtml: In the thermite reaction, why is aluminium called the reducing agent, and why is it also correct to say it loses electrons?
questions.answerHtml:
Aluminium removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide, so it reduces it: that makes it the reducing agent. Aluminium gains the oxygen, so it is itself oxidised.

In electron terms: aluminium atoms become Al³⁺ ions in Al₂O₃ — they lose electrons (oxidation). The Fe³⁺ ions in Fe₂O₃ become iron atoms — they gain electrons (reduction). The oxygen version and the electron version describe the same change.

questions.promptHtml: Pure iron is softer than steel, and a chisel is made of high-carbon steel but a car door of mild steel. Explain both facts.
questions.answerHtml:
Softer pure iron: all the iron atoms are the same size, in regular layers that slide easily. In steel the carbon atoms are a different size; they disrupt the layers, so they slide less easily and the steel is harder.

More carbon, more disruption: high-carbon steel is very hard, so it keeps a sharp cutting edge — ideal for a chisel, though brittle. A car door must be pressed into curved shapes, so it needs mild steel, which has little carbon and is still malleable.

(d) To absorb water (vapour) — it keeps the air dry 1

(e) Iron needs both water and oxygen to rust 1

markScheme.point: (a) Tube A
(b) To remove dissolved air / oxygen from the water
(c) To stop air / oxygen dissolving back into the water
(d) To absorb water (vapour) — it keeps the air dry

questions.promptHtml:
Blocks of magnesium are attached to the steel legs of an oil rig.

(a) Explain how this prevents the steel from rusting. (2)
(b) Suggest why the blocks must be replaced every few years. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Magnesium is more reactive than iron 1; so the magnesium reacts / is oxidised / corrodes instead of the iron 1 — never "rusts instead"

(b) The magnesium is used up / corrodes away over time 1

(b) The magnesium is used up / corrodes away over time

Some steel buckets are coated with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting.

questions.answerHtml:
(a) Galvanising 1

(b) Zinc is more reactive than iron 1; so zinc reacts / is oxidised / corrodes instead of the iron 1

(c) Any two of painting, oiling / greasing, plastic coating, chromium plating, sacrificial protection with magnesium blocks 1 1

(b) Zinc is more reactive than iron ; so zinc reacts / is oxidised / corrodes instead of the iron

questions.promptHtml:
A student adds pieces of zinc to four sulfate solutions. She then repeats the experiment with pieces of metal M.

SolutionZinc addedMetal M added
magnesium sulfateno changeno change
zinc sulfateno changegrey coating
iron(II) sulfategrey coatinggrey coating

(a) Name the substance that forms the brown coating on the zinc. (1)
(b) State why there is no change when zinc is added to zinc sulfate solution. (1)
(c) Deduce the order of reactivity of magnesium, zinc, iron, copper and M, most reactive first. (2)
(d) Give a possible identity for M. (1)

(a) Copper 1 — not copper ions

(b) Zinc cannot displace itself 1

(c) M above zinc, because M displaces zinc 1; full order magnesium, M, zinc, iron, copper 1 — neither metal displaces magnesium, so magnesium is top

(b) Zinc cannot displace itself

questions.promptHtml:
This ionic equation shows the reaction when zinc powder is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution.

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

(a) Explain which substance is the reducing agent. (2)
(b) Give two observations. (2)

(a) Zinc (is the reducing agent) 1; because zinc donates / loses electrons (to the copper(II) ions) 1

(b) The blue colour fades / solution becomes colourless 1; a pink-brown solid forms (zinc disappears; mixture gets warm) 1

(b) The blue colour fades / solution becomes colourless ; a pink-brown solid forms (zinc disappears; mixture gets warm)

(a) Use the same volume and concentration of acid for each metal 1; use the same mass of each metal in the same form / surface area 1; observe the rate of bubbling, or measure the temperature rise, or the volume of gas in a set time 1; the fastest bubbling / largest temperature rise / most gas shows the most reactive 1

A student uses wet iron powder to remove the oxygen from a sample of air trapped in a tube. The column of air is 50.0 cm long at the start and 39.6 cm long after a week.

(a) State why the iron powder needs to be wet. (1)
(b) Explain the advantage of using iron powder rather than pieces of iron. (2)

modules.title: Chemical Tests
modules.standfirst: Year 11 topic. It turns up on almost every paper, often as a quick "give a test for…" worth one or two marks, and sometimes as a five- or six-mark "show that this compound is…". The marks go to the exact reagent, the exact colour and what you see. Knowing roughly what happens is not enough.

PaperWhat was asked

2024 school Q6(d) (1)Test for hydrogen: lit splint, squeaky pop (a glowing splint was rejected)
2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(b) (2)Describe a test for chlorine: damp blue litmus paper is bleached / turns white

2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(b) (5)Show a compound is lithium carbonate: flame test red, add acid, bubble the gas through limewater

2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(a) (2)Show a solution contains copper(II) ions: sodium hydroxide gives a blue precipitate (or blue-green flame)

2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12(c)(ii) (2)Show the copper(II) sulfate reaction is reversible: add water to anhydrous copper sulfate, white → blue
2022 Edexcel 1C Q6(a)(ii) (1)Give the test for hydrogen

2022 Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(iii) (3)Describe a test for ammonium ions
2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(c) (2)Describe a test for carbon dioxide
2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(ii) (5)Tests to show a product is lithium chloride: flame test red; nitric acid then silver nitrate, white precipitate
2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q6(d) (2)Test to show sodium oxide contains sodium ions: flame test, yellow
2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(a) (4)Chemical test for water (anhydrous copper sulfate) and physical test for pure water (boiling / freezing point)

The mark schemes spell out exactly where these marks go.

On the lithium chloride test (2022 Edexcel 2C): "REJECT incorrect acid e.g. HCl or H2SO4". Nitric acid goes before silver nitrate. Hydrochloric acid brings in chloride ions of its own.

On the lithium flame colour (2022 and 2023): "REJECT brick red/orange red". That is the calcium colour. Lithium is just red.

On the hydrogen test (2023 Edexcel 1C): "REJECT use of glowing splint". The school's 2024 scheme says the same. Hydrogen needs a lighted splint.

On the limewater and litmus tests (2024 Edexcel 1C): "No M5 and M6 if limewater added directly to the solution." You test the gas, not the liquid.
