subsections.html: Every test here does the same job. It turns an ion or a gas you cannot see into something you can see: a colour, a precipitate, a pop, a cloudy liquid. So every answer has two halves. Say what you do (the reagent), then what you see (the result). Name the substance only after that. If either half is missing, you lose the mark.

subsections.heading: Hydrogen and oxygen — two different splints
subsections.html:
Spec 2.44 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(ii) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q6(a)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(d)(i) · 2025 school Q3(a)

Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held near it; oxygen relights a glowing splint.

GasWhat you doWhat you see
Hydrogen, H₂Hold a lighted (burning) splint at the mouth of the tubeSqueaky pop
Oxygen, O₂Put a glowing splint into the gasThe splint relights

The pop is a tiny explosion: hydrogen reacts with oxygen from the air and makes water. Oxygen does not burn. It helps other things burn, so a splint that is only glowing bursts back into flame.

✗ "Glowing splint — squeaky pop" — the wrong splint. The school's 2024 scheme and the Edexcel scheme both reject it.
✗ "It burns with a squeaky pop" — the 2023 scheme ignores this on its own. Say what you hold near the gas.
✓ "Hold a lighted splint near the gas — it burns with a squeaky pop."
✓ "Put in a glowing splint — it relights."

subsections.heading: Carbon dioxide — limewater
subsections.html:
Spec 2.44 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q1(c) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(b)

Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy).

Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution. Carbon dioxide reacts with it to make calcium carbonate, which is insoluble. The tiny white particles of solid make the liquid look milky.

Limewater turning milkyCa(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)the CaCO₃ is the white precipitate you see

The CO₂ answer — two marks

1. Bubble the gas through limewater 1

2. The limewater turns milky / cloudy 1

"White precipitate" is also allowed. "Turns white" alone is risky. Say milky or cloudy.

✗ "A lighted splint goes out" — lots of gases put out a splint (nitrogen does too). This is not a test for CO₂.
✗ "Add limewater to the solution" — the 2024 scheme gives no marks. It is the gas you test.
✓ "Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky."

subsections.heading: Ammonia and chlorine — the two litmus tests
subsections.html:
Spec 2.44 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(iii)

Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.

GasPaperWhat you seeWhy
Ammonia, NH₃Damp red litmusTurns blueAmmonia is the only common alkaline gas
Chlorine, Cl₂Damp blue litmusTurns red, then bleached whiteChlorine forms an acid in water, then bleaches the dye

The paper must be damp. A gas has to dissolve in water before it can change an indicator. Dry litmus paper does nothing.

✗ "Chlorine turns litmus red" — lots of acidic gases do that. The mark is for bleached.
✗ "Red litmus turns blue then bleaches" for chlorine — the 2024 scheme gives only M1 for this.
✓ "Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas. It is bleached / turns white." The scheme also accepts "turns red and then bleached", and damp universal indicator paper.

subsections.heading: The flame test — how to do it
subsections.html:
Spec 2.45 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q6(b)(i) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q6(d)

A clean wire carries a little of the solid into a hot Bunsen flame, and the metal ion colours the flame.

  1. Clean a nichrome or platinum wire. Dip it in concentrated hydrochloric acid, then hold it in the flame. Repeat until the wire gives no colour.
  2. Dip the clean wire in the acid again, then into the solid sample so a little sticks to it.
  3. Hold it in the hottest part of a blue (non-luminous) Bunsen flame. That means the air hole is open.
  4. Observe the colour of the flame.

Why clean the wire — the 2024 two-mark answer

1. To remove other ions / impurities left on the wire 1

2. So they do not interfere with / mask the colour of the flame 1

Why a blue flame? A yellow (luminous) flame is already coloured, so it would hide the result. A blue flame is almost colourless and much hotter.

subsections.heading: Flame colours
subsections.html:
Spec 2.46 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q6(b)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(a)

Five cations, five colours. Learn them exactly as the spec words them.

CationFlame colourMark-scheme notes
Lithium, Li⁺RedCrimson / scarlet accepted. Brick-red and orange-red rejected
Sodium, Na⁺YellowOrange or yellow-orange allowed (2022 Jan)
Potassium, K⁺LilacPale purple
Calcium, Ca²⁺Orange-redOften called brick-red
Copper(II), Cu²⁺Blue-greenGreen allowed (2023 2C)

✗ "Lithium — orange-red" — that is calcium. The two reds are the classic mix-up.
✓ Lithium = red. Calcium = orange-red. If you only remember one thing, it is that lithium has no "orange" in it.

subsections.heading: Ammonium ions — warm with sodium hydroxide
subsections.html:
Spec 2.47 · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(iii) · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(d)(ii)

Warming an ammonium compound with sodium hydroxide solution gives off ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

Ammonium ion with hydroxide — ionicNH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)the hydroxide ion takes an H⁺ off the ammonium ion
Ammonium chloride with sodium hydroxideNH₄Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH₃ + H₂Oany ammonium salt behaves the same way

The ammonium-ion answer — three marks

1. Add sodium hydroxide solution and warm 1

2. Test the gas with damp red litmus paper 1

3. The litmus turns blue (so the gas is ammonia) 1

✗ "Add red litmus to the ammonium solution" — the 2022 and 2024 schemes both reject testing the solution. Hold the paper in the gas above the tube.
✓ "Warm with NaOH(aq); hold damp red litmus at the mouth of the tube; it turns blue."

subsections.heading: Copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) — coloured precipitates
subsections.html:
Spec 2.47 · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q5(a) · 2023 school Q10(a)

Adding sodium hydroxide solution to these metal ions makes an insoluble metal hydroxide, and its colour tells you the ion.

IonAdd NaOH(aq) — what you seeHydroxide formed
Copper(II), Cu²⁺Blue precipitateCu(OH)₂
Iron(II), Fe²⁺Green precipitateFe(OH)₂
Iron(III), Fe³⁺Orange-brown (red-brown) precipitateFe(OH)₃
Copper(II) hydroxide precipitateCu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)2 OH⁻ to balance the 2+ charge
Iron(II) hydroxide precipitateFe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)green solid
Iron(III) hydroxide precipitateFe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)3 OH⁻ for the 3+ ion · orange-brown solid

The number of OH⁻ always matches the charge on the metal ion. Only the metal ion and hydroxide ion appear in the equation. The sodium ions and sulfate (or chloride) ions are spectator ions.

The school's 2023 scheme, on copper(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide: "must be what you SEE".

✗ "Copper hydroxide forms" — a name, not an observation.
✗ "It fizzes" — rejected. No gas is made.
✓ "A blue precipitate (blue solid) forms."

subsections.heading: Halide ions — acidified silver nitrate
subsections.html:
Spec 2.48 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(ii)

Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide cream, iodide yellow.

Halide ionPrecipitateColour
Chloride, Cl⁻Silver chloride, AgClWhite
Bromide, Br⁻Silver bromide, AgBrCream
Iodide, I⁻Silver iodide, AgIYellow
Silver halide precipitateAg⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)same shape for Br⁻ → AgBr and I⁻ → AgI

Why add acid first? Carbonate ions would also react with silver ions and form a precipitate, which would give a false positive. The acid reacts with any carbonate ions and removes them as carbon dioxide.

Why nitric acid, and not hydrochloric? Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions. They would give a white precipitate whatever was in the sample. Nitric acid adds only nitrate ions, and silver nitrate is soluble.

✗ "Add hydrochloric acid and silver nitrate" — 2022 scheme: "REJECT incorrect acid e.g. HCl or H2SO4".
✓ "Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate shows chloride ions." "Acidified silver nitrate" is allowed for both of the first two marks.

subsections.heading: Sulfate ions — acidified barium chloride
subsections.html:
Spec 2.48

Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate shows sulfate ions.

Barium sulfate precipitateBa²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)barium sulfate is insoluble — white solid

The acid is there for the same reason as before. It removes carbonate ions, which would otherwise form a white precipitate of barium carbonate. Hydrochloric acid is fine this time, because barium chloride is soluble. The chloride ions do not form a precipitate with barium.

✗ "Add sulfuric acid, then barium chloride" — sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so you would always get a white precipitate.
✓ "Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate forms."

subsections.heading: Carbonate ions — acid, fizzing, limewater
subsections.html:
Spec 2.48 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(d)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(b)

Adding dilute acid to a carbonate gives effervescence, and the gas turns limewater milky, so it is carbon dioxide.

Carbonate ion with acid — ionicCO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂Othe fizzing is the CO₂ escaping
Sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acidNa₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂2HCl because CO₃²⁻ needs two H⁺

The carbonate answer — three marks (2024 M4–M6)

1. Add dilute (hydrochloric) acid 1

2. Bubble the gas through limewater 1

3. The limewater turns milky / cloudy 1

The scheme says acid only. If you add a second, wrong reagent (such as silver nitrate), you lose the mark.

subsections.heading: Water — anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
subsections.html:
Spec 2.49 · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(a)(i) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12(c)(ii)

Water turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.

Anhydrous to hydrated copper(II) sulfateCuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) ⇌ CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)white → blue · heating drives it back to white

"Anhydrous" means "without water". Hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are blue. Heat them and the water leaves, so they turn white. Add water back and they turn blue again. That is why 2023 Jan Q12 used this test to show the reaction is reversible.

✗ "Add copper sulfate — it turns blue" — the 2022 Jan scheme ties M2 to saying anhydrous or white copper sulfate. Blue copper sulfate is already hydrated.
✗ "It turns from blue to white" — backwards. The 2023 Jan scheme caps you at one mark for a wrong starting colour.
✓ "Add the liquid to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. It turns from white to blue."

subsections.heading: Pure water — a physical test
subsections.html:
Spec 2.50 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q9(b)(iii) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12(b) · 2022 Edexcel 1C Q9(a)(iv) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q11(a)(ii)

Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C and freezes (melts) at exactly 0 °C.

A pure substance has one fixed boiling point. Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point. Impurities also make it boil or melt over a range of temperatures instead of at one sharp value.

The pure-water answer — two marks

1. Measure the boiling point (or the freezing point) 1

2. Pure water boils at 100 °C (or freezes at 0 °C) 1

✗ "Add anhydrous copper sulfate" — that shows water is present, not that it is pure. Salty water turns it blue too. The 2023 scheme ignores any chemical test.
✗ "Evaporate it and see if anything is left" — rejected in 2023.
✓ "Measure the boiling point. If it is exactly 100 °C, the water is pure."

subsections.heading: Identifying a compound — putting two tests together
subsections.html:
Spec 2.44 – 2.48 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q7(d)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q5(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(ii)

A compound has a cation and an anion, so a "show that this is…" question needs one test for each, and every test needs a reagent and a result.

  1. Split the formula into its two ions, for example lithium chloride → Li⁺ and Cl⁻.
  2. Pick the cation test: a flame test for Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ or Cu²⁺; NaOH(aq) for NH₄⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺.
  3. Pick the anion test: HNO₃ then AgNO₃ for halides, HCl then BaCl₂ for sulfate, acid then limewater for carbonate.
  4. For each test, write the reagent, then the observation, with the exact colour.

2024 six-marker — ammonium carbonate, (NH₄)₂CO₃

Ammonium: add sodium hydroxide solution and warm 1; test the gas with damp red litmus paper 1; it turns blue 1

Carbonate: add dilute hydrochloric acid 1; bubble the gas through limewater 1; it turns milky 1

Use separate samples for each test. Each observation mark depends on the reagent before it, so a wrong reagent can wipe out two marks at once.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Gases: H₂ — lighted splint, squeaky pop. O₂ — glowing splint relights. CO₂ — limewater milky. NH₃ — damp red litmus blue. Cl₂ — damp blue litmus bleached.

Flames: Li⁺ red · Na⁺ yellow · K⁺ lilac · Ca²⁺ orange-red · Cu²⁺ blue-green.

NaOH(aq): Cu²⁺ blue ppt · Fe²⁺ green ppt · Fe³⁺ orange-brown ppt · NH₄⁺ (warm) ammonia gas.

Anions: halides — HNO₃ then AgNO₃: Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow. SO₄²⁻ — HCl then BaCl₂: white. CO₃²⁻ — acid: fizzing, gas turns limewater milky.

Water: anhydrous CuSO₄ white → blue. Pure water boils at 100 °C.

questions.promptHtml: Why does hydrogen need a lighted splint but oxygen a glowing one? What happens if you swap them?
questions.answerHtml:
Hydrogen is a fuel. A flame sets it alight, and it reacts with oxygen in the air so fast that you hear a small explosion, the squeaky pop.

Oxygen does not burn itself. It makes other things burn better. A splint that is only glowing does not have enough oxygen in air to flame, but in pure oxygen it relights.

Swap them and neither test works. A glowing splint cannot light hydrogen properly. A splint that is already burning just burns a bit brighter in oxygen, which is hard to see. That is why the schemes reject the wrong splint.

questions.promptHtml: Why must you add dilute nitric acid before silver nitrate, and why can the acid not be hydrochloric?
questions.answerHtml:
Acid first: carbonate ions would also form a precipitate with silver ions. The acid reacts with any carbonate and removes it as CO₂ gas. Then a precipitate can only mean a halide.

Not hydrochloric: HCl contains chloride ions. They would make white silver chloride even if the sample had no chloride in it, so every test would look positive. Nitric acid only adds nitrate ions, and all nitrates are soluble.

questions.promptHtml: For the sulfate test you acidify with hydrochloric acid. Why is that fine here, when it was wrong for the halide test? And why not sulfuric acid?
questions.answerHtml:
The reagent is barium chloride. Barium ions only precipitate with sulfate (and carbonate, which the acid removes). Barium chloride is soluble, so the extra chloride ions from HCl do nothing.

Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions. It would make white barium sulfate every time, whatever the sample was. You would be testing your own acid.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the flame-test wire cleaned in concentrated hydrochloric acid, and why use the blue flame and not the yellow one?
questions.answerHtml:
Cleaning: any ions left from an earlier test would colour the flame too, and could mask the real colour. Sodium is the worst because its bright yellow hides everything else. You dip and heat until the wire gives no colour at all.

Blue flame: the yellow (luminous) flame is already coloured by glowing soot, so it would hide or confuse the result. The blue flame is hotter and almost colourless, so the colour you see comes from the metal ion.

questions.promptHtml: In the ammonium test, why must the litmus paper be damp, and why must it be held in the gas rather than dipped into the solution?
questions.answerHtml:
Damp: ammonia only acts as an alkali once it dissolves in water and makes OH⁻ ions. Dry paper has no water, so nothing changes.

In the gas: the solution already contains sodium hydroxide, which is an alkali. Dipping red litmus into it turns it blue whether or not ammonium was there. Only the gas given off proves ammonia was made. That is why the schemes give no marks for testing the solution.

questions.promptHtml: Chlorine turns damp blue litmus red and then white. Why both changes, and which one proves it is chlorine?
questions.answerHtml:
Chlorine reacts with the water on the paper to form acids, so the litmus first turns red. One of those products is a bleach, which destroys the dye, so the paper goes white.

Plenty of gases are acidic and turn litmus red. Only chlorine bleaches it. The bleaching is the mark, so always say it.

questions.promptHtml: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns blue with seawater. Why is it a test for water, but not a test for pure water?
questions.answerHtml:
The white powder turns blue whenever any water reaches it. It cannot tell whether salt or anything else is dissolved in that water.

Purity needs a physical test. A pure substance has one fixed boiling point. Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C. Seawater boils above 100 °C, because dissolved salt raises the boiling point.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium hydroxide solution gives a gas with ammonium chloride, but a precipitate with copper(II) chloride. Why the difference?
questions.answerHtml:
With the ammonium ion, OH⁻ takes an H⁺ from NH₄⁺. That makes ammonia, NH₃, which is a gas and escapes when warmed.

With copper(II) ions, OH⁻ joins the metal ion: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂. Copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble, so it appears as a blue solid, a precipitate. Iron(II) and iron(III) behave the same way, but their hydroxides are green and orange-brown.

modules.standfirst: Year 11 topic. There is a calorimetry calculation on nearly every Paper 1C, and a bond-energy or equilibrium question on nearly every Paper 2C. The marks go on the sign of ΔH, on using the mass of water, and on saying the concentrations stay constant, not equal.

The dynamic equilibrium definition has been asked three times, and the mark scheme says the same thing each time:

"REJECT concentration of the reactants and products are the same" — 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(i). The accepted wording is that they remain constant.

And on the calorimetry side, 2024 Edexcel 1C Q10(d): "REJECT no heat loss". A polystyrene cup gives less heat loss, not none.

Paper 1C tests the practical and the calculation. Paper 2C tests the triple-only parts: bond energies, reaction profiles and equilibrium. There are no school-paper questions on this topic yet, so the real papers are your guide.

subsections.html: This module has two halves. Energetics is about the heat a reaction gives out or takes in: how to measure it, how to calculate it, and where it comes from (bonds). Equilibria is about reactions that go both ways, and how temperature, pressure and catalysts affect them.

subsections.heading: Exothermic and endothermic
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(i)

An exothermic reaction gives out heat energy to the surroundings; an endothermic reaction takes in heat energy from the surroundings.

TypeHeat energyTemperature of surroundingsSign of ΔHExamples
ExothermicGiven outRisesNegativeCombustion, neutralisation, displacement, thermite, respiration
EndothermicTaken inFallsPositiveThermal decomposition, dissolving ammonium nitrate, photosynthesis

The "surroundings" are the water or solution the thermometer is in. When a reaction gives out heat, the water warms up — the chemicals themselves have lost energy. That is why ΔH is negative when the thermometer goes up.

2024 Edexcel 1C Q2(b)(i) mark scheme: heat energy is given out — "IGNORE energy on its own".
✗ "Energy is released."
✓ "Heat (thermal) energy is given out to the surroundings."

subsections.heading: Calorimetry 1 — burning a fuel
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2, 3.8 · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q8 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q7

Burn a fuel under a copper can of water; the heat that warms the water is the heat the fuel gave out.

  1. Weigh the spirit burner and fuel (with its cap on).
  2. Measure, say, 100 cm³ of water into a copper can and clamp it above the burner.
  3. Record the initial temperature of the water.
  4. Light the wick. Stir the water with the thermometer.
  5. When the temperature has risen by about 20–35 °C, put the flame out (cap on).
  6. Record the final temperature and immediately reweigh the burner. The mass lost is the mass of fuel burned.

Why stir? So the heat is spread evenly through the water and the thermometer reads the true temperature. Why reweigh straight away, with the cap on? The fuel is volatile — it evaporates from the wick, which would make the mass loss too big. Why copper? It is a good conductor, so heat passes quickly into the water.

2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(a): the bottom of the can turns black. That is carbon (soot) from incomplete combustion.
✗ "Copper oxide" or "smoke".
✓ "Carbon."

subsections.heading: Calorimetry 2 — reactions in solution
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2, 3.8 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q10 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q10

For neutralisation, displacement and dissolving, the reaction happens in the water itself, so you do it in an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid.

  1. Measure the solution (e.g. 25 cm³ of acid) into a polystyrene cup with a measuring cylinder or pipette. Stand the cup in a beaker so it does not tip.
  2. Record its starting temperature.
  3. Add the second reactant — 25 cm³ of alkali, a weighed amount of metal powder, or a weighed amount of a salt.
  4. Put on the lid, stir, and record the highest temperature (or the lowest, for an endothermic change).
ChangeExampleTemperature
NeutralisationHCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂ORises — exothermic
DisplacementZn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + CuRises — exothermic
Metal + acidMg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂Rises — exothermic
DissolvingAmmonium nitrate in waterFalls — endothermic

Why polystyrene, not glass — 2024 Edexcel 1C Q10(d), two marks

1. Polystyrene is a (good) insulator / poor conductor of heat 1

2. so there is less heat loss to the surroundings 1

"No heat loss" is rejected. A lid reduces heat loss further.

subsections.heading: The calculation — Q = mcΔT, then ΔH
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3, 3.4 · 2024 Edexcel 1C Q10(c) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q8(c) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q10(b)

First find the heat energy the water gained, Q; then divide by the moles that reacted and give ΔH in kJ/mol with a sign.

Heat energy changeQ = m × c × ΔTQ in J · m = mass of the WATER or SOLUTION heated, in g (1 cm³ ≈ 1 g) · c = 4.2 J/g/°C · ΔT = temperature change in °C
Molar enthalpy changeΔH = −Q ÷ nQ in kJ (divide J by 1000) · n = moles of the reactant that was used up · negative if the temperature rose
  1. Work out ΔT = final − initial temperature.
  2. Q = m × 4.2 × ΔT, using the mass of water (not the fuel, not the metal).
  3. Find n of the reactant that was completely used up: the fuel burned, or the limiting reactant (the one not in excess).
  4. Divide Q by n, and convert J to kJ (÷ 1000).
  5. Add the sign: temperature went up → negative. Round as the question asks.

Worked example 1 — metal + acid (2024 Edexcel 1C Q10)

40 cm³ of nitric acid rises from 16.0 °C to 32.4 °C when 0.12 g of magnesium reacts. [Aᵣ Mg = 24]

  1. ΔT = 32.4 − 16.0 = 16.4 °C
  2. Q = 40 × 4.2 × 16.4 = 2755 J
  3. n(Mg) = 0.12 ÷ 24 = 0.005 mol
  4. 2755 ÷ 0.005 = 551 000 J/mol = 551 kJ/mol
  5. ΔH = −550 kJ/mol (2 s.f., with the minus sign)

Worked example 2 — combustion (2023 Edexcel 1C Q8)

Burning pentanol heats 100 cm³ of water by 35.0 °C. The burner goes from 90.11 g to 89.75 g. [Mᵣ = 88]

  1. Q = 100 × 4.2 × 35.0 = 14 700 J
  2. Mass burned = 90.11 − 89.75 = 0.36 g, so n = 0.36 ÷ 88 = 0.0041 mol
  3. 14 700 ÷ 0.0041 ≈ 3 600 000 J/mol = 3600 kJ/mol
  4. ΔH = −3600 kJ/mol

Worked example 3 — displacement: choose the limiting reactant

Excess zinc powder is added to 50 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate. The temperature rises by 10.0 °C.

  1. Q = 50 × 4.2 × 10.0 = 2100 J = 2.1 kJ
  2. The zinc is in excess, so use the copper(II) sulfate: n = 0.20 × 50 ÷ 1000 = 0.010 mol
  3. ΔH = −2.1 ÷ 0.010 = −210 kJ/mol

Worked example 4 — dissolving: an endothermic answer

4.0 g of ammonium nitrate (Mᵣ = 80) dissolves in 50 cm³ of water. The temperature falls by 6.0 °C.

  1. Q = 50 × 4.2 × 6.0 = 1260 J = 1.26 kJ
  2. n = 4.0 ÷ 80 = 0.050 mol
  3. The temperature fell, so ΔH is positive: ΔH = 1.26 ÷ 0.050 = +25.2 kJ/mol
Rearranged for the temperature riseΔT = Q ÷ (m × c)2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(i): 2880 ÷ (50 × 4.2) = 13.7 °C, then add the starting 21.0 °C → 34.7 °C

✗ Using the mass of fuel (0.36 g) as m in Q = mcΔT.
✗ Using the final temperature (50.9 °C) instead of the change (35.0 °C).
✗ "+550 kJ/mol" or "550" — 2024's M4 needed "correct sign" and 2 s.f.
✓ m = mass of water; ΔT = change; answer in kJ/mol, minus sign for a temperature rise.

subsections.heading: Why the answer comes out too small — errors
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2 · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(c) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q10(b)(ii) · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q8(a)

Almost every school calorimetry result is smaller than the data-book value, because not all the heat from the reaction ends up in the water.

ErrorWhy it makes ΔH too smallImprovement
Heat lost to the surroundingsHeat warms the air, the can and the clamp instead of the waterDraught shield, lid, insulate the can, polystyrene cup
Incomplete combustion (fuels)Some fuel burns to carbon (soot) and carbon monoxide, releasing less energyGood air supply
Fuel evaporates from the wickMass loss is bigger than the mass actually burned, so n is too bigKeep the cap on; reweigh immediately
Heat absorbed by the copper canOnly the water's mass is in Q = mcΔT(Usually just stated as heat loss)

2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(c) gave −910 kJ/mol against a data-book −1367 kJ/mol. The mark scheme took any two of: heat lost, incomplete combustion, ethanol impure or evaporating.

✗ "Human error" / "the thermometer was wrong" — not specific, no mark.
✓ "Heat was lost to the surroundings" and "incomplete combustion of the ethanol".

subsections.heading: Energy level diagrams (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5C · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(d)(ii)

An energy level diagram shows the reactants and products as two horizontal lines, with ΔH as a vertical arrow from the reactants to the products.

  1. Label the vertical axis energy.
  2. Draw the reactants line (e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂) and label it with formulae.
  3. Exothermic: the products line (CO₂ + 2H₂O) is lower. Endothermic: it is higher.
  4. Draw a vertical arrow from the reactants level to the products level and label it ΔH (e.g. −890 kJ/mol).

The arrow therefore points down for an exothermic reaction and up for an endothermic one. The products are lower in an exothermic reaction because the chemicals have lost energy to the surroundings.

2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(d)(ii): "REJECT arrow pointing from products level to reactants level".
✗ An upward arrow for an exothermic reaction.
✓ Arrow starts at the reactants and ends at the products; a double-headed arrow is also accepted.

subsections.heading: Reaction profiles — ΔH, Ea and the catalysed curve (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.14C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(ii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q5(b)

A reaction profile is an energy level diagram with the hump drawn in: the activation energy is the height of the hump above the reactants. Module 7 (Rates of Reaction) explained why a catalyst speeds a reaction up — an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. Here you just have to draw it.

  1. Reactants line on the left, labelled (e.g. H₂ + Cl₂).
  2. A curve rising to a peak, then falling to the products line on the right, labelled (e.g. 2HCl).
  3. Ea: vertical arrow up from the reactants level to the top of the peak.
  4. ΔH: vertical arrow from the reactants level to the products level — down if exothermic, up if endothermic.
  5. Catalysed curve: starts at the same reactants level, has a lower peak, ends at the same products level.

A catalyst lowers Ea but does not change ΔH — the reactants and products are the same substances with the same energies. For an endothermic reaction, Ea is always bigger than ΔH, because the peak must be above the products.

2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(ii): Ea arrow "REJECT arrow pointing down"; ΔH arrow for this exothermic reaction "REJECT arrow pointing up".
✗ Ea drawn from the products level, or from the axis.
✗ Catalysed curve that ends at a different products level.
✓ Both arrows start at the reactants line; catalysed curve has the same start and end, lower peak.

subsections.heading: Bond breaking and bond making (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.6C · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(b)(iv) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q6(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(b)

Breaking bonds takes in energy (endothermic); making bonds gives out energy (exothermic). ΔH is the difference between the two.

  • If more energy is released making the new bonds than is taken in breaking the old ones → exothermic, ΔH negative.
  • If more energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making them → endothermic, ΔH positive.
  • If the same bonds are broken and made → ΔH ≈ 0.

Why is it exothermic? — 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(b)(iv), two marks

1. Bond breaking requires (takes in) energy and bond making releases energy 1

2. More energy is released making the bonds than is taken in breaking them 1

The ester reaction is the classic ΔH ≈ 0 case. In CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, one C–O and one O–H bond are broken, and one C–O and one O–H bond are made. Same bonds broken as made → the energy taken in equals the energy given out → ΔH ≈ 0.

✗ "Breaking bonds releases energy." — the single most common error in this topic.
✓ "Breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds gives out energy."

subsections.heading: Bond energy calculations (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.7C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(i) · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(d)(i)

Add up the energy of every bond broken in the reactants, add up every bond made in the products, and subtract: broken minus made.

Enthalpy change from bond energiesΔH = (energy of bonds broken) − (energy of bonds made)all in kJ/mol · a negative answer = exothermic · include the sign
  1. Draw or read the displayed formulae so you can count every bond.
  2. Multiply by the numbers in the balanced equation (3N₂H₄ means three molecules).
  3. Total the bonds broken (reactants).
  4. Total the bonds made (products).
  5. ΔH = broken − made. Keep the sign.

Worked example — H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (2024 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(i))

H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol

  1. Broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
  2. Made: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ
  3. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol

The mark scheme: "(+)184 scores 2" — the sign is worth a whole mark.

Worked example — hydrazine, 3N₂H₄ → 4NH₃ + N₂ (2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(b))

N–N 158, N–H 391, N≡N 945 kJ/mol. Each N₂H₄ has one N–N and four N–H.

  1. Broken: 3 × 158 + 12 × 391 = 474 + 4692 = 5166 kJ
  2. Made: 4 NH₃ has 12 N–H, plus one N≡N: 12 × 391 + 945 = 5637 kJ
  3. ΔH = 5166 − 5637 = −471 kJ/mol

Worked example — finding an unknown bond energy (2022 Edexcel 2C Q7(d)(i))

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 463. Find C–H.

  1. Broken: 4 × (C–H) + 2 × 498 = 4(C–H) + 996
  2. Made: 2 × 805 + 4 × 463 = 3462
  3. 4(C–H) + 996 − 3462 = −890
  4. 4(C–H) = 1576, so C–H = 394 kJ/mol

✗ "made − broken" — gives the right number with the wrong sign.
✗ Forgetting the big numbers in the equation: 2H₂O has four O–H bonds.
✓ Broken − made, every bond counted, sign shown.

equations.name: Enthalpy change from bond energies
equations.formula: ΔH = (energy of bonds broken) − (energy of bonds made)

subsections.heading: Reversible reactions — copper(II) sulfate and ammonium chloride
subsections.html:
Spec 3.17, 3.18 · 2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12(c) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(c)(ii)

A reversible reaction can go in both directions: the products can react to re-form the reactants. The symbol ⇌ shows this.

Dehydration of copper(II) sulfateCuSO₄·5H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l)blue hydrated → white anhydrous on heating · add water: white → blue, and it gets hot
  • Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate drives off the water of crystallisation. It turns white. This direction takes in heat — endothermic.
  • Adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns it blue again and gives out heat — exothermic.
  • That colour change is the test for water: add the liquid to anhydrous (white) copper(II) sulfate — it turns blue.
Heating ammonium chlorideNH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g)white solid at the hot end breaks down · white solid re-forms in the cooler part of the tube

Heat ammonium chloride at the bottom of a test tube. The white solid seems to disappear as it decomposes into two gases. Higher up, where the tube is cooler, the gases recombine and a white solid forms on the glass again.

2023 Jan Edexcel 1C Q12(c)(ii): "Max 1 mark if incorrect starting colour".
✗ "Add copper sulfate; it turns blue." — which copper sulfate? Hydrated is already blue.
✓ "Add the liquid to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, which turns from white to blue."

subsections.heading: Dynamic equilibrium (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.19C, 3.20C · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(i) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(c)(iii)

In a sealed container a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium: the forward and reverse reactions go on at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

  1. At the start there are only reactants, so the forward reaction is fast and the reverse is zero.
  2. As reactants are used up, the forward rate falls. As products build up, the reverse rate rises.
  3. Eventually the two rates are equal.
  4. Now products are made exactly as fast as they are used up, so the concentrations stop changing.

Dynamic means both reactions are still happening — it has not stopped. Sealed container (a closed system) matters: if a gas escapes, the reverse reaction cannot happen and equilibrium is never reached.

The definition — two marks, asked three times

1. The forward and reverse (backward) reactions occur at the same rate 1

2. The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant 1

✗ "The concentrations of reactants and products are equal." — rejected in 2022 Jan and 2023 Jan.
✗ "The reaction has stopped."
✓ "The concentrations remain constant (do not change)."

subsections.heading: Catalysts do not move the equilibrium (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.21C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q7(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(c)(ii)

A catalyst speeds up the forward and the reverse reactions by the same amount, so the position of equilibrium — and the yield — does not change. Equilibrium is just reached sooner.

The catalyst lowers the activation energy of the pathway in both directions (look at the catalysed reaction profile: the peak is lower whether you climb from the left or the right). Both rates rise equally, so they stay equal to each other at the same concentrations.

The catalyst answer — two marks

1. A catalyst increases the rate of the forward and backward reactions 1

2. equally (by the same amount) — so no effect on the position or the yield 1

✗ "The catalyst increases the yield because the reaction is faster."
✗ "A catalyst speeds up the forward reaction." — only half of it.
✓ "No effect on the yield: it increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally."

subsections.heading: Changing temperature and pressure (triple only)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.22C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)

Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction; raising the pressure shifts it towards the side with fewer moles of gas. (Lowering them does the opposite.)

Change madeEquilibrium shifts towards…
Temperature increasedThe endothermic direction
Temperature decreasedThe exothermic direction
Pressure increasedThe side with fewer moles of gas
Pressure decreasedThe side with more moles of gas
Catalyst addedNo shift — equilibrium reached sooner

The ΔH given with the equation is for the forward reaction. The reverse reaction has the same size ΔH with the opposite sign.

Worked example — 2023 Edexcel 2C Q7(c)

CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g)   ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

  1. Temperature lowered (700 °C → 600 °C): the forward reaction is endothermic, so equilibrium shifts to the left (the exothermic direction). The yield of hydrogen decreases.
  2. Pressure lowered (5 atm → 4 atm): left side has 1 + 1 = 2 mol of gas, right side 1 + 3 = 4 mol. Lower pressure shifts to more moles of gas — the right. The yield of hydrogen increases.

Each is marked as a pair: the effect on yield 1, then the reason 1. The reason mark depends on the effect being right.

Count only gas moles, from the numbers in front of each formula. If both sides have the same number, as in H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), pressure has no effect on the position. Raising the temperature or pressure also makes both reactions faster, but that is a rate effect, separate from the position.

✗ "Increasing the temperature favours the forward reaction." — only if the forward reaction is endothermic.
✗ "Fewer molecules on the right" — count moles of gas from the balanced equation.
✓ "Yield decreases, because the forward reaction is endothermic, so equilibrium shifts to the left."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Calorimetry: Q = m × 4.2 × ΔT with m = mass of water; ΔH = −Q ÷ n, in kJ/mol, with a sign. Use n of the fuel burned or the reactant not in excess.

Too small? Heat lost to the surroundings; incomplete combustion; fuel evaporated.

Bonds: breaking takes in energy, making gives out energy. ΔH = broken − made.

Profiles: Ea and ΔH arrows both start at the reactants. Catalyst: lower peak, same ΔH.

Equilibrium: forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant. Temperature up → endothermic direction. Pressure up → fewer moles of gas. Catalyst → no change, reached sooner.

questions.promptHtml: In the pentanol experiment, 0.36 g of fuel heated 100 g of water. Why does Q = mcΔT use 100 g and not 0.36 g?
questions.answerHtml:
Q = mcΔT measures the heat that went into something whose temperature you measured. The thermometer is in the water, and c = 4.2 J/g/°C is the specific heat capacity of water. So m must be the mass of the water.

The fuel comes in later, when you divide by its moles to get the energy per mole. Mass of water goes into Q; mass of fuel goes into n.

questions.promptHtml: The temperature of the solution goes up, yet ΔH is negative. Why is that not a contradiction?
questions.answerHtml:
ΔH describes the energy of the chemicals, not the water. The reacting chemicals lose energy, and it goes into the water as heat. The water gets hotter because the chemicals got lower in energy.

On an energy level diagram that is why the products line is below the reactants for an exothermic reaction. Thermometer up → chemicals down → ΔH negative.

questions.promptHtml: A student's value for the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is −910 kJ/mol. The data book says −1367 kJ/mol. Explain why school values are almost always too small, never too big.
questions.answerHtml:
Every common error makes Q too small or n too big:

  • Heat lost to the air, the can and the clamp → less heat reaches the water → Q too small.
  • Incomplete combustion → some fuel becomes carbon or carbon monoxide, which releases less energy → Q too small.
  • Fuel evaporates from the wick → the mass loss counts fuel that never burned → n too big.

All three push Q ÷ n down. There is no everyday error that adds extra heat to the water, so the answer is nearly always too small.

questions.promptHtml: If breaking bonds always takes in energy, how can any reaction be exothermic?
questions.answerHtml:
Because a reaction also makes new bonds, and making bonds gives out energy. The overall ΔH is the balance.

In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, breaking one H–H and one Cl–Cl takes in 678 kJ. Making two H–Cl bonds gives out 862 kJ. More out than in → exothermic, ΔH = −184 kJ/mol.

The "hump" on the reaction profile is the bond-breaking part: energy has to go in first before the new bonds can form. That is the activation energy.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the enthalpy change for making an ester from an acid and an alcohol about 0 kJ/mol?
questions.answerHtml:
Look at which bonds change. One C–O and one O–H bond are broken in the reactants, and one C–O and one O–H bond are made in the products. Every other bond is untouched.

The same bonds are broken and made, so the energy taken in to break them equals the energy given out making them. Broken − made ≈ 0.

It is only "approximately" 0 because the same bond in different molecules has a slightly different energy — data-book bond energies are averages.

questions.promptHtml: At dynamic equilibrium the colour and pressure of the mixture stay the same for hours. Why is it wrong to say the reaction has stopped?
questions.answerHtml:
Both reactions are still happening. Reactant particles are still turning into products, and product particles are still turning back into reactants.

They happen at the same rate, so every product molecule made is balanced by one used up. The amounts do not change, so nothing looks different — but it is dynamic, not static.

That is also why the concentrations are constant but not necessarily equal. There could be far more products than reactants, or the other way round.

questions.promptHtml: A nickel catalyst is added to CH₄ + H₂O ⇌ CO + 3H₂. The forward reaction speeds up. Why doesn't the yield of hydrogen go up?
questions.answerHtml:
The catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy — and it is the same pathway in both directions. So it speeds up the backward reaction by the same amount as the forward one.

Both rates rise equally, so they are still equal at the same concentrations. The position does not move and the yield is unchanged. The only benefit is that equilibrium is reached sooner.

questions.promptHtml: Raising the temperature increases the yield of hydrogen from CH₄ + H₂O ⇌ CO + 3H₂, but decreases the yield of ammonia from N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
A rise in temperature always shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Which way that is depends on the sign of ΔH.

Methane + steam: ΔH = +206 kJ/mol, so the forward reaction is endothermic. Heating shifts it to the right → more hydrogen.

Ammonia: ΔH is negative, so the forward reaction is exothermic and the reverse is endothermic. Heating shifts it to the left → less ammonia.

Always read the ΔH before answering. "Hotter means more product" is only true for an endothermic forward reaction.

questions.answerHtml:

Hydrogen reacts with bromine: H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366.

modules.title: Alcohols, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Polyesters
modules.standfirst: Year 11 topic, all triple only. It is on Paper 2C almost every year, often as a whole 10–15 mark question. The marks go on three things: drawing formulae with every bond shown, naming esters the right way round, and the hydration-versus-fermentation comparison.

Two mark schemes, one formula, opposite rulings. In January 2022 the question asked for the molecular formula of ethanol:

"C2H6O … REJECT C2H5OH"

In June 2023, in the fermentation equation, the scheme said "if C2H6O given no M1".

So: molecular formula = C₂H₆O (all the atoms counted, nothing grouped). In an equation, write C₂H₅OH (or CH₃CH₂OH), so the –OH group shows it is ethanol. Read which one the question asks for.

subsections.html: This module is three families of carbon compounds and how they turn into each other. An alcohol can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid. An alcohol plus a carboxylic acid make an ester. Join acids and alcohols with two functional groups each and you get a polyester. Homologous series and alkenes are in module 10, equilibrium in module 15 and addition polymers in module 16. This module links to them rather than repeating them.

subsections.heading: Three functional groups
subsections.html:
Spec 4.29C, 4.34C, 4.38C · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(a)(i) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(a)(i)

A functional group is the group of atoms that gives a family its reactions: –OH for alcohols, –COOH for carboxylic acids and –COO– for esters.

FamilyFunctional groupDisplayedName ending
Alcohol–OH–O–H-ol (ethanol)
Carboxylic acid–COOHC with a double-bonded O, and an O–H-oic acid (ethanoic acid)
Ester–COO–C with a double-bonded O, and an O joined to another carbon-yl …-oate (ethyl ethanoate)

The carboxylic acid group and the ester group, displayed:

  O                    O
  ║                    ║
──C──O──H            ──C──O──
carboxylic acid      ester

"Ring the functional group" questions: 2022 Jan scheme said "REJECT any other atoms in the ring."
✗ A ring round the whole CH₃COOH molecule, or round just the O–H.
✓ In ethanoic acid, ring exactly the –COOH: the C, both O atoms and the H on the oxygen.

subsections.heading: The four alcohols — names and formulae
subsections.html:
Spec 4.30C, 4.3 · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(a), (b)(iii) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q3(d)(ii) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1(c)(ii)

The alcohols form a homologous series: each has one more CH₂ than the last, and every one ends in –OH.

CarbonsNameStructural formulaMolecular formula
1MethanolCH₃OHCH₄O
2EthanolCH₃CH₂OH (or C₂H₅OH)C₂H₆O
3Propan-1-ol (propanol)CH₃CH₂CH₂OHC₃H₈O
4Butan-1-ol (butanol)CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OHC₄H₁₀O

The "-1-" means the –OH is on the end carbon. The spec only uses the end-carbon versions, and "propanol" and "butanol" are accepted.

   H                 H  H
   │                 │  │
H──C──O──H        H──C──C──O──H
   │                 │  │
   H                 H  H
methanol          ethanol

   H  H  H           H  H  H  H
   │  │  │           │  │  │  │
H──C──C──C──O──H  H──C──C──C──C──O──H
   │  │  │           │  │  │  │
   H  H  H           H  H  H  H
propan-1-ol       butan-1-ol

Homologous series — the two-mark list (2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(a))

Any two of these:

1. Same general formula 1

2. Same functional group 1

Also accepted: similar chemical properties; a trend in physical properties; consecutive members differ by CH₂. The scheme ignored "same chemical properties", so say similar.

2024 scheme on the methanol drawing: "Penalise once only if O - H bond not shown".
✗ H–C–OH, with the OH written as one lump.
✓ H–C–O–H, with every bond drawn. Each carbon has four lines, the oxygen two, each hydrogen one.

subsections.heading: Burning alcohols — complete combustion
subsections.html:
Spec 4.31C · 2023 Edexcel 1C Q8(d)

In plenty of oxygen, an alcohol burns completely to carbon dioxide and water, just like a hydrocarbon. Burning is one of the three ways ethanol can be oxidised.

Complete combustion of ethanolC₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂Ocount the O in the alcohol too: 1 + 6 = 7 on the left, 4 + 3 = 7 on the right

Balancing any alcohol combustion, in order

  1. Carbon: number of C atoms → that many CO₂.
  2. Hydrogen: count all the H atoms (C₅H₁₁OH has 12) → half that many H₂O.
  3. Oxygen: count the O on the right, subtract the one O already in the alcohol, then halve to get the O₂.
  4. A half is allowed (7½O₂), or double everything.

Pentanol: C₅H₁₁OH → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O. Right side has 10 + 6 = 16 O. Minus 1 in the alcohol = 15 O atoms = 7½O₂.

Complete combustion of pentanolC₅H₁₁OH + 7½O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O2023 Edexcel 1C Q8(d) — formulae one mark, balancing the second; multiples allowed

✗ C₂H₅OH + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O — forgot the oxygen already inside the alcohol.
✓ C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

subsections.heading: Oxidising ethanol to ethanoic acid
subsections.html:
Spec 4.31C, 4.37C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(b)

Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid in two ways: slowly by microbes using oxygen in the air, or quickly by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

Microbial oxidation. Leave wine open to the air and microbes use oxygen to oxidise the ethanol. It turns sour: the ethanoic acid makes vinegar, which is an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid.

Microbial oxidation of ethanolC₂H₅OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂Ooxygen from the air; microbes do it · this is why wine left open goes sour

Potassium dichromate(VI). Heat ethanol with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid. The dichromate is the oxidising agent.

  1. Add potassium dichromate(VI) and dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) to the alcohol.
  2. Heat.
  3. The solution changes from orange to green.
  4. The ethanol has become ethanoic acid.

The same thing works on the other alcohols: methanol → methanoic acid, propanol → propanoic acid. The carbon count stays the same.

2024 scheme: orange and green "must be in the correct order".
✗ "from green to orange" — no marks.
✗ "the ethanol turns green" — ethanol is colourless; it is the dichromate that changes.
✓ "The potassium dichromate(VI) changes from orange to green."

subsections.heading: Making ethanol 1 — hydration of ethene
subsections.html:
Spec 4.32C · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q1(c) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q3(b)

Ethene reacts with steam at about 300 °C and 60–70 atm, with a phosphoric acid catalyst, to make ethanol. "Hydration" means adding water across the C=C double bond.

Hydration of etheneC₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OHsteam · phosphoric acid catalyst · about 300 °C · 60–70 atm
  • Reactants: ethene and steam. The ethene comes from cracking crude-oil fractions (module 10).
  • Catalyst: phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄).
  • Temperature: about 300 °C. Pressure: about 60–70 atm.
  • It is fast, it runs continuously, and the ethanol made is pure.

2022 Jan scheme accepted any pressure "between 60 and 70 atm". It had to be in that window.
✗ "high temperature and high pressure" — the question wants numbers.
✓ "300 °C and 60–70 atmospheres, with a phosphoric acid catalyst."

subsections.heading: Making ethanol 2 — fermentation
subsections.html:
Spec 4.32C, 4.33C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q3(a), (c)

Enzymes in yeast turn glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, at about 30 °C and with no air.

Fermentation of glucoseC₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂enzymes in yeast · about 30 °C · absence of air · atmospheric pressure

Check it: 6 C, 12 H and 6 O on each side. Write ethanol as C₂H₅OH here. The 2023 scheme gave no formula mark for C₂H₆O in this equation.

Why no air — either of these two-mark chains:

  1. Oxygen in the air would oxidise the ethanol …
  2. … to ethanoic acid (the wine turns to vinegar).

or: fermentation must be anaerobic so ethanol forms; with oxygen the yeast respires aerobically and makes only carbon dioxide and water.

Why about 30 °C — the optimum temperature:

  1. Colder: the enzymes work slowly, so fermentation is too slow.
  2. Hotter: the enzymes in the yeast denature (their active sites change shape), so fermentation stops.
  3. About 30 °C gives a reasonable rate without denaturing the enzymes.

The product is a dilute solution of ethanol in water, so it has to be purified by fractional distillation.

✗ "No air, or the yeast would die." — not the reason given in any mark scheme.
✗ "At high temperature the enzymes are killed." — enzymes are not alive.
✓ "Oxygen would oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid." · "Above the optimum the enzymes denature."

subsections.heading: Hydration or fermentation — the comparison answer
subsections.html:
Spec 4.32C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q3(b)

Fermentation uses a renewable raw material and gentle conditions, but it is slow, runs in batches and gives impure ethanol. Hydration is the opposite on every point.

FeatureHydration of etheneFermentation of glucose
Raw materialEthene and steamAqueous glucose (from sugar cane etc.)
SourceCrude oil — finite, non-renewablePlants — renewable
CatalystPhosphoric acidEnzymes in yeast
TemperatureAbout 300 °CAbout 30 °C
Pressure60–70 atm1 atm (atmospheric)
RateFastSlow
ProcessContinuousBatch
ProductPure ethanolImpure — dilute, needs distilling

The four-mark answer — advantage and disadvantage of fermentation

Advantage: uses a lower temperature and pressure 1, so less energy is needed 1

or: glucose comes from plants, so it is renewable, whereas ethene comes from crude oil, which is finite.

Disadvantage: fermentation is slower 1, and it is a batch process whereas hydration is continuous 1

or: the ethanol is impure, so it has to be purified. Or: growing sugar cane uses land that could grow food crops.

2023 scheme: "IGNORE cheaper" and "IGNORE reference to yield".
✗ "Fermentation is cheaper."
✓ "Fermentation uses a lower temperature, so less energy is needed." Every advantage needs a reason linked to it.

subsections.heading: Carboxylic acids — names and formulae
subsections.html:
Spec 4.34C, 4.35C, 4.37C · 2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(b)(iii) · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(a)(ii)

subsections.heading: Carboxylic acid reactions — metals and carbonates
subsections.html:
Spec 4.36C · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(b) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(a)(iii)

Carboxylic acids react like any acid: with metals they give a salt and hydrogen, and with carbonates a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

Ethanoic acid and magnesium2CH₃COOH + Mg → Mg(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂salt = magnesium ethanoate · fizzing · hydrogen gives a squeaky pop
Ethanoic acid and sodium carbonate2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂salt = sodium ethanoate · fizzing · CO₂ turns limewater milky
Methanoic acid and sodium carbonate2HCOOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2HCOONa + H₂O + CO₂2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(b) · salt = sodium methanoate

The salts are named -oate: methanoate, ethanoate, propanoate, butanoate. The metal replaces the H of the –COOH, so sodium ethanoate is CH₃COONa.

Carboxylic acids are weak acids. They do the same reactions as hydrochloric acid, only more gently: slower fizzing at the same concentration.

Test for a carboxylic acid (not using an indicator) — two marks

1. Add a named metal such as magnesium or zinc — or a carbonate such as sodium carbonate 1

2. Effervescence (bubbles, fizzing) 1

An alcohol or an ester gives no fizzing. That is how you tell them apart.

2022 Jan scheme: the metal "must be a named metal" and "REJECT Group 1 metals". 2022 June: "REJECT NaCOOH" and, for the observation, "IGNORE gas given off".
✗ "Add sodium; a gas is given off."
✓ "Add magnesium ribbon; effervescence." · Salt formula HCOONa, not NaCOOH.

subsections.heading: Esters — making ethyl ethanoate
subsections.html:
Spec 4.38C, 4.39C, 4.40C · 2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(a), (c)(i) · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q6(a) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(a)(ii)

An alcohol and a carboxylic acid react, with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, to make an ester and water.

Making ethyl ethanoateCH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂Oethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water · catalyst: concentrated sulfuric acid

The –OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol's –OH leave together as water. The rest joins through the new –COO– link.

   H  O                     H  H
   │  ║                     │  │
H──C──C──O──H    +    H──O──C──C──H

Ethyl ethanoate: structural formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, molecular formula C₄H₈O₂.

The reaction is reversible (⇌), so it reaches equilibrium and never fully converts (module 15). The sulfuric acid is a catalyst. That is why its moles do not change during the reaction (2023 Jan Edexcel 2C Q6(c)(i)).

  1. From the alcohol: methanol → methyl, ethanol → ethyl, propanol → propyl, butanol → butyl.
  2. From the acid: methanoic → methanoate, ethanoic → ethanoate, propanoic → propanoate, butanoic → butanoate.
  3. Name = alcohol part + acid part, e.g. ethyl ethanoate, propyl methanoate.
  4. Formula = the acid part (the side with C=O) written first, then the alcohol chain: ethyl ethanoate is CH₃COOCH₂CH₃.

subsections.heading: Why esters matter — smells, uses and the practical
subsections.html:
Spec 4.42C, 4.43C · 2023 Edexcel 2C Q6(a)(i), (ii)

Esters are volatile and have distinctive, usually fruity, smells, so they are used as food flavourings and in perfumes. "Volatile" means they evaporate easily, which is how the smell reaches your nose.

Practical 4.43C — preparing ethyl ethanoate:

  1. Put a little ethanol and ethanoic acid in a test tube.
  2. Add a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (the catalyst).
  3. Warm in a hot water bath for a few minutes. No naked flame, because ethanol and the ester are flammable.
  4. Pour the mixture into a beaker of sodium carbonate solution (or water). The carbonate neutralises the leftover acids and fizzes.
  5. The ester forms an oily layer on the surface. Waft it carefully: it has a sweet, fruity smell, like pear drops or nail-polish remover.

2023 scheme for "how would you know an ester has formed": distinctive, sweet or fruity smell, and it would also "ACCEPT an oily layer forms".
✗ "It changes colour." / "It fizzes." (the fizzing is the sodium carbonate reacting with leftover acid, not the ester).
✓ "It has a fruity smell" or "an oily layer forms on the surface."

subsections.heading: Polyesters and biopolyesters
subsections.html:
Spec 4.48C, 4.49C, 4.50C · 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(d) · 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(e)

A dicarboxylic acid and a diol join through ester links to make a polyester, and a molecule of water is lost at every link. This is condensation polymerisation.

Each monomer has a functional group at both ends, so the chain can keep growing in both directions. Compare addition polymers (module 16): one monomer with a C=C, and nothing else is made. Here there are two different monomers and water is made too.

      O  O                    H  H
      ║  ║                    │  │
H──O──C──C──O──H        H──O──C──C──O──H
                              │  │
                              H  H
ethanedioic acid        ethanediol

The acid loses –OH from each end. The diol loses H from each –OH. Those join to make water, and the C and O join to make ester links. The repeat unit:

  ┌                    ┐
  │  O  O     H  H     │
  │  ║  ║     │  │     │
 ─┼──C──C──O──C──C──O──┼─
  │           │  │     │
  │           H  H     │
  └                    ┘ n
Making a polyestern HOOC–COOH + n HO–CH₂CH₂–OH → –[OC–COO–CH₂CH₂–O]ₙ– + 2n H₂Oethanedioic acid + ethanediol → polyester + water · two ester links, so two waters, per repeat unit
  1. Draw the acid with no –OH on either end: –OC–(middle)–CO–.
  2. Draw the diol with no H on either O: –O–CH₂CH₂–O–.
  3. Join them: acid part then diol part. Every C=O carbon should now be bonded to an O on one side.
  4. Add brackets, an extension bond through each bracket, and n.

How 2022 Jan Edexcel 2C Q7(e) marked the repeat unit — two marks

1. The right carbons from each monomer (three from that dicarboxylic acid, two from the diol) and the ester linkage 1

2. –OH lost from the dicarboxylic acid and –H lost from the diol 1

The scheme allowed a structure without extension bonds and ignored brackets and n. The marks are on the atoms, so get those right first. Still draw the brackets, extension bonds and n.

2022 June scheme on drawing the monomers: "REJECT OH--C once only". The bond must go from the carbon to the O, not to the H.
✗ HO–CH₂ drawn with the line joining H to C.
✓ H–O–CH₂: the oxygen is bonded to the carbon.

Biopolyesters (spec 4.50C). Some polyesters, called biopolyesters, are biodegradable: microorganisms can break them down. That matters because addition polymers such as poly(ethene) are inert and do not biodegrade. They last for centuries in landfill, and burning them can release toxic gases (module 16). A biodegradable polyester rots away after use, so it causes fewer disposal problems.

✗ "All polyesters are biodegradable." — only some: the biopolyesters.
✓ "Biopolyesters are biodegradable, so they are broken down by microorganisms and do not build up in landfill."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Groups: alcohol –OH · carboxylic acid –COOH · ester –COO–. Draw every bond, including O–H.

Oxidation of ethanol: burning → CO₂ + H₂O; microbes + air → ethanoic acid (vinegar); acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heat → ethanoic acid, orange to green.

Hydration: ethene + steam, phosphoric acid, 300 °C, 60–70 atm. Fermentation: glucose, yeast enzymes, 30 °C, no air: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

No air: oxygen would oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid. 30 °C: colder is too slow, hotter denatures the enzymes.

Acids + metal → salt + hydrogen. Acids + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂. Salts are -oates.

Esters: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst. Name: alcohol-yl, acid-oate. Fruity, volatile, flavourings and perfumes.

Polyester: dicarboxylic acid + diol → polyester + water, condensation polymerisation. Biopolyesters are biodegradable.

questions.promptHtml: Fermentation must happen in the absence of air. Give the two different explanations the mark scheme accepts, and say why both lead to less ethanol.
questions.answerHtml:
Route 1 — oxidation: oxygen in the air would oxidise the ethanol that has formed into ethanoic acid. That is exactly how wine left open turns into vinegar. The ethanol is made and then destroyed.

Route 2 — respiration: with oxygen, yeast respires aerobically and breaks glucose all the way down to carbon dioxide and water. No ethanol is made at all. Fermentation is the anaerobic route.

Either way, air means less ethanol: one route stops it forming, the other destroys it after it forms.

questions.promptHtml: Why is about 30 °C the best temperature for fermentation, when for most reactions hotter simply means faster?
questions.answerHtml:
Fermentation is catalysed by enzymes, which are proteins.

Below 30 °C it behaves like any reaction: less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions, a slow rate.

Well above 30 °C the enzymes' active sites change shape. They denature and stop working, so the rate collapses. That never happens with phosphoric acid in hydration, which is why hydration can run at 300 °C.

About 30 °C is the optimum: as fast as possible without denaturing the enzymes.

questions.promptHtml: One mark scheme rejected C₂H₅OH and wanted C₂H₆O. Another gave no mark for C₂H₆O. How can both be right?
questions.answerHtml:
They were asking different things.

A molecular formula is just the total number of each atom: 2 C, 6 H, 1 O = C₂H₆O. C₂H₅OH groups the atoms to show structure, so it is not a molecular formula.

In an equation for making ethanol, the examiner wants to see that it is ethanol. C₂H₆O does not show an –OH group. The same atoms could be arranged as a different compound, with the O between the two carbons. C₂H₅OH shows the alcohol group.

Rule: molecular formula → count atoms. Equation or structural formula → show the –OH.

questions.promptHtml: A country has plenty of sugar cane but no crude oil. Another has an oil refinery and little farmland. Which method of making ethanol suits each, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
Sugar-cane country → fermentation. Its raw material is renewable and local. The gentle conditions (30 °C, 1 atm) need little energy and cheap equipment. It accepts the downsides: slow batches and ethanol that must be distilled.

Oil-refinery country → hydration. Cracking gives ethene. Hydration is fast, continuous and gives pure ethanol. It accepts the downsides: high temperature and pressure cost energy, and crude oil is finite.

The exam version asks for one advantage and one disadvantage. Each must be a feature plus its consequence, not a bare "cheaper".

questions.promptHtml: In the ester name "ethyl ethanoate" the alcohol comes first. In the formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ the acid comes first. How do you avoid mixing them up?
questions.answerHtml:
Tie each part to its ending. -yl always comes from the alcohol, and -oate always from the acid, just as the acid's salts are ethanoates.

In the formula, find the C=O. The carbon chain on the C=O side, including that carbon, is the acid part. The chain on the far side of the single-bonded O is the alcohol part.

CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃: C=O side has 2 C → ethanoate. Other side has 3 C → propyl. Name: propyl ethanoate. Made from propanol and ethanoic acid.

questions.promptHtml: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added when making an ester, and its amount is the same at the end. What is it doing, and why does the reaction still not turn all the acid and alcohol into ester?
questions.answerHtml:
It is a catalyst. It speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the number of moles of sulfuric acid does not change.

The reaction is reversible: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water. As ester and water build up, the backward reaction speeds up until both rates are equal. That is dynamic equilibrium (module 15). A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so it gets to equilibrium sooner but does not change how much ester is there.

questions.promptHtml: Poly(ethene) forms from ethene with nothing else made. A polyester forms with water as a by-product. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Addition polymerisation (module 16): the C=C double bond opens and the monomers join end to end. Every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer, so nothing else is made.

Condensation polymerisation: each link forms when the –COOH of the acid reacts with the –OH of the diol, exactly like making an ester. That reaction gives out water, one molecule per ester link. The monomers need a functional group at both ends (a dicarboxylic acid and a diol) so the chain can keep growing.

questions.promptHtml: Ethanol, ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate are three colourless liquids. Describe tests to tell them apart, using only what is in this module.
questions.answerHtml:
Add sodium carbonate solution or magnesium to each. Only ethanoic acid fizzes, because only the carboxylic acid reacts with carbonates and metals.

Warm the other two with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Ethanol is oxidised, so the colour turns from orange to green. The ester does not change it.

Smell is a clue too: the ester has a strong fruity smell, and ethanoic acid smells of vinegar.

questions.promptHtml:
An organic compound has this percentage composition by mass: C = 54.5%, H = 9.1%, O = 36.4%. [Aᵣ: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

(a) Show that the empirical formula is C₂H₄O. (3)
(b) The relative formula mass of the compound is 88. Deduce its molecular formula. (1)
(c) The compound fizzes when sodium carbonate is added. It has an unbranched chain. Name the compound and explain how the fizzing shows it is not an ester. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 54.5 ÷ 12, 9.1 ÷ 1, 36.4 ÷ 16 1; = 4.54, 9.1, 2.275 1; divide by the smallest (2.275): 2.0 : 4.0 : 1.0, so C₂H₄O 1

(b) Mᵣ of C₂H₄O = 44; 88 ÷ 44 = 2, so C₄H₈O₂ 1

(c) Butanoic acid 1; carboxylic acids react with carbonates to give CO₂, but esters do not (ethyl ethanoate is also C₄H₈O₂, but it would not fizz) 1

Modelled on 2022 Edexcel 2C Q5(a).

questions.promptHtml:
A factory ferments 90 kg of glucose. C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ [Mᵣ: glucose = 180, ethanol = 46; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³]

(a) Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol, in kg, that can be made. (3)
(b) Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in dm³, made at the same time. (2)
(c) The factory actually obtains 36.8 kg of ethanol. Calculate the percentage yield. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) n(glucose) = 90 000 ÷ 180 = 500 mol 1; n(ethanol) = 2 × 500 = 1000 mol 1; mass = 1000 × 46 = 46 000 g = 46 kg 1

(b) n(CO₂) = 2 × 500 = 1000 mol 1; volume = 1000 × 24 = 24 000 dm³ 1

(c) 36.8 ÷ 46 × 100 = 80% 1
